On account of the Vedic revelation, there should be an entitlement based on birth. Jaimini 3.3.1.
Thus, having determined the application through indicative mark (*liṅga*), the application through syntactical connection (*vākya*) and other means is now determined.

In this context, "syntactical connection" (*vākya*) is defined as the proximity of heard words conducive to the construction of a meaning consisting of either an objective reference (*uddeśyatā*) or a causal factor (*kārakatva*) that constitutes a subordinate element.
And such [proximity] exists in the case of: "The cow is the sacrificial fee" (*dhenurdakṣiṇā*).

In such cases as "The *ṛc* is performed loudly" (*uccair ṛcā kriyate*) and "With the remnant of the *prayāja*," the term "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*) here intends to denote merely that cognition which is distinct from the presentation of word-meanings generated by their primary denotative power (*śakti*), and which pertains to relations such as objecthood (*karmatva*) or instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), regardless of whether it arises through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or other means.

Therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in cases such as "the cow is the sacrificial fee" (*dhenurdakṣiṇā*), where the instrumentality appears as a mode of relation (*saṃsarga-vidhayā*). In reality, however, because the mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*) between two inflected words is unestablished by grammatical tradition, and in accordance with the necessary postulation of their connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), the word "cow" (*dhenur*)— being in the nominative case— indicates instrumentality, while the word "fee" (*dakṣiṇā*) indicates the objecthood residing in its effect, and the word "kalpanā" [indicates the action].
Only that which is an apprehension produced by indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is intended [by the definition].
In cases such as *uccaiḥ* ("loudly"), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), because the instrumental sense—which is elided—is indicated by the nominal stem itself.

Alternatively, since it is possible for the instrumental sense to appear in cases like *uccaiḥ* precisely as a relational factor (*saṃsarga-vidhayā*), both [types of apprehension] are intended by the term "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*).
In passages such as *prayājaśeṣeṇa*, the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the objecthood by the instrumental case-ending and the instrumentality by the verbal root is quite evident.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for the proximity of the heard word to produce the cognition of objecthood and so forth without the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), the word functions as an indicator of the logical mark (*liṅga*) consisting in that competency.

This is because, by accepting that the very heard word indicates the objecthood and so forth, there is no need to postulate a further scriptural text (*śruti*) in the form of a word expressing that [objecthood].

Moreover, since that which has been heard [the word] is postulated as possessing the property of having that [intended meaning] as its purport, its status as a creator of a *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) is established.
Consequently, the sentence (*vākya*) serves as the means of valid knowledge for subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) by first postulating an indicative power (*liṅga*) and then a *śruti*.

Thus, in this case of the Jyotiṣṭoma, the loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*) and so forth, which are enjoined by the sentence "The Ṛg-verse is recited loudly," etc., [are understood] through that [sentence] which provides the objective referent (*uddeśya*).

Regarding the inquiry as to whether the words "Ṛk" and so forth indicate that only the *mantras* beginning with the Ṛgveda are the objects of reference, or whether— by virtue of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the opening section stating "the three Vedas were born"— they refer, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), to all *mantras* that constitute parts of the rituals enjoined by the Ṛgveda and the others: even though the word "Veda" occurs in the opening section, because it resides in an explanatory passage that is subordinate and intended for another purpose, [it must yield] to the words "Ṛk" and so forth which reside in the primary injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*).

Since there is no doubt [regarding the primary meaning], it is impossible for the word "Veda" to indicate the Rigveda and so forth as its parts through the logic of the conflict between the quality and the subordinate member (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*); therefore, the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) applies to the word "Veda" itself as a part of that whole.
In reality, however, there is no indication of the word "Veda" even with respect to its parts, because the property of being a Veda (*vedatva*) resides in each individual part.

Otherwise, there would be no fault incurred by a Śūdra upon hearing a single sentence [of the Veda]. This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), [the siddhāntin replies]: From the hearing of the word "Veda" at the beginning, it is understood that since the Veda is being praised here, its status as either the subject (uddeśya) or the predicate (vidheya) must necessarily be intended in the sentence. And since the predicate—such as "being recited loudly" (uccaiḥ)—is already obtained elsewhere, it follows by elimination that the Veda is understood to be the subject; thus, in reality, the words "Ṛk" and so forth are merely restatements (anuvāda) intended to designate that subject.

Therefore, since there exists a Vedic word situated at the beginning (*upakrama*) that is not contradicted by anything else and which serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the term *ṛk* and so forth must be taken as indicating, by way of secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*), the mantras that constitute parts of the rituals prescribed in the Ṛgveda and other Vedas—on the basis of their abundance therein.

Nor can there be a sublation of what is understood from the beginning by something subsequent, according to the principle of the section on "separation" (*apacchedādhikaraṇanyāya*); for in this case, because the injunction requires praise (*stuti*), it necessarily forms a single syntactical unit with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and thus the subsequent [word] does not even arise due to its dependence on the preceding [word], and consequently cannot function.
Nor is there a contradiction with the introductory statement on the grounds that the property of being a Veda (vedatva) is fully present even in the *Ṛg* and other [Vedas];
for vedatva resides only in a specific collection of texts consisting of a totality of mantras and brāhmaṇas, and thus it does not reside in individual parts.
Otherwise, the requirement of the injunction to study would be fulfilled by the study of even a single sentence.
The prohibition against a Śūdra hearing even a single word [of the Veda], however, is not untenable, just like the prohibition against eating parts of a *vṛntāka* (eggplant) and so forth.
Furthermore, how such a prohibition differs from a positive injunction (*vidhi*) in this regard should be examined in the Kaustubha.

Therefore, in accordance with the introductory context (*upakrama*), the qualities such as loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*) belong specifically to the mantras that are constituent parts of the rites prescribed in the *Ṛgveda*.

And thus, since the property of being a Veda (*vedatva*) is not pervasive enough to apply to every sentence situated within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), it is impossible for the context to restrict the sentence to its own particular domain. Consequently, one understands from the sentence that the rule regarding accents is enjoined with reference to all rites whatsoever that are prescribed by anything delimited by the property of being a Veda.
Even if there is sublation by the context, there is no harm. // 1.35 //
Thus ends the first section concerning the fact that loudness and other such qualities are properties of the Veda.

(B2) Oṃ. Since *liṅga* (indicative power) functions as an applicator by postulating a *śruti* (direct Vedic statement), it is to be examined immediately after the section on *śruti*, just as the four means beginning with *vākya* (syntactical connection) are to be examined after the section on *liṅga* because they function as applicators by postulating both *liṅga* and *śruti*. Thus, demonstrating this "immediate sequence" (*anantara-saṅgati*) in the form of an "occasion" (*avasara*), [the author] proceeds to the consideration of the application useful for that which is to be understood through the means of knowledge that postulate *liṅga*.
He asserts that it is the meaning of the word "pāda" with the words "evam" (thus).

By the phrase "vākya, etc.," the author indicates that since the four means of application— sentence (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*)— are being determined as the factors of application within this very chapter (*pāda*), they constitute the purpose of the chapter. Consequently, the commentators [hold] that because *vākya* involves a great deal of material to be investigated,
it serves as the purpose of the chapter, whereas *prakaraṇa* and the others do not, due to the absence of such abundance.
The argument that— because each of those [four means of knowledge] is to be considered individually and thus lacks a multiplicity of subjects for inquiry,

whereas the consideration of their relative strength (*balābala*) is common to all— it was stated that [the *balābala* section] should come first— that has been refuted; for, in this investigation of the four means of knowledge, since the first sentence must necessarily be examined as it is the basis (*upajīvya*) for the subsequent ones, the result follows incidentally from that initial inquiry.

The meaning is that, since there is no evidence to establish that a multiplicity of deliberations (*vicāra*) is the cause [of a particular application], it is impossible to exclude the possibility that all [deliberations] are the cause for the application of a verse.
Among the four means of proof mentioned therein, the application established by syntactical connection (*vākya*) is examined first, because it is that which must be relied upon (*upajīvya*).

In the *Bhāṭṭabhāskara*, although the definition of a sentence (*vākya*) is formulated as either "syntactic unity of words" (*padaikavākyatā*) or "syntactic unity of sentences" (*vākyaikavākyatā*), this definition suffers from the defect of under-extension (*avyāpti*). This is because, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the rule] "loudly for the *ṛc*" and so forth pertains to the properties of the *ṛc* and other mantras, it is accepted that this very sentence serves as the authoritative means of application (*viniyojaka*); thus, the definition does not extend to that case. Furthermore, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), although the syntactic unity of words functions to provide the specific qualifier for the subject (*uddeśya*), it is accepted that the application is established by the authority of the sentence "loudly," etc., and thus the definition remains under-extended.
Intending to state that this is correct, he himself provides the definition of a sentence: "In that regard, what is called a sentence... and so forth.
"The proximity of the heard word."
The meaning is: the utterance of two heard words in a specific proximity conducive to the cognition of a single syntactic connection.
The phrase "conducive to conceptualization" is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of [direct] hearing.
The two terms "proximity to the heard word" are employed in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of a *liṅga* (inferential mark).
"This exists."

The meaning is that there is a definition [of implication] consisting in the proximity of such words, which possesses a suitability for the postulation of the sprinkling of ghee upon the elevated cow and the status of being an action residing in the Ṛg-verses remaining from the sacrificial fee and the fore-sacrifices;
this occurs by way of the relation of connection (saṃsarga-vidhayā).

When the word *dhenu* (cow), whose meaning is co-occurrent with the word *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee)—which denotes a substance that effects the *ānati* (propitiation)—is construed through identity, as in the case of "the blue pot," then the cow is understood by way of the relation of identity with the substance that effects the *ānati*. Similarly, in the case of "loudly" (*uccaiḥ*) as well, when the *ṛc* (verse) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the meaning of the co-occurrent word "loudly" is construed through identity; and by virtue of this relation of identity, the status of being an instrument is perceived as belonging to the loudness itself. Thus, [the loudness] possesses an instrumentality that appears by way of the relation of identity (*saṃsarga*).
The meaning is that there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

Since it will be stated later that the postulation of a Vedic text (*śruti*) is impossible in a case where the instrumentality appears as a mode of relation (*saṃsarga-vidhayā*), weakness (*daurbalya*) relative to the *śruti* would not result; therefore, he states another position: "In reality, however..."—namely, that it is simply the presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Although, in cases such as "A three-year-old castrated animal is the means for purchasing Soma," it cannot be maintained that there is no cognition produced by secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) because the status of being a means for the purchase of Soma is understood through the suffix *lyuṭ* itself in that syntactical application (*vākyīyaviniyoga*);

nevertheless, since the suffix *lyuṭ* denotes a substance that is the locus of instrumentality (*sādhanatā*), it does not denote the specific causal factor (*kāraka*) consisting of the abstracted power (*śakti*) which constitutes the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*).
The point is that there is no fault, because it is necessary to indicate the meaning of such case endings as "one should effect the purchase of Soma with a castrated animal."

Since the nature and definition of the three—context (*prakaraṇa*) and the others—will be stated hereafter, he sets them aside and demonstrates that it is *vākya* alone that brings about the inference of *liṅga* and *śruti*: "without the knowledge of compatibility" means without the cognition of compatibility in the form of "the word-meanings possess the fitness for mutual connection," provided that the words have been heard;
"having that as its purport" [is the meaning].

The meaning is that words such as *dhenu* (cow) are recited in the form of words—such as "one should accomplish the purpose of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) by means of a cow"—and thus they possess the character of a scriptural text (*śruti*). Having thus postulated both the indicative power (*liṅga*) and the scriptural text (*śruti*), [the author] indicates by the phrase "therefore" (*ataśca*) that the capacity of syntactical connection (*vākya*) to enjoin application is established by the very section concerning other sentences (*vākyāntarādhikaraṇa*), since it is no different in its role as an enjoiner of application in both the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Consequently, [he mentions] the delimiting property of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) which is useful for the application understood through that [syntactical connection].
He provides an example to indicate that this determination of the section (adhikaraṇa) of the chapter is for the purpose of definition, saying: "In that case... (tadiha).
By means of such [passages] as these.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the two [rules] "the *yajus* is whispered" (*upāṃśu yajuṣā*) and "the *sāman* is loud" (*uccaiḥ sāmnā*) are included.
Likewise: "Prajāpati created these three Vedas; once they were created, they oppressed him; he squeezed them out from them..."

"Earth, Atmosphere, Heaven"—from these syllables [the Vedic meters] flowed forth: from "Earth" the Ṛg-verses flowed forth, and that became this world; from "Atmosphere" the Yajus-formulas flowed forth, and that became the intermediate world; from "Heaven" the Sāman-chants flowed forth, and that became the heavenly world. Therefore, if an offering should be made in excess or improperly, one should go toward the Gārhapatya fire and offer with "Bhūḥ Svāhā! For the Gārhapatya is indeed this world. This...
The world is the *Ṛgveda*; it indeed satisfies this world and the *Ṛgveda* with its own essence.
Now, if a deficiency should occur in respect of the *Yajus*, one should go to the *Anvāhāryapacana* fire and offer an oblation with the words, "Bhuvaḥ Svāhā!

The *Anvāhāryapacana* fire is the intermediate region (*antarikṣaloka*), and the intermediate region is the *Yajurveda*. It indeed satisfies both the intermediate region and the *Yajurveda* with its own essence.
"He satisfies it with its own essence; now, if it should become excessive on account of the Sāman, one should go to the Āhavanīya fire and offer an oblation with 'Svaḥ svāhā!

For the Āhavanīya is indeed the heavenly world, and the Sāmaveda is the heavenly world; therefore, he satisfies both the heavenly world and the Sāmaveda with their own essence. This should also be understood as applying to the section on expiations found in the fifth section of the first chapter of the *Tāṇḍaka-Brāhmaṇa*.

By the phrase "denoting the subject-matter" (*uddeśyasamarpaka*), it is stated that both in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is only words such as "deer" (*mṛga*) that denote the subject-matter, and not the word "Veda" in the case of the conclusion; thus, the meaning is that the inquiry concerns only the specific sense of that [subject-matter].
It is being established.

And therefore, since that which is performed with a *ṛk* mantra is done "aloud" (*uccaiḥ*), the conclusion is that even those *ṛks* originating from the Yajurveda must be recited aloud and not in a whisper (*upāṃśu*). This is the meaning [of the passage]. [The phrase] "by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) situated at the beginning" [is used].
“Prajāpati alone was this [universe] in the beginning; he performed austerity. From him, performing austerity, three gods were created: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya. They performed austerity.

From them, performing austerity, the three Vedas were created: from Agni the Ṛgveda, from Vāyu the Yajurveda, and from Āditya the Sāmaveda. This is the explanatory passage (arthavāda) found at the beginning of the text as recorded in the Bhāṣya.

In that regard, in the ninth section (anuvāka) of the third chapter of the second book [of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka], it says: "In the beginning, indeed, nothing whatsoever existed here. Regarding the meaning of the word *tepāna* occurring there in the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*, the Vedic commentary (*Vedabhāṣya*) has shown that it means "he performed austerity" (*tapas taptavān*), thus [the word] *tepānaḥ* [is derived from] *tasmāt*.

Similarly, here too, one should establish the word *tepāna* by applying the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) to the root *tap* in the sense of "he performed austerity," and then, after performing the substitution of *e* for the *śānac* suffix, the meaning of that word should be understood.
"Of the mantra alone."

Furthermore, since the word *ṛk* refers to the Veda, when it is ordained that "that ritual which is performed with the Ṛgveda is to be done loudly," loudness cannot directly apply to the ritual itself; rather, it applies by way of the mantras that constitute parts of the rituals prescribed by that Veda. Consequently, the meaning is that only those mantras that are constituent parts of rituals prescribed by that [specific] Veda must be recited loudly. Therefore, there is no requirement for loudness in the case of the *ṛks* being recited by the Adhvaryu priest as constituent parts of rituals belonging to the Yajurveda.
Furthermore, the intended meaning is that the conclusion is simply that [the mantra] must be recited in a whisper (*upāṃśu*). The word *mātra* is used for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

In that context, since there exists a proximate expression denoting the subject (*uddeśya*) which is not subordinate to anything else, it is not possible to claim that the word "Veda" occurring in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is intended to denote that subject, namely the enjoined mental realization (*bhāvanā*) of loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*).

Now, even if it is impossible for that [word] to denote [the object], one might argue that because it is accepted as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the word "Ṛk" and so forth itself refers to that [object] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Even so, since it is possible for the literal meaning alone to constitute the objective factor (*uddeśya*) of the unity of the Ṛk and so forth, the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) cannot be the basis [for such an interpretation].

Furthermore, although the words "Ṛk" and so forth and the word "Veda" have mutually contradictory meanings, the impossibility of their co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "Veda" found in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) may serve as the basis [for the argument].

Nevertheless, intending that it is more appropriate for that [intention] to reside in the words of the Veda itself, he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words: "Of the introduction" (upakramasya).
"Without doubt."

Since it has been established in the second [pāda] that the terms "ṛcs," "sāmans," and "yajus" refer exclusively to mantras because they are so used in the Veda, the fact that there is no doubt [regarding their meaning] indicates that they do not fall within the scope of the *aktādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the word "anointed").

By this, the following objection is refuted: "In expressions such as ‘Ṛgveda’ or ‘Ṛk-branch,’ since the words ‘ṛk’ and so on are also used for the Veda, the application [of the term] is possible through the relationship of general and particular; therefore, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) does not arise.
The meaning is that once it is certain that these terms refer only to mantras, such usages are easily explained as being based on metaphorical extension (*bhūman*).

Now, one might object: since in the section of the twelfth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] stating "Or rather, the primary [is followed], because of the prior injunction, as in common worldly practice," it will be taught that when there is a conflict between the properties of the primary and the secondary, the property of the primary is to be favored; therefore, by that same principle, since the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is primary in the present case, it alone should be followed. How then can this be the prima facie view? To this, he says: "Because of the quality of the subordinate... (*aṅgaguṇa*).

Just as, by the sentence "He who desires [such-and-such]," when there is a conflict between the time of the full-moon and new-moon sacrifices (*parvakāla*) prescribed for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other offerings and the principal Soma sacrifice on the one hand, and the alternative of having one or more days of initiation (*ekādidīkṣā*) on the other, it will be stated— by way of an exception to the principle of the preceding section, namely "In case of a conflict between a subordinate and a quality, [the quality is set aside] because of its being for that purpose"— that the time of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other subsidiaries must be sublated in favor of the time of the principal Soma sacrifice, since they are merely its subsidiaries.
Similarly here as well, even though [the word] is primary, it is logical that it should favor the words contained within the principal injunction; such is the meaning.

In reality, however, because "Vedic-ness" (*vedatva*) is a pervading property (*paryāpta*), even though the related object is delimited by a subordinate property (*vyāpyadharma*), it is still related to that which possesses the pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*); thus, the praise is logically established, and there is no need for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For "Vedic-ness" is not pervasively present (*paryāpta*) in the entire text consisting of both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa.

If that were the case, then for a Śūdra who studies two or three sentences [of the Veda], the fault resulting from the prohibition against Vedic study would not arise. Or, let it be granted that such a fault does arise;

nevertheless, since even a constituent part of the enjoined object is connected to the whole through a traditional lineage, a praise by means of the word "Veda" is appropriate here—just as the praise of reeds and *avakā* grasses [is understood] through a praise of water. Thus, there is no [contradiction].
There is a contradiction;
intending to show that because of this impossibility, metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) is necessary for words such as "Ṛg-veda" and so forth, he says: "But in reality... (vastutastu).

And therefore, the injunction regarding loudness and so forth is for the purpose of the action to be accomplished by the *ṛk* mantra; the meaning is that there is no evidence for [applying it to] figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, even though the word "Veda" occurs within an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because it is the first thing to present itself, its own primary meaning serves as the object of the praise.

Since praise is impossible for that which is not subject to injunction, [the word "Veda"]—even though it appears as something to be enjoined—does not imply other enjoined properties such as high pitch (uccaiṣṭva) because those already exist;
rather, by process of elimination, it makes known its role as a constituent of the objective (uddeśyatā).
And thus, since the fact that the referent of the word "Veda" is a constituent of the objective is determined to be free from contradiction, subsequently, with reference to that very objective...

Because it occurs subsequent to the determination of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), the word "sight" (*dṛk*) and others are not capable of conveying that their own referent constitutes a factor in the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatā*);

thus, due to its subordinate nature, its contradiction having already arisen, and its character as a restatement (*anuvāda*), it undergoes figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just like the word "adhvaryu" in the sentence "He who is the *hotṛ*, he is the *adhvaryu*.

For this very reason, when the injunction requires an object of reference and the object of reference in the form of the Veda—indicated by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—is obtained as the first thing to present itself...
Furthermore, since that which is connected as the object of praise cannot be connected as a constituent of the subject (*uddeśya*), there arises a need for another word to present it;

and in this regard, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the words *ṛk* and so forth—presented through syntactic proximity (*samabhivyāhāra*)—acting as its presenters by means of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

Therefore, because the sequence of requirement establishes that the words *ṛk* and so forth do not convey the status of being a constituent of the subject as presented by other means of knowledge, it is understood—by virtue of conforming to the word "Veda" occurring in the opening statement—that there is indeed a sublation (*bādha*) characterized by non-arising with respect to that [subject].
For this very reason, this [conflict] is treated as one where the sublation is not yet established (*aprāptabādha*).

For this very reason, although the injunction (*vidhi*), being the primary element, possesses the status of being the objective referent (*uddeśyatā*) for the meanings of the Vedic words, there is no contradiction; and since words such as *viruddha* (contrary) are included within the injunction itself, the principle of the "subordinate quality" (*aṅgaguṇanyāya*) does not apply.

For this very reason, that [principle of *aprāptabādha*] applies only in cases such as the Soma sacrifice, where both the primacy [of the Soma] and the subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are established by other means of knowledge (*māna*), and thus there is no need to consider the relative strength or weakness of the preceding or succeeding words.
As for the argument that— in the sentence "ya iṣṭyā" (he who [performs] an *iṣṭi*)— the word *iṣṭi* occurs at the beginning (*upakrama*) while the word *soma* occurs at the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*),

and that therefore the latter cannot possibly intend another action without contradicting the former, and since the latter intends its own literal meaning which is primary, the principle of the conflict between a subordinate and a quality (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*) indeed subverts the principle of the opening statement (*upakramanyāya*) in this case.

Since that logic does not apply here, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "In the introduction" (*upakrame*), intending that the term *ṛk* and so forth is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in the Veda because it consists predominantly of those [mantras].
Regarding the word "sentence" (vākya):
The word "foremost" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
[Regarding the phrase] "the definition of mantra":

Although it might be argued that since the mantra can be brought to mind through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the Veda alone—by means of the maxim of "uselessness [of the whole] when its parts [are already known]" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*)—there is no need for the indication of the end of that [Veda];

nevertheless, the statement regarding the indication of the end of that [Veda] is made with the intention of asking: "Even if indication is necessary, why should the delay in its presentation, caused by logical reasoning (*nyāya*), be tolerated?
And in this case, where there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), the maxim of the beginning (*upakramanyāya*) possesses greater force.

However, in cases such as "He who [performs] the *iṣṭi*," where the acceptance of three distinct sentences occurs through the individual application (*anuṣaṅga*) of the governing words (*tantrapada*) from "he should sacrifice" and "on the new moon day," there is a state of separate sentential unity (*bhinnavākyatva*). [this refers to] "immediately preceding."
The meaning is that at the time of application (prayoga), since origination (utpatti) is separated [from it], the application (viniyoga) occurs immediately prior [to it].

[Objection: In that case, by the same logic, would it not follow that even for the subsidiary elements of the Darśapūrṇamāsa—such as the stotras and śastras belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma—the quality of *upāṃśutva* (low-voiced recitation), which is based on the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*), would necessarily apply? To this, he says: "provided there is no subverting factor" (*asati bādhake*).

The meaning is as follows: In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, although the *prayogavidhi* (injunction of performance) would result in all parts being recited in a low tone (*upāṃśu*) according to their respective rules of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*), the specific rule "the *yājyābhāgas* are in a low tone, while the subsequent *anuyājas* and so forth are in a medium and high tone" prescribes the accentuation of the *bhāga* elements by way of overriding what was previously obtained. Thus, the low tone (*mandra*) and other accents apply there; furthermore, in some instances, due to specific statements, the high tone (*uccais*) and so forth are applied.

Thus, even for those modifications (*vikṛti*) that are not performed out of desire (*akāmyā*), since their assistance is already established in respect to the principal part, the archetypal auxiliary parts, and the auxiliary parts that have taken over the function of those [archetypal ones], the accent remains archetypal, just as in the case of a different performer in the *Śyena* sacrifice.
Even in respect to the non-archetypal auxiliary parts, it is indeed archetypal;

for since the accent in the archetype is a property of the constituent parts (*bhāgadharma*), even if it resides in non-archetypal procedures that initiate those parts, it does not result in performing a non-archetypal function.

Regarding the optional modified sacrifices (*kāmyavikṛti*), although the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is prescribed by the statement, "The optional sacrifices belonging to the *Atharva-veda* are indeed to be performed in a whisper," this whispered quality applies only to the principal act (*pradhāna*)— just as in the case of the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*)— because there is an absence of the third [and subsequent] case endings and thus no injunction for the ritual with its subsidiaries (*sāṅgavidhi*). Consequently, in the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), the original (*prākṛta*) mode remains.
In this case as well, sublation by specific statements should be observed here and there.

Thus, even in the Jyotiṣṭoma, when various Vedic accents would apply according to their respective rules of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*), there is sublation by the archetypal accent (*prākṛta-svara*) regarding those subsidiaries that have the Darśapūrṇamāsa as their archetype, according to the logic of the Śyena sacrifice. Furthermore, in that context, the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) enjoined by the rule, "Whatever is prior to the Agnīṣomīya [offering], with that they proceed in a low voice,"—being an auxiliary of the elements occurring before the Agnīṣomīya—is like the various Vedic accents; it sublates even the archetypal accent.
It sublates the [general] pitch.

Furthermore, the specific pitches prescribed by particular injunctions—such as, "One should recite at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* with whatever degree of voice one desires; [with a] low [pitch] at the *prāyaṇīyā*; [with a] lower [pitch] at the *ātithyā*"—being without scope for application elsewhere, sublate [the general rule] only with respect to the primary portions of those respective *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites.

Therefore, since the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is already established for the *upasads* by virtue of their occurring prior to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, one should not even suspect the redundancy of the separate injunction, "The *upasads* are whispered.

This is because it is appropriate to accept that the term *upasat* functions merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all ritual acts other than those with no other scope, serving simply as a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of praising the accentuation of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites.
For this very reason, there is no subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*) of the *agnīṣomīya* sentence by this [injunction].

In the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and others which have the Darśapūrṇamāsa as their archetype, there is indeed the archetypal threefold accentuation (*traisvarya*). However, in those sacrifices that do not have that as their archetype, there is the accentuation of various Vedas (*nānāvedasvara*), according to the injunctions governing the application (*viniyoga*) of each respective rite.

But at the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing), by virtue of the injunctions such as "they proceed with a low tone (*mandra*) during the morning pressing," which apply equally to both the subsidiaries and the principal rites, [the low tone prevails].

In the sequence of the *savanas*, there is a sublation of the natural accent at the beginning of the *savanīya* offerings by means of the low (*mandra*), middle (*madhyama*), and high (*uttama*) tones; likewise, there is a sublation of the various Vedic accents at the beginning of the *stotras*.

Nor should it be suspected that, because the words *prātaḥsavana* and so forth here denote merely the respective repetitions (*abhyāsa*) of the Soma sacrifices, they would subvert the accents already established for their constituent parts (*aṅga*); for, due to the co-occurrence with the verb *caranti*, which expresses performance, it is understood that the word *prātaḥsavana* also indicates a part of the performance composed of its own denotatum—thus differing from terms such as *prāyaṇīya*. Consequently, in those rites performed after the *sutyā* which have the Darśapūrṇamāsa as their archetype (*prakṛti*), the original (*prākṛta*) [accents apply].
But in the case of *apūrva* rites, there is the accentuation of various Vedas;
this should likewise be understood to apply to the modifications (*vikāra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
And thus, wherever there exists such a specific injunction of accents and so forth that serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*), [the general rule is set aside].

In that regard, even where there is a sublation of the accent by a specific injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*), wherever such a sublating factor is absent, there the accent belonging to the various Vedas is indeed employed as prompted by the injunction of application.
For example, in the case of *darvī* oblations, the low-voiced (*upāṃśu*) quality prescribed in the Yajurveda applies;
this is because no other sublating factor is present.

Likewise, because injunctions such as "the *prātaḥsavana* [should be] in a low tone" (*mandram*) are eternal, they have no connection with non-eternal optional (*kāmya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rites; thus, since they apply only to eternal matters and do not operate in non-eternal ones, there is no sublation [of their force]. Therefore, whatever optional or occasional rite is performed by means of the *Ṛgveda* or *Sāmaveda*, in that case the Vedic loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*) alone applies. In the present instance, however, the low tone (*upāṃśutva*) applies to the *ādhāna-sāmans*, as it is necessitated by the injunction governing their specific application. This is the general direction.

In this context, the application of the ear by one standing at a distance constitutes loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*). The application of the mind to soundless effort constitutes softness (*upāṃśutva*). That tone in which the application of sound is perceived in the chest region is the *mandra* (low) tone. That tone in which the application of sound is perceived in the throat region is the *madhyama* (middle) tone, because it occupies the intermediate position between the *krauñca* and *kruṣṭa* tones.
The *krauñca* is to be understood as that which is suitable for hearing from a distance; the *kruṣṭa* is to be known as that which is suitable for hearing when nearby;
and it is where the application of sound is perceived at the location of the head.

Its characteristics, such as being the "supreme tone" (*uttama-svara*)—which is another synonym for the *tārakruṣṭa*—and so forth, should be understood from the *Taittirīya-Prātiśākhya* and other ritual treatises (*yājñika-grantha*).
Thus ends the second section concerning the low-voiced nature of the chanting during the Ādhāna.
— — — — — — — (B1) (Section 3 / [A.3 Pāda 3 Adhikaraṇa 3]) "By virtue of abundance, there is the scriptural mention of both.
(Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.10) Where a single ritual action is mentioned in relation to many [texts], [it is that which is intended].
In this regard, when there arises the inquiry as to where the origin [of the rite] occurs and where its mention is heard for the purpose of enjoining a subordinate quality (*guṇa*),
the answer is that the origin occurs where there is a plurality of subsidiaries (*aṅga*); just as the location of a king is determined by the number of his attendants.

In reality, however, it is the completeness of the constituent factors— such as the substance and the deity— which characterize the essential nature of the ritual act that serves as the decisive factor.
Even within that, although both are external factors, it is the deity alone that is non-deviant [with respect to the rite].
But it is not so for the substance; this and other points should be inferred accordingly.
Therefore, when such a definitive [injunction] exists, the production occurs right there;
elsewhere, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that [substance] with the addition of another non-contradictory quality.
But where there is a contradiction, there is indeed a difference based on the quality [of the action].
Likewise, where there is an absence of any restrictive factor whatsoever, there too the difference arises from repetition.
For in this case, according to the principle of other recensions (*śākhāntara*), even if all [texts] have the purpose of origination, there is no unity of the ritual act.

Likewise here, because there is no difference among the students, it is established by the force of this restrictive rule that the accent is based solely on the Veda in which the [mantra] originates. // 3.37 //
Thus ends the third section concerning the Yajurvedic nature of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

(B2) Since there is an inquiry as to whether the two accents prescribed by the sentences beginning with "uccair ṛcā" are to be employed optionally in a single ritual act, or whether only one accent is to be used as a rule, the connection to the chapter, the section, and the context is established; likewise, the incidental connection and the immediate sequence of topics need not be stated here as they are clear. Furthermore, because the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is already restricted by the accents prescribed for its respective libations (*savana*s), [the question arises].

Since there is no room for the prima facie view based on conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pūrvapakṣa*) nor for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) based on the natural state of the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*), [the author], disregarding the example of the Jyotiṣṭoma cited in the Bhāṣya and other texts, intends instead to refer to rituals such as the Agnihotra; thus, without specifying a particular subject, he explains the general nature of the principle: "In a case where there is only one... and so forth.

Although it might be argued that since only the high pitch (*uccaiṣṭva*) of the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* is prescribed, the determination of which one of them is the object of the injunction (*vidheya*) regarding the ritual action is not useful for the specific accentuation— and with this in mind, the phrase "in both scriptural texts" (*ubhayaśrutī*) was used in the Sūtra, making the expression "among many" (*anekesu*) inappropriate— nevertheless, it should be understood as being included merely for the sake of comprehensive inclusion.

Although the non-restricted and the restricted have been shown in some places to be objects of investigation, since it is the purpose of the investigation that constitutes their objectivity, [the author] demonstrates that only the cause of that [investigation] is its object, in order to indicate the absence of objectivity for those two themselves; thus he says: "In that regard... (tatra).

Considering the weakness of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) first, according to the method of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*): "Where [there is] the auxiliary... and so forth.

Intending to show that the restrictive principle stated by the author of the Bhāṣya— that the smallness or largeness of the probans (the smoke, etc. is not the determining factor because one observes the inference of fire even from a small amount of smoke— is incorrect, he states the restrictive principle as set forth in the Vārttika,
beginning with "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*).
The meaning is that only the substance, deity, and so forth possess the quality of being determinative because they are never found apart from [the rite].
Regarding the phrase "in two ways":
The meaning is that there is a twofold division: in one Veda there is the mention of the substance (*dravya*), while in the other there is the mention of the deity (*devatā*).
With the intention of showing that the substance is more internal according to the principle of the eighth [chapter], it was stated "even though the deity is external.
The word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "of the deity alone" is to be connected with the subsequent statement regarding its determinative power.
"There is an absence of a controller."
The meaning is that there is the existence of a repeated hearing of an injunction not intended for anything else.
Thus, even in cases where only the ritual action is heard in its own sentence,
while in another sentence there is an injunction regarding a deity, [the same principle applies].

In another case, where there is no injunction of that [original element] but rather the hearing of another contradictory quality, since the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are heard in both instances, if both were injunctions, then in one case—where it is co-occurrent with an injunction regarding a deity and so forth—it would be an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*); whereas in the other, since it lacks the purport of origination, its purpose would be to revitalize the context (*prakaraṇa*) for the application (*viniyoga*) of qualities introduced by another sentence. This detailed discussion should be seen in the *Kaustubha*.
It is based solely on that cognition.
Where there is an audition of a substance, a deity, and so forth, it is precisely there that [the mantra] is enjoined as something to be performed;
therefore, the meaning is that the accent is based solely on that knowledge.
The purpose [of this rule] is not stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the third section concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice being prescribed by the Yajurveda.
— — — — — — (B1) (4th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.3 Pā.3 Adhi.4) "That which is not connected [by direct statement] belongs to the context, because of its requirement for a procedure" (Jaimini 3.3.11).
Thus, having determined the nature of syntactical connection (*vākya*), the nature of context (*prakaraṇa*) is now being determined.
Now, what indeed is this so-called "context" (prakaraṇa)? It is certainly not mere proximity;
for if it were, even the *godohana* vessel and the like would incur the status of being subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*).
Nor is it merely the state of having an expectancy; for that would result in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) also having such an expectancy regarding the archetypal subsidiaries (*prākṛtāṅga*).
Nor is it being recited in proximity while possessing expectancy; [for this definition is too narrow].
Otherwise, that [status] would result even for subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) and the like.
If, on the other hand, it is defined as being qualified by mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣatva*),
then that would also result for mantras and the like which are established in their own forms.
Furthermore, since the *prayāja* offerings and so forth have no expectancy [for a purpose], they would not apply [to the sacrifice].

If you argue that although the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) have their own purposes through other means, an expectancy for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is nonetheless established, and thus "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is appropriate—
then what exactly is this so-called "state of being a procedure"?
It cannot be a cooperative factor with respect to either the fruit or the unseen potency (*apūrva*),
because that would result in [the sacrifice] being primary;
furthermore, it would lead to the consequence that the *Āgneya* sacrifice, like the *prayāja* offerings, would be extended by injunction (*atideśa*) into the modified ritual (*vikṛti*).
Nor can it be the status of being a producer of an instrument, because that would be contradicted in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.

If this is argued, we say no; for the meaning of "context" (*prakaraṇa*) consists precisely in the requirement, as a procedure (*itikartavyatā*), of something proximate, fruitful, and whose subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) has not yet been understood, with respect to a particular ritual act.

The first qualification is for the purpose of excluding items such as the *prayāja* offerings from being subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices when they are not present [in the context];
the second, "that which possesses a fruit" (*phalavataḥ*), is for the purpose of excluding items such as the *anuyāja* offerings;

and the third is for the purpose of excluding items such as the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)—which are already assigned by the triad of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth—from being the subject matter of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

The fourth [point] is that mantras and the like, which have an established form but are not specifically enjoined by a *liṅga* (indicative mark), must be included within the context (*prakaraṇa*) for the sake of establishing their status as *itikartavyatā* (procedural requirements).
And being *itikartavyatā* consists in being an auxiliary to the *karaṇa* (the instrument of action).
For it is beyond dispute that since that which lacks power cannot function as a cause, power necessarily resides in every cause.
Furthermore, whether that delimiting factor of causality is itself of the nature of a cause is another matter.
The general rule is that if it subsists in produced things, it is simply a product;
the exception is that when the causal complex is not obtained, it is ultimately beginningless.

In that context, the requirement for the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is precisely the requirement for that causal complex (*sāmagrī*). And by means of that [requirement], there arises the cognition of the status of subsidiary (*aṅga*) for the *prayāja* and other such elements that are present,
because the *prayāja* and so forth constitute that causal complex.

Furthermore, since an accomplished entity such as a substance cannot constitute a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) without the infusion of an operation (*vyāpārāveśa*), it is not apprehended by that [complex]. In this context, the requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) residing in the principal [action], when conjoined with the requirement for a purpose (*prayojanākāṅkṣā*) residing in the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, brings about the construction of a syntactical unit (*vākya*)— known as "proximity" (*sannidhi*)— consisting of the conventional words which are parts of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), even though each individual sentence has already reached completion in its own respective subordinate sentence-meaning (*avāntaravākyārtha*).

And through the presentation of their own respective meanings by means of the etymologically explained words (*nirukta-pada*), as well as by the postulation of unmentioned other words (*aśruta-padāntara*) based on the inference (*liṅga*) consisting in a fitness conducive to that [postulation], and further by the postulation of a scriptural statement (*śruti*) in the form of unmentioned words expressing the nature of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)— such as "He performs the *samit* sacrifice" and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices"— there is authoritative validity regarding the status of being a factor in the performance (*kṛti-kārakatva*) in the form of the procedure.
For it is indeed possible that even the *prayāja* offerings and the like are connected with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) by virtue of generating the aforementioned capacity.
Therefore, it is established that "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is the fourth means of proof (*pramāṇa*).

As for what was stated here by Pārthasārathi—that this is not "context" because we observe that actions and the like, even when unsupported, initiate conjunction and disjunction—[that objection is refuted].

However, it might be argued that, having accepted that the general sense of activity (*vyāpāra*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the requirement for the *itikartavyatā* (the "how-to") is simply a requirement for its specific details; and by means of that very [requirement], the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are connected as such [details], and that alone constitutes *prakaraṇa*. That is not correct; for if that were the case, it would be impossible for the aforementioned *prakaraṇa* to convey subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) that is not constituted by those [specific details].
Furthermore, if the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries were themselves the *bhāvanā*, it would follow that they alone must be connected to the result;

however, in our view, since effort (*yatna*) alone is the *bhāvanā*, and its purpose is fulfilled simply by being the generator of the sacrifice, such a consequence does not arise—this constitutes the difference.

Moreover, if this were the case, then even though the primary act is inherently devoid of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), it would follow that in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries would become constituent parts (*aṅga*) of it solely through the mutual expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*).

Furthermore, when the bhāvanā in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) requires specific details, its expectancy is satisfied by the proximate upahomas themselves—even though their assistance has not been previously established—so that there is no occasion for the assumption of an extended application (atideśa); such is the detailed explanation in the Kaustubha.
Thus ends the fourth section concerning the application of context (prakaraṇa).
(B2) He demonstrates the connection (*saṅgati*) of the present discussion concerning the application (*viniyoga*) of what is to be performed by the words "Thus" (*evam*).

In the sūtra *śeṣaḥ parārthatvāt* ("The subordinate is that which exists for the sake of another"), since it is impossible to define subservience (*pārārthya*) without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the six means of valid cognition— direct assertion (*śruti*) and so forth— are introduced. Among these, because the application of direct assertion (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*) was explained in the section on "That Which Is Already Present" (*tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*), and the application of indicative power (*liṅga*) was explained in the section on "Capability" (*sāmarthyādhikaraṇa*), the first two quarters [of the second book] have merely defined the delimiters of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal.

In this section, however, having already determined the application based on syntactical connection (*vākya*), the definition, characteristics, and manner of application of *prakaraṇa* (context) are now being established, as the opportunity for such a discussion has arisen. The meaning is that although there is no immediate logical connection due to the subject matter belonging to a different section (*prakaraṇāntara*), there is no harm [in proceeding with this].

Now, one might object: "Since the very nature of the context (*prakaraṇa*) is unestablished, how can it be proposed as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for being an auxiliary (*aṅga*), such that its investigation would constitute the subject matter promised? With this in mind, he raises the doubt with the word "nanu" (now, surely).
"By way of being undesired."
The phrase "in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
[This applies] even to the offering to Agni.

The meaning is as follows: since the *paramāpūrva* (the ultimate transcendental result) is not produced from the Āgneya [sacrifice] alone—being independent of the Agniṣomīya—the latter also becomes a constituent of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) in that context due to its cooperation with the Agniṣomīya; consequently, just as in the case of the Prayāja offerings and others, there would be the consequence of an extended application (*atideśa*).
This is what is meant by "because of sublation" (*bādhāt*).
The meaning is that, because the substance and the deity are the generators [of the sacrifice], that [efficacy] is sublated in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and others.
In order to exclude [the objection] that this is a subject matter for a specific topical discussion (*prakaraṇa*).

Since the status of threshing and other such acts as being subsidiary to rice and other materials is understood through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means alone, there is no need for a "context" (*prakaraṇa*) in the form of proximity (*sannidhi*), which is termed "qualification" (*adhikāra*); or rather, according to the method stated in the *Bhaṭṭālaṅkāra*, because proximity (*sannidhi*) constitutes "position" (*sthāna*), it cannot logically function as "context. Therefore, when multiple sentences—each possessing an intermediate intention regarding various meanings—possess a single "context" termed "qualification" in the form of a great intention directed toward one specific point, this context serves to grasp the intention that consists in the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the delimiting factor of subsidiarity (*aṅgitāvacchedaka*) within a word such as "rice."

The meaning is: "In order to exclude that [the status of being a subsidiary], because it lacks the character of being a subject matter of a context (*prakaraṇa*) consisting in the expectation of what is to be done for the sake of joy (*pīti*)."

And it is not the case that— despite the fact that being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) which serves as a means to the *apūrva* is understood through direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth— the status of being an auxiliary to the sacrifice, or the status of being an auxiliary to the *apūrva*, is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) consisting of the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*)—

because the status of being an auxiliary to the *apūrva* is established by implication (*arthasiddha*), since it is logically untenable without being an auxiliary to the *apūrva*, and thus does not depend on the operation of the context.

Therefore, the sense is that even when there is an omission of acts such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), the expiation for a lapse in a subsidiary element of the sacrifice (kratvaṅga) is not difficult to obtain, just as in the case where subsidiariness is understood through the context (prakaraṇa).

In this context, it should be understood that since context (*prakaraṇa*) and the other [means of proof]—by the method to be explained—indicate subsidiarity only through the postulation of preceding means of proof, they function more slowly;
consequently, they cannot indicate subsidiarity regarding the domain of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth. Thus, it is established by itself that these do not apply to the domain of context;
therefore, the phrase "regarding a subsidiary whose status is not yet known" has been included for the sake of clarity.
"Not enjoined by a mark."

In the section concerning mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*), it was stated by the Teacher that mantras whose purpose is to illuminate meaning are to be accepted as part of the context by means of the act of illuminating meaning— according to the principle that they do not connect with intermediate actions; therefore, the phrase "not assigned by *liṅga*" is used to demonstrate their distinction from that [category].

Therefore, since an indicative mark (liṅga) depends upon a means of knowledge that establishes a general connection, context (prakaraṇa) is also presented in the section on indicative marks (liṅgapāda) as a means of establishing a general connection, just like order (krama) and name (samākhyā).

And this statement— that threshing (*avaghāta*) and other such *sannipātin* acts, which are enjoined by the triad of direct assertion (*śruti*) and the rest, do not fall within the scope of the context (*prakaraṇa*)— was made following the explanation in the *Nyāyasudhā*, relying on the sūtra’s word "unconnected" (*asaṃyukta*). The authors of the *Prakāśa*, however, accepting that the direct assertion and the rest are concerned solely with providing the means (*dvāra*) and the purpose (*idamarthya*), maintain that the status of threshing and other such acts as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) arises solely through the requirement of the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*) expectancy, based on the natural sense of the *Śāstradīpikā*, which aims to demonstrate that even *sannipātin* acts like threshing are grasped by the context.
In this regard, at the conclusion of this section, for what purpose is the inclusion of the term "unconnected" (*asaṃyukta*)?

It is for the purpose of precluding the application by context (*prakaraṇa*) of those [elements] that are connected by direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), or syntactical connection (*vākya*), such as the injunctions regarding the singular or plural forms of the *pratipad* verses, and the words "Pūṣan" and so forth along with their remnants;

or rather, it serves to exclude from contextual application those things which are "unconnected"—that is, not in conflict with the context—while being connected with elements that are themselves not in conflict, such as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) and "the seat of the gods, the sacrificial grass" (*barhir devasadanaṃ*).

Since [the acts] such as "I give" and "she buys with red [cattle]," when connected with the rice, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and the purchase mentioned within the context (*prakaraṇa*), are logically included in that context;

and since that [inclusion] is established by their own inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), it was not explicitly stated by the author of the Sūtras. Thus, the Vārttika alone is the root for these two views; therefore, there is no need for effort here in extracting one particular view. This is the direction [of the argument].
He refutes the objection that "the nature of being an *itikartavyatā* (procedure) is difficult to define" with the words: "And as for the nature of being an *itikartavyatā*..."

In our own view, since *bhāvanā* consists of effort (*yatna*), even though it has no need for auxiliary factors (*anugrāhaka*) therein, there is indeed a requirement for those [auxiliaries] with respect to the production of the *apūrva* by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which serves as its instrument (*karaṇa*) by way of the fruit. Thus, the status of being a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consists in being an auxiliary to the instrument. The meaning is that "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is precisely that expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) of the *bhāvanā* for the generation of the power residing in its own instrument;
this is what is meant by the phrase "attaining the totality of conditions" (*sāmagryalābha*).

Just as, out of fear of the fault of infinite regress regarding the causal capacity residing in a staff and so forth, one accepts beginninglessness when the requisite totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) is not obtained;

for if the capacity residing in the staff were itself produced, then the staff would have to be the cause of that capacity by virtue of possessing it, and if that [capacity] were again to be caused by the staff in that same manner,
there would result the fallacy of infinite regress.

In the case of the *prakṛti* (archetypal sacrifice), however, when there is a requirement for a cause for the power residing in the sacrifice—which is conducive to the production of the *apūrva*—if the sacrifice itself were the cause, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. Since the requirement for a proximate purpose and the capacity to convey the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatā*) in the form of being a causal factor (*kāraka*)—such as the *prayāja* offerings—is inherent in the context (*prakaraṇa*), the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) grasps [the auxiliaries] by way of their being causal factors in the form of generating the power residing in the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is the nature of the expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*).
The meaning is "the context";
[it means] "the grasping by that."

Because established entities such as substances, deities, and the Vāmadevya-sāman produce a single instrument through a perceptible means, they do not require a further purpose; thus, they are not grasped as producing a power residing in the instrument.

As for that unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the restrictive rule (*niyama*), since it arises only after the completion of the sacrifice, it cannot be a cause with respect to the sacrifice; therefore, it does not require [the sacrifice] as the generator of a potency residing within it. However, because it is assisted by the unseen merit of the restriction, the conventional designation of "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*) is applied in the scripture to substances and the like when they are joined with intermediate actions—this is the meaning rooted in this very principle.

Thus, having described the nature of the treatise as being authoritative, he now demonstrates the manner in which it serves as the basis for the conception of each preceding means of valid cognition and as that which applies them, stating: "In this regard..."
"Of the etymologically explained words."
The meaning is: of the subordinate sentences that occupy the place of the aforementioned technical terms. "Residing in that" (tanniṣṭhā) [refers to this].
The meaning is that it culminates in the sense of the intermediate sentence-meaning.
He demonstrates the capacity to convey subsidiarity by means of a dramatic gesture, saying: "For it is possible..."

The meaning is that in the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), the *prayāja* and other such elements denoted by the word "thus" (*ittham*) are connected through a mediated sequence as generators within the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the phrase "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*).

Consequently, because they convey the status of being a causal factor (*kārakatā*) for the volitional effort (*kṛti*) that constitutes a subordinate element (*aṅga*), the authority of the context (*prakaraṇa*)— defined by the mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) between them— is established.
He concludes the established tenet with the words: "Therefore."

Having thus established that the nature of *prakaraṇa* consists in the desire for assistance, in order to confirm this, [the author] restates and refutes that entirely different definition of the nature of *prakaraṇa* which was formulated by Pārthasārathi through his critique of such a [definition]: "As for what [he said] here..."

The meaning is that although the context (prakaraṇa) makes known the connection with specific elements such as the *prayāja* offerings, it cannot logically make known [the status of] being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*), because that status is not comprised within it.
This refers to "the *prayāja* and so forth."
In your view, if the specific activity conducive to the production of another [result] belongs to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth,

then there must be the postulation of an *apūrva*. Consequently, at the stage when the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is first presented, it is not possible for the *apūrva* to be syntactically connected [to the action],
because it does not yet exist.
Nor can it belong to the sacrifice, because that is sublated by the fact that [the sacrifice] is produced by the *prayāja* and other such rites;
what remains, therefore, is the fruit alone.

In that regard, just as the sacrifice is connected to the fruit because the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of the sacrifice has the fruit as its objective (*bhāvya*), so too, since the productive operations of the *prayāja* offerings and others are likewise *bhāvanās*, it would be difficult to avoid the consequence that the *prayāja* offerings—which are their respective objects—would also be connected to the fruit.
Nor can it be restricted by the scriptural mention within the same word (*samānapada-śruti*) that the sacrifice alone possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the fruit;
for since the *prayāja* offerings and others also possess their own operations in the form of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), their status as instruments is difficult to deny.

Since the sacrifice is not expressed directly as the result—because it is not conveyed by the same word [as the result]—it is expressed only by means of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force); and because, in comparison to that, it is more appropriate for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, which are themselves of the nature of *bhāvanā*, to be the instruments (*karaṇa*), the consequence of their connection with the result is unavoidable. This is the meaning.
Furthermore: "Moreover" (*kiñca*).

The meaning is that since the sacrifice, even though it requires only its own performance for the production of another [result], is inherently devoid of expectancy due to the absence of any further requirement, the status of the *prayāja* and other rites as subsidiaries would follow solely from the mutual expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*) between them.
Therefore, it is logical that the sacrifice’s very need for assistance (*anugrahākāṅkṣā*) constitutes the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Since the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is for the sake of a result—either by the logic of the *viśvajit* sacrifice or the logic of the *rātrisatra*—there is no extension (*atideśa*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is; however, this has not been stated because it is self-evident.
Thus ends the fourth section concerning the application of the ritual context.
— — — — — — (B1) (5th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.3 Pā.3 Adhi.5) "And sequence [is a means of proof] because of the commonality of location" (Jaimini 3.3.12).
Position (*sthāna*) is the fifth authority for being a subsidiary (*aṅga*).
This refers to the proximity of two sentence-meanings that are unfit to be related as *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance).

Unfitness as *itikartavyatā* is twofold: in some cases due to a lack of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), as for instance in the case of subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) and the like within a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
Because there is no further expectancy once the requirement is satisfied by the archetypal auxiliary elements whose assistance has already been established;
and because in some cases,
such as with mantras for recitation (*japa*) and the like, they do not consist of an active operation.

And here, it is stated as "vākya" (syntactic connection) because proximity (*sannidhi*)—such as that of the *vrīhi* grain and the sacrifice mentioned within a single sentence—would otherwise also result in being such [a means of proof].

The first qualification is for the purpose of excluding the possibility that the *prayāja* offerings and so forth would fall under the scope of "position" (*sthāna*). That [proximity] has two kinds, which are synonymous with "co-location" (*sādeśya*).
[The proximity of recitation] consists of proximity of textual recitation (*pāṭhasādeśya*) and proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhānasādeśya*).
The former is of two kinds:
recitation in sequential order (*yathākrama-pāṭha*) and recitation in close proximity (*sannidhi-pāṭha*).
This triad is also of two kinds: that which arises from mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) and that which arises from one-sided expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*).
Here, the primary expectancy constituting mutual expectancy should be understood as distinct from the expectancy for the procedural details (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*).

In that regard, by virtue of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras associated with optional sacrifices (*kāmya-iṣṭi*) function as subsidiaries to those optional sacrifices.

However, because it is recited in proximity to the injunction for the cleansing of the *sānnāyya* vessels, the mantra "śundhadhvam" (be ye purified) is subordinate to that [injunction]. Furthermore, due to the proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*), the characteristics of the animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*) are subordinate to the *daikṣa* animal.

Even though these [characteristics] are applied by other means of proof such as indicative power (*liṅga*), and since sequence and the like merely serve to indicate the intended meaning—namely, the status of being a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*)—they do not possess authority regarding subordination itself.
Nevertheless, non-overlapping examples for all six types of sequence (*krama*) should be inferred according to the method stated in the *Kaustubha*.

Here, in all six types of sequence, in the case of an indirectly contributing factor (*ārādupakāraka*), the capacity to establish a context (*prakaraṇa*) arises because the expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) must be postulated.

Even in the case of a directly contributing factor (*sannipatyopakāraka*) such as a mantra, although the mantra does not produce the sacrifice by its own nature, [the sacrifice is produced] when it is endowed with the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the respective restrictive rules (*niyama*).

Because it produces that [context], the assumption of *prakaraṇa*—which consists in the nature of being an *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) defined as the production of a capacity residing in the instrument—is indeed necessary.
For this very reason, it is weaker than that [context].
Furthermore, among the six types of *krama* (order), that characterized by one-sided expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*) is weaker than that characterized by mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*).

Even in that case, because proximity in performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*)— that is, proximity in the context of the injunction (*vidhi-sannidhāna*)— is more immediately manifest than the order of recitation (*pāṭha-krama*),
proximity is stronger between those two.
Because it consists of a single work, etc.; this should be examined in the Kaustubha. // 3.39 //
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the application [of mantras] based on position.

(B2) Indicating the contextual connection (*avasara-saṅgati*) in the determination of the applicative force of *krama* as a means of proof—which was introduced in the same manner as before—the author promises to define *krama* under the guise of explaining synonyms for the word *krama* used in the Sūtra: "And position (*sthāna*)."
The word "pramāṇa" is to be supplied [in the compound] as that which follows;
and since its nature is not known, he states its nature by way of its definition with the words "And that... (tacceti).
Regarding the phrase "in the case of mantras such as japa, etc. [it means]: in the case of mantras for recitation and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), there is an inclusion of mantras such as the *anumantraṇa* and the *yājyā*.
In the phrase "by the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtha*), the word "meaning" (*artha*) includes the proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhānasādeśya*).
[The phrase] "by the expectancy of either one" (*anyatarākāṅkṣayā*)...
The meaning is that it is sixfold in this manner;
[it is] differentiated by the expectancy for the "how-to" (itikartavyatā).

The meaning is that it is the expectation regarding the mere recollection of the substance and deity, which is distinct from the general expectation concerning the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) of the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
That it is an auxiliary element of the optional sacrifice (kāmyeṣṭi).
The phrase "as has been established previously" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
In the [sūtra] *liṅgakramasamākhyānāt*, it was stated that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) depends upon sequence and so forth;

however, here, the lack of redundancy should be understood as resulting from the resolution of the objection: how can sequence itself—which in some cases must depend on the indicative mark—be a factor in application (*viniyojaka*).
This is also an illustration regarding the consecratory formulas (mantras).

For instance, in the *Adhvaryava-kāṇḍa*, the rites dedicated to Agni, the Upāṃśuyāja, and Agni-Soma are prescribed in their respective order; and in the *Yājamāna-kāṇḍa*, the mantras pertaining to those same rites are likewise prescribed in that same order.

“By the sacrifice to the god Agni, may I become an eater of food”; “You are the piercer; may I become unpierced; may I pierce so-and-so”; “By the sacrifice to the gods Agni and Soma, may I become a slayer of Vṛtra.

In these cases, even in the absence of commonality of location with the performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*), the mantra is applied in the mantras over exactly as much space as the primary rite is recited in the Brāhmaṇa.

When there is a mutual requirement between these two as principal and subordinate, their proximity occurs through the principle of corresponding order (*yathāsaṃkhyanyāya*) because they occupy the same position.
Seeking a mantra for the first primary act, one examines the recitation of the mantras starting from the beginning;
consequently, the first mantra comes to mind.
And since there is no reason for its transgression, that very [first] one is accepted.
Likewise, by this same process, a mantra that requires a principal (śeṣin) becomes connected with the first principal;
and consequently, by this same principle, it is also connected with the second principal.
Although the context— characterized by words such as *ghātukā*, *āyudha*, *vāc*, and *abdhi*— and the power of the mantras remain applicable even to the *Āgneya* and other offerings, nevertheless,

since those [offerings] are already encompassed by mantras with clear indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as those addressed to Agni, this mantra with indistinct marks cannot be optionally substituted due to its inferior status. Furthermore,
because the consecratory mantras (*anumantraṇa-mantra*) serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) by means of reviewing the sacrifice whether it has been performed or not, they must apply specifically.
Because a cumulative application is untenable, the mantra belongs to the Upāṃśuyāja situated in the middle, according to the order of recitation.

Nor can the mantras be understood as serving all purposes on the basis of the *prakaraṇa* (context), because mantras, not being of the nature of action (*akriyārūpatva*), cannot be grasped by the context; and since their indicative marks (*liṅga*) are not explicit, it is impossible to determine that their function of denotation (*abhidhānakriyā*) pertains specifically to the Āgneya and other sacrifices, and thus they cannot be grasped by the context even through that function.

Therefore, due to the absence of any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a general connection in the form of *prakaraṇa*, the mantras do not serve the purpose of the Āgneya and other such rites.
Furthermore, that designation (*samākhyā*) as the "invocation for the sacrifice" (*yāgānumantraṇa*) is not exclusive to the Āgneya and other offerings.
