And thus, although the word *asi*—by virtue of ending in the second person singular (*madhyama-puruṣa*), which has your [the sacrificer] as its referent—possesses the capacity to manifest all the subjects under discussion, such as the Āgneya and others, in a common manner; nevertheless, because of the extreme proximity of the Upāṃśuyāja due to its immediate sequence (*sādeśya*), and because the vocative case (*āmantraṇa-vibhakti*) pertains to one who is present before [the speaker], [the invocation applies specifically to the Upāṃśuyāja].

Since the *upāṃśuyāja* is understood to be present before the mantras because it requires them for its performance, one infers the presence of the "capacity for denotation" (*liṅga*), which pertains specifically to the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Thus, by virtue of being the denotable object, the *upāṃśuyāja* alone—due to its extreme proximity—stands [before the mantras], and therefore the mantra is indeed an ancillary (*aṅga*) to that sacrifice.
"But because of proximity," [it is said].

The meaning is as follows: after the vessels have been set down, there is the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and cleansing (*śundhana*). Because of the capacity of the mantra recited in proximity to that rule—"Be cleansed for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods"—to manifest cleansing, it directly sets aside the application [of the mantra] to the *sānnāyya* sacrifice obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*) by means of its indicative power (*liṅga*).

Furthermore, since the indicative power is not explicit regarding specific vessels, the mantra's status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the sprinkling of the *sānnāyya* vessels is established according to the sequence of proximity to the injunction for sprinkling those specific *sānnāyya* vessels.
Although, in the *Adhikaraṇamālā*, it was stated that because this mantra is not recited in proximity to the injunction for the cleansing of the *sānnāyya* vessels—
and because the subsequent mantras beginning with "O Gharma of Mātariśvan" (*mātariśvano gharmosi*) clarify the *kumbhī* vessel and other *sānnāyya* vessels through their recitation in that context—
this mantra, despite clarifying the act of cleansing in general, is nonetheless an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the cleansing of the *sānnāyya* vessels.
It is not the case that [the statement] "because it is recited in proximity to the injunction for that" refers to the proximity to the injunction for cleaning the vessels;
nevertheless, there is no fault, as this should be understood with reference to other Vedic branches (śākhā).
"Of those whose nature is that of cattle."

Even though the *daikṣa* [animal sacrifice] arises in proximity to the purchase [of the Soma], since it is understood from another scriptural statement that it is to be performed on the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*), it remains present in the mind; furthermore, because it requires the properties of the animal sacrifice, possesses the necessary fitness, and— by virtue of being recited in the same location as its own injunction— is understood to be something that ought to be performed,
it is accepted as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the animal-sacrifice properties such as the *upākaraṇa* (dedication), which require a purpose and possess the requisite capacity.
The meaning is that the status of being a "grasper" (the agent of performance) arises from proximity in the ritual procedure (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*).

However, in the section concerning the common injunction for the animal sacrifice (*paśu-sāmānavidhyādhikaraṇa*), this very point is raised as an objection—namely, whether by virtue of the general context (*prakaraṇa*) it serves all purposes, or by virtue of the intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*) it serves only the *savanīya* sacrifice—and is then resolved; thus, one should understand that there is no redundancy.
Thus, the examples for the sequence have been stated according to the method of the Easterners (Prācām); as if objecting to them, he states the distinction: "And although of these... and so forth.
The application of the *kāmya-yājyā-anuvākyā* mantras and the previously mentioned *anumantraṇa* mantras through their indicative power (*liṅga*) is indeed clear.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "through indicative power and so forth," the fact that the animal-rites (*paśudharma*) serve the purpose of the animal is included by means of the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā-śruti*) and other such direct scriptural statements.

In the phrase "of order and so forth" (*kramādīnām*), since it is specifically the sequential arrangement of the text that is intended by the word "order" (*krama*), the terms "proximity" (*sannidhi*) and "commonality of location in performance" (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*) are included by the word "and so forth."
"In some cases" means:

In the *Taittirīyabrāhmaṇa*, after reciting the passage, "Prajāpati created the sacrifice; its two vessels (*ukhā*) became loose," and then stating the application of the mantra, "Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods," it is established that the explicit textual mention (*vācanika*) of the vessel being caught between the two [vessels] by the formula, "Thou art the cauldron (*gharma*) of Mātariśvan," is sufficient to indicate the intended meaning—that this constitutes the means for producing the transcendental result (*apūrva*). Thus, the status of being a subsidiary to the *sānnāyya* offering is secured.
With the intention that proximity (*sannidhi*) also lacks the capacity to apprehend that specific intended meaning (*tātparya*), it was stated "in some cases."

Furthermore, since this mantra is prescribed in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa itself for the sprinkling of the vessels used for the *pauroḍāśika* (cake-offering), it is incorrect to establish the conclusion that it is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) for the sprinkling of the *sānnāyya* (milk-offering) vessels based on proximity alone;
the details of this should be seen in the Kaustubha.
According to the manner stated by Kaustubha.

And it is as follows: where one action with a fruit is prescribed, and in another place an action without a fruit is prescribed by way of a general injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*) as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*),
and both of these are to be performed independently at the same time according to their two respective scriptural statements;
In that case, although it is fruitless, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that which possesses a fruit arises merely from the commonality of location in performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*).

Regarding this, the distinction is as follows: when [the model sacrifice] possesses a fruit and is an *apūrva* by virtue of being a *darvī-homa*, [the subsidiary] is a modification (*vikṛti*) through mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*); whereas in other cases, it is so through one-sided expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*).

And thus, where there is an injunction in the Brāhmaṇa or the Mantra-section for the recitation of various mantras— such as those for silent recitation (*japa*)— which have distinct results and multiple primary acts, and which follow a sequential order that is not governed by indicative power (*liṅga*), there the respective injunctions indicate their corresponding primary acts solely through the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*).
This is because the recitation of the specific mantra as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to each respective primary act follows the order of the sequential text.

Even in that case, the distinction is as follows: when sacrifices with different results have different measures of authority, they are considered *apūrva* (independent rites) by virtue of being *darvihomas*; however, if they are *vikṛtis* (modified rites), it is because of mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*), whereas if they are not, it is because of one-sided expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*).

Thus, the meaning is that examples where the categories do not overlap should be inferred in this manner, such as the status of the *upahomas* as subsidiaries of a *vikṛti* due to their recitation in proximity (*sannidhipāṭha*).

Having thus stated that sequence is a factor of application (*viniyojaka*), [the author] now examines its relative strength and weakness in this context by way of explaining how it brings about the assumption of a section (*prakaraṇa*). He begins with the words: "In this regard... (*atrety*)...
The state of being a creator of contexts.

And thus, in a case where there is proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*) between those that have no mutual expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), since the expectancy of the principal (*pradhāna*) itself must be postulated, [proximity of performance] is weaker than context (*prakaraṇa*). However, in a case where there is proximity of performance between those that do have mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*), nothing need be postulated regarding the matter of remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*);

nevertheless, because proximity of performance is not mentioned in the scriptural injunction for the remote auxiliary, it is weaker than context, which is constituted by mere proximity to the recitation of the injunction (*vidhi-pāṭha-sannidhi*).
The meaning is that the proximity of the injunction (vidhi) presents itself first [to the mind].
This should be understood to apply likewise in cases of remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) that are enjoined by other sequences.
[The phrase] "in the form of mantras and so forth" [is used].

In that case, because it serves as the basis for inferring *prakaraṇa* (context)—which consists of a twofold expectancy—there is a weakness [of *sthāna*]. This is because [the latter] involves the postulation of a primary element and its recollector through the requirement of expectancy, and the postulation of the status of being an *itikartavyatā* (procedure) by means of the postulation of its own expectancy, whereas [the former] does so by way of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
The phrase "in comparison to that" refers to this.
By the first word "that" (tat), the context (prakaraṇa) is grasped; by the second word "that" (tasya), the sequence (krama) is grasped.
"In that case as well" means:

The meaning is: where there is a conflict between the two types of proximity—proximity of recitation (pāṭhasādeśya) and proximity of performance (anuṣṭhānasādeśya)—and the order characterized by mutual expectancy (anyatarākāṅkṣālakṣaṇakrama) is weak;
[this occurs] because of its immediate manifestation (puraḥsphūrtikatvāt).
The meaning is that when there is proximity in performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*), it is the performance itself of the primary act that first presents itself to the mind, not the injunction;

whereas in the case of textual order (*pāṭha-krama*), it is the reading of the injunction alone that is proximate, and thus it presents itself before the performance. Therefore, proximity in performance is weaker than textual order.
"But as for those two..."
The meaning is that there is a mutual conflict between the order of recitation (*pāṭhasādeśya*) and proximity (*sādeśya*).

The point is that because the order of recitation does not involve being located within a single text, whereas proximity involves being located within a single text and thus presents itself more immediately, the order of recitation is weaker than proximity.
The purpose has not been stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the application [of mantras] based on position.
— — — — — — — (B1) (The sixth section on the six topics; A.3 Pāda 3 Adhikaraṇa 6) *Ākhyā caivam atadarthatvāt* (Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.13).

In the Veda and by ritualists (*yājñika*), designations such as *hautra* (pertaining to the *hotṛ*) and *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the *adhvaryu*) are applied to the constituent elements (*padārtha*) prescribed in the Ṛgveda and other Vedas. This is because [these names] do not have any other purpose [than to indicate the specific performers].

That [etymology] also serves as proof for its being a subordinate element (*aṅga*). For instance, in all cases, a word whose constituent parts have established meanings is of two kinds: that which has a meaning connected to the sentence-meaning in the context of the injunction under discussion, and that which is different from it.

Among these, the first refers to words such as *nirmanthya* in passages like "He bakes the bricks with fire produced by friction" (*nirmanthyeneṣṭakāḥ pacati*) and "He threshes with the mortar and pestle that have been sprinkled" (*prokṣitābhyām ulūkhalamusalābhyām avahanti*).

In those cases, since the act of churning and so forth are subsidiary to the baking and so forth solely by virtue of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), there is no application based on name (*sāmākhyānika-viniyoga*).
The second, however, refers to [words] such as *ādhvaryavam adhīte* ("he studies the office of the Adhvaryu") and *praitu hotuś camasaḥ* ("let the cup of the Hotṛ come forward").

In that case, once the connection of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), namely the *kāṇḍa* itself, has been established within the context of the injunction under discussion, the application (*viniyoga*) of the qualifier—such as its being performed by the Adhvaryu priest—is inferred because its mention as an established fact would otherwise be inexplicable.
Thus, in this instance, the application is determined by name (*samākhyā*).

Here, since the relationship between the two constituent meanings of the name is already understood through the principle of semantic integration (*saṃsargamaryādā*), there is no need to postulate an independent injunction based on the inexplicability of that mention.
Because that would result in an undue burden [of interpretation],
it is rather merely a word that effects the syntactic unity between the sentence concerning the placing of fuel (*anvādhāna*) and the sentence "he chooses the Adhvaryu priest," namely:
"the one whom he chooses as Adhvaryu, he [that same person] places the fires."

And since that [connection] exists in some way within a single cognition of the two injunctions, one first postulates a location (*sthāna*) of this kind; then, by means of postulating a *prakaraṇa* (context) consisting of an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) that makes known the nature of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) belonging to the Adhvaryu, one postulates a *vākya* (syntactic connection) in the form of word-proximity (*pada-sannidhi*), which is called being a part of a single great sentence (*mahāvākya*) for those two injunctions.

And by that, through the postulation of an *liṅga* (indicative power) in the form of fitness residing solely in the Adhvaryu, one postulates a *śruti* (direct statement) in the form of words that effect syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). Thus, it is logical that this [proximity] possesses the status of a sixth means of proof (*pramāṇa*). // 3 // 40 // //
Thus concludes the sixth section concerning the application [of mantras] by means of name.

(B2) Since the authority of the designation (*samākhyā*), which was introduced as before, finds its occasion for investigation five steps later, and since the "contextual connection" (*avasara-saṅgati*) with the present investigation of authorities is clear, [the author] does not state it explicitly; instead, he demonstrates the nature of the authoritative designation by saying: "The *Ṛgveda*, etc. (*ṛgvedādi*).
In rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Jyotiṣṭoma prescribed by the Ṛgveda, there is the designation *hautra*; in those prescribed by the Yajurveda, *ādhvaryava*;
and in those prescribed by the Sāmaveda, *audgātra*. Likewise, in the case of specific vessels, there are designations such as *hotṛcamasa* and *pauroḍāśika*.

The meaning is that [terms] such as "soma-cup" (somacamasa) and others are employed in the ritual items of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (dārśapaurṇamāsika) within the Veda, and likewise employed by common people and by those engaged in sacrifice.
In that case, there would be an application [of the term] through designation (samākhyā) based on its etymological nature (yaugikatva).
Nor is etymological derivation possible here;

for while words such as "pāṭhaka" (reciter) are appropriately used in an etymological sense because their connection with the agent of the act of reciting is understood through perception and other means, in this case, since no such connection is known prior to the name itself, etymological derivation cannot be the cause. Therefore, terms such as "ādhvaryava" (pertaining to the Adhvaryu) are purely conventional (*rūḍha*).

Furthermore, because the designation *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu) is not observed in the case of worldly objects performed by the Adhvaryu, and because the etymological connection (*avayavayoga*) is thus inconsistent,
there is no possibility of a designation consisting of a derivative word (*yaugika-śabda-rūpa-samākhyā*).

Even if such a possibility were somehow granted, since that designation would only produce a cognition of a general relationship, it could not produce a cognition of "subservience" (*śeṣatva*) known as "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*).

Even though the Adhvaryu and others have been acquired through the acts of choosing (*varaṇa*) and appointing (*bharaṇa*), and thus possess a requirement for their purpose (*kaimarthyākāṅkṣā*), and even though the *anvādhāna* and other rites possess a requirement for an agent (*kartṛpekṣā*), it is impossible for the name (*samākhyā*) to convey the sense of being for the sake of something (*tadarthya*)— as understood through an injunction (*codanā*)— because, being a mere word, the name lacks the nature of an injunction.

Even if one were to somehow accept a relationship [between the name and the act] through another means of knowledge, such as the case of "cook" (*pācaka*), the name would not possess authority regarding that relationship.

If one were to assume a relationship based solely on the force of the name (*samākhyā*), there would arise the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), because the name itself depends upon the establishment of that very relationship; thus, in order to refute this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding its lack of authority, he says: "That too...

By the phrase "having its constituent parts already established in their power," it is indicated that when a derivative meaning (*yaugikatva*) is possible, it is improper to assume a conventional (*rūḍhi*) sense.

Furthermore, the avoidance of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is to be understood by the logic set forth in the *Udbhid* section; thus, the nature of the name as being derivative in character has been indicated.

The meaning is that here, as in the case of words such as *aśvakarṇa*, there is no sublation (*bādha*) or impossibility (*asaṃbhava*) that would cause one to abandon the perceived etymological connection (*yoga*); for since the state of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) is possible, it cannot be sublated, and furthermore, the demonstration of that state of being for that purpose is also possible according to the method to be explained later.
If this designation were something that had a beginning in time, then it would have to be applied only after the relationship [between the name and the object] has first been known;

yet, since there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a person who applies it to make that relationship known, the designation itself would have to be the means of valid cognition in that case, resulting in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

And this [conventional usage] is beginningless because there is no recollection of its originator and because it is employed in the Veda; since causes such as delusion or a desire to deceive are untenable, and since the subsequent employment is established simply by observing previous employments, and since the relationship is not denotative but is understood through mere co-utterance (samabhivyāhāra), it is possible for even that which was previously unperceived to serve as the ground for application (pravṛttinimitta). Furthermore, even if one does not grasp its prior perception, the performance [of the rite] remains possible.

Intending to show that there is no risk of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya)—just as in the case of grasping the convention for words such as "cow" (*gavādi*)—he establishes the application [of mantras] by means of traditional designation (*samākhyā*). His reasoning is as follows: because the stream [of linguistic usage] is beginningless, one first understands the relationship between action and its factors through direct perception alone; thus, since the practical application of words is established, and since no other basis is possible for those who know the system of logic (*nyāyavid*), it is possible to assume the comprehension of that relationship based on traditional designation itself. Therefore, he establishes the application by means of *samākhyā*.
"By nature," it is said.
"By the sentence alone."
And this [term] is also an indicator for the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof.

For this very reason, even in the case of derivative names such as *āgneya* ("belonging to Agni"), since the status of Agni and the others as deities is established by the direct statement of the secondary nominal suffix (*taddhita-śruti*) itself, there is no application (*viniyoga*) of Agni and the others based on the name (*samākhyā*).

Therefore, wherever a derivative word brings to mind only those meanings of its constituent parts that are capable of entering into a relationship of subordinate and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*), [the application is determined by the derivative suffix].

However, the traditionalists maintain that in cases such as "he sprinkles the rice grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), where there is a relationship between the subordinate and the principal, the designation (*samākhyā*) consisting of words such as *hautra* or *camasa* is the sixth means of proof.

As for that which is stated in the *Śivatattvaviveka*— namely, that "samākhyā" (designation) is derived from the etymology *samā* (same) and *ākhyā* (name), meaning that the identity of name serves as the cause for a connection between what is established in one place and what is established elsewhere; for example, the identity of the name *ādhvaryava* serving as the cause for the mutual connection between mantras such as "May Agni, knowing, heat the sacrifice" and the *atimukti* oblations— this alternative definition of *samākhyā* is to be disregarded, because it is not universally applicable (*avyāpaka*) when these names are used to assign the role of agent (*kartṛtva*).

In the section on the animal sacrifice (paśubandha), regarding the four *atimukti* oblations prescribed by the text "he offers the four *atimuktis*," no connection with the previously mentioned mantras is established through direct naming (*samākhyā*);
rather, it is only as found in the *Āpastamba-sūtra*. Therefore, it should be understood that for that purpose, such a nature [of the mantras] which contradicts the Mīmāṃsakas is not authoritative.
This is because [the mantras] are subordinate to the cooking and other such acts.

In that case, since the substantive element (viśeṣya) is already established through implication and by being mentioned in another word, the sentence serves as the application (viniyoga) because its intended meaning (tātparya) lies in its function as a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa). This is the sense.
"Of the qualifier."

The meaning is as follows: since the agent—such as the *adhvaryu* priest—and the act of consuming for the purpose of the *camas* cup do not connect with the study [of the Veda] because they function as qualifiers, it is impossible for there to be an application [of the injunction] by means of a word denoting that action. Therefore, having postulated an injunctive sentence according to the method to be described, by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and so forth, one attains the cognition of a relationship in the form of agency and the like.
The formulation of an independent injunction.
The meaning is that one should assume an injunction such as "the *adhvaryu* should perform the ritual items beginning with the *anvādhāna*, as recited in the [relevant] section";
thus [it says], "he [should kindle] the fires."
By this, the avoidance of the absence of an injunction for the Adhvaryu’s agency and the difficulty regarding its being subject to the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*) is indicated.

In reality, however, because there are many subsidiary sentences (*aṅgavākya*), one would incur the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) by having to postulate numerous specific words to effect the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of each respective sentence.

Therefore, it is more appropriate—given that the burden of complexity is equal—to postulate, on the basis of the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject matter (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*), a single injunction for the application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) of the entire section (*kāṇḍa*) itself as being performed independently by the Adhvaryu priest.

In this regard, although we observe such references in the injunctions regarding study (*adhīte*) and so forth, as well as in the mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), which appear to refer to established facts;

Since such an injunction can only be postulated through the impossibility of its being otherwise (*tadanyathānupapatti*), it is not tenable to claim that the application (*viniyoga*) is based on the name (*samākhyā*) alone; thus, it cannot be said to be "based on name.
Nevertheless, because the impossibility of the etymological word-meaning being otherwise is the specific cause in that case, it is designated by that [name] in common usage.

However, where something is established solely through common usage among ritualists (*yājñika*), it should be understood that since even the injunction (*vidhi*) must be inferred merely from the fact that otherwise [the practice] would be inexplicable, such conventional usage is indeed appropriate.

In this regard, the ancients maintain that in the case of *krama* (order), its authority arises from the assumption of *prakaraṇa* (context) and so forth, because it merely arouses the primary expectancy (*pradhānākāṅkṣā*)—namely, that there is a relationship between place and the general characteristic [of the rite] as perceived by direct observation.

In the case of *samākhyā* (name), however, on the strength of a name denoting only a specific ritual element, one first assumes a relationship, thinking, "Surely there must be some connection between these two.
Thereafter, the expectancy for the *anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel) and other such acts—which had been eclipsed by the *kathaṃbhāva* (the "how-to") of the fruit-bearing *bhāvanā*—is revived.
It has been stated that authority is established by postulating [the word] *kalpya* through the assumption of sequence and context;
however, that is incorrect.

For in the case of the term *ādhvaryavam*, when both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) present their own respective literal meanings as well as a general relation, it is by virtue of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) that...

Since it is appropriate to understand [the word] as referring to a specific relationship characterized by agency and so forth, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of postulating a relationship that cannot logically serve as the basis for determining the position [of the mantra].

Therefore, accepting the already established presence of the relationship, he demonstrates the determination of the position that is favorable to what was stated—that the assumption of merely the word itself brings about syntactic unity—by saying: "And that... and "as the procedure...
(itikartavyatātve).

The meaning is that, just as before, by postulating for the *adhvaryu* priest the status of a procedure (*itikartavyatātva*) through the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from those restrictive rules, one then postulates the *prakaraṇa*—in the form of a requirement for such a procedure—for the *anvādhāna* rite.
The rest is clear in meaning.

The purpose [of this discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is no restriction regarding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in those various Vedic rites enjoined by the respective Vedas which constitute the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices;
whereas, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is a restriction. This has not been explicitly stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the sixth section concerning the application of ritual elements through designation.
(B1) (Section 7) (Topic 7:

A.3 Pāda 3 Adhikaraṇa 7) "In the case of a conflict between direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each subsequent one is weaker because of its remoteness from the purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.14).
Thus, having defined the six means of proof (*pramāṇa*), the relative strength and weakness in cases of contradiction is now determined.

Furthermore, there is conflict when two means of proof exist for a single subsidiary (śeṣa) with respect to two principals (śeṣin), such as when the Aindrī mantra is [by] direct statement (śruti) a subsidiary to the Gārhapatya fire, yet by indicative mark (liṅga) a subsidiary to Indra; or alternatively, when there are two means of proof enjoining two subsidiaries for a single principal,
such as when the Aindrī mantra is [enjoined] to the Gārhapatya by direct statement, but [the same] Āgneya [mantra] is [enjoined] by indicative mark.

Furthermore, this application of the two remaining [means of proof] serves as the determinant of relative strength only when there is identity of the object (*śeṣin*), and not even when there is a difference between them;

for instance, although the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice and the *prayāja* offerings share a single object through both syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), such [relative strength] does not apply there.
However, where there are two means of proof for a single subordinate element (*śeṣa*) with respect to one and the same principal element (*śeṣin*), [the conflict arises].

In that regard, when there is inequality, only the stronger [text] possesses the power of application for the sake of a specific purpose; however, when they are equal, one has the power of application while the other, being a repetition (*punar-śruti*), is assumed to have a different purpose.
In the absence of a restrictive factor, both are assumed either to possess an exalted result (*abhyudayaśiraskatva*) or to denote a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

Thus, in cases such as "one purchases with redness" (*āruṇayā krīṇāti*), where there are three means of proof for the fact that redness serves the purpose of the purchase which is a means to the *apūrva*, it is the *śruti* alone that possesses the power of application (*viniyojakatva*), and not anything else;
for the syntactical connection (*vākya*) merely provides the object to be designated.
Therefore, in the case of the phrase *naindyā*, there is no conflict between the gender (*liṅga*) and the sentence (*vākya*);

for although the sentence functions as an auxiliary to the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) by providing the mere object of reference (*uddeśya*), it lacks the power of application (*viniyojakatva*) consisting in the cognition of its being a factor in the performance (*kṛtikārakatva*).

Context (*prakaraṇa*), however, is merely a grasper of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*) regarding the status of being a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva-sādhanatva*), but even that is not an applicator (*viniyojaka*), due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*).

Therefore, just as the relative strength or weakness of the means of application (*viniyojaka-pramāṇa*) must be examined, so too must the relative strength or weakness of the means that apprehend the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka-pramāṇa*).

Thus, here, when there is a conflict between two direct scriptural statements (*śruti*), the *aindrī* mantra is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *gārhapatya* fire by virtue of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*), and not an auxiliary to Indra and others by virtue of the *taddhita* suffix;
for that [suffix], being a *sūkta-taddhita*, denotes primarily the relationship of the hymn and lacks the capacity to express the status of a factor of action (*kāraka*).
And therefore, because it lacks the status of primary direct statement (*śruti*), it is weak.
Thus, this mantra’s subservience to Indra by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*) serves as the very example for the conflict between direct statement and indicative power;
for in all such cases, the authority of each subsequent means of proof is established only by its dependence upon the preceding one, as will be demonstrated in their respective examinations.

Because each subsequent [element] is established by the preceding one, there is a sublation of the assumption of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) for that which has already been understood, since the relationship between the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) is rendered free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) by the preceding [element].

Nor is it tenable that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) should lead to the assumption of a *śruti* merely through the expectancy of Indra and others— just as the assumption of an extended application (*atideśa*) occurs through the expectancy of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) even when the subsidiaries are themselves free of expectancy because they serve the purpose of the archetype (*prakṛti*)—
because [the deity] can be remembered through other means such as meditation (*dhyāna*), and thus lacks the kind of necessary expectancy found in the case of a *vikṛti*.

Therefore, by direct statement (*śruti*), it is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *gārhapatya* fire. Nor should it be argued that there is no conflict between direct statement and indicative mark (*liṅga*) because the direct statement merely expresses instrumentality, whereas its being related to the *gārhapatya* depends on syntactical connection (*vākya*). Even if that were the case, since it is a Brāhmaṇa passage, it is established as more powerful than the indicative mark of a mantra—just as in the case of the rule "even if the animal is dedicated to another deity."
In reality, however, there is no contradiction with the sentence (vākya) either, just as there is none with the direct statement (śruti) alone;
for this is logically consistent, as [the word "near"] can mean "in the vicinity of the Gārhapatya fire.

Therefore, even though there is a contradiction with both, it is cited as an example of the conflict between *śruti* and *liṅga* according to the maxim: "Designations are made by means of the principal factor."
When there is a conflict between two indicatory marks (*liṅga*), the primary one sublates the secondary one by virtue of its superior capacity. However,

regarding the conflict between an indicatory mark and syntactical connection (*vākya*), the entire mantra is [sublated] because the first half, "syonaṃ te" (pleasant for thee), which illuminates the preparation of the seat, and the second half, "tasmin sīda" (sit upon that), which illuminates the act of sitting, form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) due to their mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*) as to what "that" might be.

Whether the application (*viniyoga*) of this [mantra] is intended to occur in one of the two places— namely, the *sādana* (seating) or the *sadana* (establishing)— or in both, or indeed in the act of establishing alone, by means of a sentence consisting of the proximity of the word "in that" (*tasmin*), then, because the syntactic indication (*liṅga*) which has already functioned previously establishes that there is no evidence for assuming that the primary subject of each respective verb— which conveys its own meaning— is subordinate to another; and because the pronoun "that" (*tat-śabda*) can refer to an object presented by another sentence, just as in the case of the phrase "That [offering] belongs to the Viśvedevas" (*sā vaiśvadevī*).
Because their purpose has been fulfilled, the application [of the quality] is to each [part] individually.

When there is a conflict between two sentences, the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*)—on account of its syntactic unity with the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) which is separated [from it] in the sentence "This is indeed the secret part (*tsarā*) of the sacrifice"—is a property of the constituent parts of the sacrifice;

therefore, it is set aside by the property of the ritual act as understood through its syntactic unity with the proximate word "whatever" (*yatkiñcit*) in the sentence "Whatever is prior to the Agniṣomīya, that they perform in a whisper."

Furthermore, when there is a conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), the status of the *vaimṛdha* offering as a subsidiary of the Full Moon sacrifice—understood through syntactical connection—sublates its status as a subsidiary of the New Moon sacrifice understood through context.

As for the example cited—that the contextual purpose of the words "this oblation" (*idaṃ haviḥ*) and so forth, which are part of a single sentence with terms such as "Agni-Soma," namely the manifestation of the deities of the New Moon sacrifice, is sublated by syntactical connection—that is incorrect; because the *sūktavāka* is employed by direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative power (*liṅga*), it is established in form and thus does not fall within the scope of context (*prakaraṇa*), and therefore there is no possibility of its being applied to the primary context.

This should be understood as intending to set aside that [subordinate context], because even here the subordinate context known as *adhikāra* (qualification) is applicable as a determinant of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) by way of defining [the action] as a means to the *apūrva*.
When there is a conflict between two contexts, the major context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) prevails over the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

When there is a conflict between context (*prakaraṇa*) and order (*krama*), although actions such as gambling (*videvana*) enjoined in passages like "He plays with dice" would—due to their proximity—be expected to be subsidiary to the Soma sacrifice called *Abhiṣecanīya*, they are instead established as subsidiary to the *Rājasūya* by virtue of the [major] context.

Nor can there be a suspicion of [the *abhiṣecanīya*] being the subject of the context (*prakaraṇa*), because it is a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) and thus lacks such a requirement; for as a modified sacrifice, its expectancy has already been satisfied by the archetypal auxiliary elements whose assistance is already established.

Furthermore, even in a modified sacrifice, when an auxiliary belonging to the modification is enjoined by a direct scriptural statement (*vācanika*) in reference to an archetypal auxiliary—such as the spottedness (*pṛṣattā*) and so forth—[it does not constitute a case of *prakaraṇa*].

It should not be argued that, since the expectancy for subsidiary elements (aṅga) in their modified form has not yet ceased, it is logical for a new subsidiary occurring after the primary rite—which is sandwiched between them—to be grasped by context (prakaraṇa) precisely because it is to be enjoined; and that, as for the dice-playing (videvana) and so forth, they too are logically grasped by context because they are recited in the text as occurring after the Abhiṣecanīya rite and before the aforementioned consecration (abhiṣeka). [Reasoning: This is because even when the expectancy for subsidiaries in their modified form has not ceased, since [the new element] is to be enjoined, it is appropriate for a new subsidiary occurring after the primary rite—which is situated between them—to be grasped by context alone; and as for the dice-playing and so forth, they are indeed grasped by context because they are recited in the text as occurring after the Abhiṣecanīya and before the consecration described in the aforementioned manner. Thus it must be stated.

Even for a new subsidiary (*apūrvāṅga*) prescribed by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to an archetypal subsidiary (*prākṛtāṅga*), the prescription occurs only when the requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) of the modification (*vikṛti*) has already ceased—just as in the case of the *upahoma*s.

For only that new subsidiary whose prescription is made because it takes the place of an archetypal function (such as the *audumbara* wood or the *śara* grass) is included within the context of the modification (*vikṛtiprakaraṇa*), provided its requirement has not yet ceased; this applies equally to a subsidiary that is conjoined with such an element, or one that precedes it, or one that follows the principal rite (*pradhāna*).

However, since the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) does not fall under the category of a primary ritual act (*prākṛtakārya*), it is not tenable that the acts previously mentioned—such as the gambling (*videvana*) and so forth—should be included within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the consecration-rite (*abhiṣecanīya*).

In reality, although the consecration arises independently, its status as a subsidiary element of the Rājasūya is understood from the context; thus, regarding the statement “he is consecrated facing the Māhendra-stotra,” it will be explained that the connection with the word *prati* indicates a connection for the purpose of time (*kālārtha-saṃyoga*).

Therefore, when it would follow that all [acts] from the gambling (videvana) up to the consecration (abhiṣeka) are subsidiary to the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice by virtue of their proximity (sannidhāna) and so forth, that [conclusion] is set aside by the context (prakaraṇa).
Nor is it the case that there is an absence of context for the Rājasūya because each of its parts is a modified sacrifice (vikṛti);

for, beginning from the Pavitra and extending up to the Kṣatrasya Dhṛti, there is a scriptural injunction (vācanika) of subsidiaries under the heading of the "Rājasūya-characteristics," and thus it is logical that the gambling and other acts interwoven within that [sequence] are to be grasped by the context.
In this manner, examples for the *prakaraṇa* (context) may also be inferred through other sequences.

Thus, when there is a conflict between two sequences (*krama*), and it occurs that by virtue of proximity (*sannidhāna*) both *yājyā* verses could indifferently serve as subsidiaries to the two optional *aindrāgna* offerings, the first verse serves as the subsidiary to the first offering according to the order of the recitation.

When there is a conflict between sequence and name (*samākhyā*), the mantra beginning with "śundhadhvam," which is recited in the section named *pauroḍāśika*, becomes a subsidiary to the *sānnāyya* offering due to its proximity [to that offering].
Nor does the context (adhikāra) set aside the proximity (sannidhi),
because the latter is also stronger due to its being conjoined with a scripturally enjoined subsidiary element (vācanikāṅga).
Nor, in this way, does it follow that [proximity] becomes the context (prakaraṇa).
Because a mantra, being of an accomplished nature and lacking a specific indicative mark (*liṅga*) for application, does not fall within the scope of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Furthermore, proximity (*sannidhāna*), like name (*samākhyā*), possesses relative strength or weakness only in its capacity to indicate the intended meaning—namely, that something is a means to the *apūrva*—but not in the actual application itself.
In that regard, another example must be sought.

Thus, when there is a conflict between two designations (*samākhyā*), the general designation, "pertaining to the Adhvaryu" (*ādhvaryava*), is sublated by the specific designation, "pertaining to the sacrificer" (*yajamāna*).

In this same manner, examples of the conflict between earlier and later means of knowledge—such as those separated by two or three intervening steps—as well as cases involving multiple subsidiary elements, should be consulted in the *Kaustubha*.
Furthermore, this sublation of direct assertion (*śruti*) by indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is a case of "sublation of what has not yet been established" (*aprāptabādha*).

And the reality [of sublation] consists in the obstruction of the means of knowledge—such as indicative marks (*liṅga*) and the like—which would otherwise establish subsidiary status (*aṅgatā*). For once subsidiary status has been determined by each preceding means of knowledge, the subsequent means of knowledge no longer give rise to the postulation of a preceding one, because the requirement for it has already been satisfied. This, then, is "sublation by non-attainment" (*aprāptabādha*).
The same applies in cases such as the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice, where it is stated: "He performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings," and so forth.

In other cases—such as with general rules (*sāmānya*), specific rules (*viśeṣa*), obligatory rites (*nitya*), occasional rites (*naimittika*), and so forth—there is sublation by what has been obtained (*prāptabādha*).
This consists in the capacity of an already established cognizer to obstruct the application of a rule to a specific object.
For, by a specific rule (*viśeṣaśāstra*) and the like, only the applicability of a general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*) and the like to objects such as the *padahoma* sacrifice is obstructed.

But it is not even the general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*), because that is already established and thus need not be postulated, and because its falsity could not be postulated either, as that would entail the absence of the *āhavanīya* fire in other oblations as well.

Therefore, for one who has first considered only the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*), it is precisely the error produced by the non-perception of the particular (*viśeṣa*) that is sublated by the particular rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) regarding that particular object. Likewise, even in cases such as "He does not perform those two [rites] on the sacrificial animal" (*na tau paśau karoti*), where there is a prohibition of what was established by a scriptural injunction, the establishing rule must necessarily have a particular scope; for since the prohibition depends upon the prior establishment [of the practice] and thus subsists upon it, its absolute sublation is untenable.

Nevertheless, because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is accepted in that case, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the stated definition, since the absence of that [construction] is precluded by its having a specific object.

And just as in that case, one accepts sublation (*bādha*) of what is obtained through error—similar to a prohibition obtained through passion—and does not accept conceptual construction, so it should be seen in the *Kaustubha*;
and this will also be explained here in the tenth chapter.
Therefore, it is established that sublation is twofold. // 3.41 //
Thus ends the seventh section, on the relative strength and weakness [of arguments].

— — — — — — (B2) At the beginning of the chapter, in the first sūtra—"Now, therefore, the definition of the subsidiary" (*athātaḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam*)—the commentator has demonstrated the fivefold thesis by summarizing: "What is the subsidiary? By what reason is it subsidiary? How is it applied? What are the means of application, such as direct assertion (*śruti*) and the rest? And in case of conflict among them, what is their relative strength? In that regard:

Having deliberated up to the promise to define the means of application (*viniyoga*) such as direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, we now consider—taking advantage of the present occasion—the relative strength and weakness (*balābala*) promised immediately thereafter. This is done because it is useful for setting aside applications based on weaker authorities. Thus, by way of "occasion" (*avasara-saṅgati*), the direct connection to the chapter is stated here in this section on sentences (*vākya-pāda*), concerning the very investigation of the relative strength and weakness of the authorities beginning with sentence and ending with name (*samākhyā*) which were mentioned therein.

Even though it is appropriate to discuss [the relative strength of the means of proof] here, [the author], while indicating that the investigation of those very means of proof— namely *śruti* and *liṅga*— is present in the mind, thus suggesting the topical connection (*pādasaṅgati*) consisting in their presence in the intellect; and likewise, because the determination of all means of proof serves as the support for the investigation of relative strength (*balābala*), and because the determination of the means of proof ending with *samākhyā* acts as the cause for that investigation of relative strength, thus suggesting the immediate connection (*anantara-saṅgati*) in the form of a cause-and-effect relationship, he makes the formal proposition regarding the subject matter to be investigated in this section.
Thus it is so.
"Contradiction."

Even when there is a conflict, if there is no single object of application—as in the case of a horse and a buffalo—there is an absence of relative strength (balābala). Therefore, even though the sentence concerning "redness" (*aruṇā*) exists, since redness has as its single object the sense of being for the purpose of the purchase that serves as a means to the *apūrva*, and since there is no conflict between direct statement (*śruti*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), and context (*prakaraṇa*), such [relative strength] is absent. It is with this meaning that the following is stated in the Sūtra: "When there is a conflict and a single object of application, relative strength is determined."
The term *samavāya* has been explained.
This very point is stated under the guise of demonstrating that contradiction (*virodha*) has a single locus: "And contradiction... [and so forth].
Because of the absence of that.

The meaning is that the purpose by which the *prayāja* and other rites possess the status of being subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices does not apply to the *vaimṛdha* offering; for when there is a difference in the assistance produced by each, there is no identity of the means (*dvāra*), and thus no co-inherence (*samavāya*) in that case.
Likewise, in the two instances of co-inherence cited above, regarding the relative strength and weakness of the two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is simply the sublation (*bādha*) of one.

In the first case, however, since both are established as constituent parts by two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there is a combination (samuccaya) rather than both being constituent parts [in the sense of an option].
In the second case, however, there is an option (vikalpa), just as in the case of rice and barley; such is the sense. As for the phrase "where, however" (yatratu):

Just as, with respect to the single fruit consisting of heaven, there are two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that convey the subsidiarity (*śeṣatā*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices— namely, the two statements "the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* for all [desires]" and "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*"—

wherein, despite a discrepancy arising from one being a general statement and the other a specific statement, it is assumed that the specific statement alone is the applicator (*viniyojaka*) with respect to heaven, and thus the general statement is assumed to have a scope other than that.

And the purpose of that [distinction] is as follows: by making known that [the two results] are delimited by distinct delimiters of causal efficacy (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), there arises—through the rule that from a single performance only one thing delimited by a single delimiter of causal efficacy can be produced—the establishment of a rule regarding the production of either of the two fruits, such as a son or cattle, as delimited [by their respective delimiters].

Nevertheless, there is no obstruction to the production of the fruit consisting of both a son and heaven, because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) to its production as being delimited by a distinct delimiter of causal efficacy [namely, heaven].
Therefore, the meaning is that for the sake of accomplishing such another purpose, only a strong [means of proof] possesses the power of application;
this is what is meant by "the postulation of another purpose."

Just as in the case of two statements regarding heaven recited in different branches of the Veda, one must assume a distinct purpose consisting in making them known to their respective individual students;
therefore, the meaning is that in such instances, because there is no coexistence [of the texts], they do not constitute a subject for deliberation.
He extends [the argument] by stating "in this same way," indicating that because inherence (samavāya) does not exist elsewhere either, it is not an object of investigation.

For here, by the direct statement (*śruti*) of the instrumental case-ending, redness (*āruṇya*) is established as a subordinate element (*aṅgatva*) with respect to action in general; by the syntactical connection (*vākya*) characterized by its co-occurrence with the verb *krīṇāti* (he buys), it is established with respect to the specific action of buying; and by the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is established with respect to the specific means for producing the transcendental result (*apūrva*).

Thus, although there is a convergence of these three, it is the direct statement of the instrumental case-ending alone that conveys the status of being a subordinate element. As for the other [means], they serve merely to provide the object to be qualified for the purpose of formulating a restrictive injunction (*viśeṣaṇa-vidhi*); therefore, because there is no identity of objective domain, [the means] do not [conflict].
The meaning is "inherence."

Although it has been stated that among all means of proof (*pramāṇa*), there is a relative weakness when they are in conflict, and not when only two are involved; nevertheless, since a collection such as *śruti* and so forth lacks the capacity to enjoin at a single point, the relative strength or weakness residing therein must—according to the principle of repetition with respect to each primary element (*pratyadhānāvṛttinyāya*)—result in the injunctive force belonging to each one individually. This is because of the inherent logic of the Sūtra regarding each individual [means of proof].
When weakness is to be discussed, the presentation of strength elsewhere is stated by way of its opposite; thus, it is not improper to examine the relative strength and weakness of each pair.

Just as the examination of the relative strength and weakness of *śruti* and *liṅga* is undertaken here in this section (*pāda*) as an incidental discussion, so too, because the reasoning is identical, the examination of two *śrutis* and two *liṅgas* will also be conducted incidentally.

In that regard, regarding the example of the conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), in the case of the injunction "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī [verse]," there is no conflict between the direct statement of the instrumental case and so forth and the indicative mark of the mantra in their own forms; for it is impossible for the instrumental case to exclude Indra's status as the subordinate element (*aṅga*).
It is only when the rule "the Gārhapatya" is established that a conflict between the two arises.

Since this [conflict] between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and indicative power (*liṅga*) arises here from the fact that both are produced by a sentence consisting of the co-utterance with the term *gārhapatya*—just as in the case of the "red" (*aruṇā*) and the "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*)—there is no possibility of a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative power (*liṅga*).

Anticipating this objection, the author refutes it here in passing, for the sake of providing an example of the conflict between *śruti* and *liṅga* which will be discussed later, stating: "For this very reason... (*ata eva*).
The status of being the object (*uddeśyatā*) of the *aindrī* verse as it pertains to the *gārhapatya* fire would be understood solely through syntactical connection (*vākya*);

for subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) consists in being a factor (*kāraka*) in the activity directed toward that object. Since the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), which denotes the [verse] primarily by virtue of its connection with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), is predominant according to the maxim "designations are made according to the principal," the indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than the words *gārhapatya* and *aindrī*.

The meaning is that because there is a necessity for a separate status as an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) established by the direct statement (*śruti*), there is a contradiction with the cognition of its status as an auxiliary established by the indicative power of the mantra (*mantraliṅga*); thus, it is designated as an example of the conflict between *śruti* and *liṅga*.

In reality, however, since the *āgneyī* verse would already be established for the Gārhapatya fire by its own indicative power (*liṅga*), just as it is established for Indra, the sentence (*vākya*) would become redundant; therefore, one must necessarily maintain that the status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣitva*) expressed by the direct statement (*śruti*) as "the Gārhapatya" refers to objects other than the *āgneyī*, and the status of being an "instrument" (*karaṇatva*) expressed by the direct statement as "the *aindrī*" refers to objects other than Indra. Thus, there is indeed a conflict with the indicative power even regarding the general form expressed by the direct statement, and not merely a conflict created by the sentence; hence, there is no fault.
Furthermore, this very doubt will be refuted by [the author] himself through another method.
"For this very reason."
Context and the other [criteria] serve as indicators of the intended meaning (tātparya) characterized by being the means to an unprecedented result (*apūrva*).
For this very reason, they also acquire relative strength or weakness regarding application (*viniyoga*) at the final stage; that too must indeed be examined here.
For example, in the application of the *pūṣānumantraṇa* mantra by means of indicative power (*liṅga*), because it is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—

The meaning is that, since the context (prakaraṇa) would be obtained as the indicator of the purport regarding the characteristic of being tall, it will be stated that the name (samākhyā) alone is the indicator of that purport because of its contradiction with the indicative mark (liṅga).
But not by virtue of the direct mention of a secondary derivative (taddhita).

The meaning is that, although the term *aindrī* is derived from the sense of "that which has Indra as its deity" (*yasyā indro devatā*) according to the rules for secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), since the secondary suffix reveals that Indra is the deity whose nature is to be manifested, Indra is perceived as primary by virtue of being the object of manifestation; therefore, the mantra does not convey subservience to Indra, because it expresses the status of being the objective (*uddeśyatā*) which constitutes the subordinate element (*aṅgatva*).

Furthermore, regarding the rule "niveśanaḥ saṅgamano vasūnām," it is heard in the context of the *cayanam* (fire-piling) that the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire is to be performed with a verse addressed to Indra (*aindrī*);
and regarding the rule "kadācana starīḥ," it is heard in the context of the *agnihotra* that the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire is to be performed with a verse addressed to Indra.

Since in both cases Indra is not the intended object of the rite, and thus the worship addressed to Indra is not to be performed, how could there be any possibility of Indra being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) [of the worship] based on the direct statement of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-śruti*)?
Therefore, even in the case of a conflict between *śruti* and *liṅga*, this is not an example of a conflict between two *śrutis*;

rather, one should simply say that "he takes up the horse's halter" is the correct [view]. For just as the status of being a subordinate part (*aṅgatva*) is established in the *bhakṣa-mantra* by assuming an injunction for taking [the cup] based on the *liṅga* "that which is to be consumed," so too here, the status of being a subordinate part is established by assuming an injunction for the worship of Indra based on both the *śruti* "Indra" and the *liṅga*.
The sense is that there is no fault [in this view], because it follows from the rule that one should perform the *aindrī* worship while standing near the *gārhapatya* fire.

Even though predominance (*prādhānya*) is the meaning of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), since predominance is not presented by the suffix as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), it does not fall under the definition of being "directly Vedic" (*mukhya-śrauta*).

Furthermore, predominance is not the meaning of the suffix in the form of "desirability" (*īpsitatva*), which constitutes the factor of being a subordinate element (*aṅgatva*); rather, it is merely the status of being the substantive within the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in relation to other qualifiers.

Therefore, having characterized that [object] as being "intended" (īpsitatva) by virtue of its stated predominance, he says "of that" (tasya), meaning that its application (viniyoga) would not be understood through the direct statement of the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita-śruti) alone; thus, it is weaker than the direct statement of the case-role (kāraka-śruti).

Thus, the examples illustrating the relative strength and weakness in cases of conflict between two *kāraka* (syntactic) indications, between two *vijātīya* (heterogeneous) indications, and between two *samānajātīya* (homogeneous) indications are to be found in the *Kaustubha*.
"Thus" [concludes the section].

Nor is there a redundancy with the section concerning the *aindrī* mantra; for while that section merely established that the figurative capacity is supported by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), this section avoids redundancy by refuting the suspicion that Indra might be a subordinate element (*aṅga*) based on indicative power (*liṅga*).
An inferential mark (*liṅga*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by itself;

for, according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that "the entire Veda is the root of Dharma," it is established that only the Veda— whether directly perceived or inferred— is restricted as the means of knowing Dharma,
and because [inference] would otherwise necessitate the unwarranted importation of meanings (*arthādhyāhāra*).
Furthermore, the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*), which is constituted by the fact of being enjoined, is not possible without the postulation of an injunction (*vidhi*).

And since that [injunction] is cognizable solely through words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), the postulation of such words is necessarily required. With this in mind—that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) functions as the applicator (*viniyojaka*) precisely by postulating a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) consisting of words expressive of that [auxiliary], so that the very factors such as the causal efficiency (*kṛtikārakatva*) presented by those words may be construed [with the primary act]—[the author proceeds].
It establishes weakness [of the opponent's position] with the words: "For here... (atrāhi).
"As in the case of a transformation."

The meaning is that there is a disparity [between the two cases]: because in the case of a modified ritual (*vikṛti*), the requirement for auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) such as deities is not satisfied by mere implication (*ākṣepa*), it is not improper to restrict [the auxiliaries] to those of the archetypal ritual (*prakṛti*) presented through a specific similarity.
Furthermore, in this context, regarding the subject of the sublated gender, the word "Indra" alone is the object;
since the remaining words form a single syntactical unit with it, they belong to Indra as their auxiliary, and thus do not have that [gender] as their own scope.

However, there is a contradiction with direct statement (*śruti*) because of the sentence form that constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the word "Indra. Alternatively, once the word "Indra" is established by direct statement as being subsidiary to the Gārhapatya fire, it follows that the remaining words, by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with it, must likewise be subsidiary to the Gārhapatya; thus, the operation of direct statement does not extend even to that portion [of the sentence], as that is the actual state of the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
It should be understood that since [the cognition] has as its object only the locus of Indra, there is no contradiction between the Śruti and the sentence regarding that portion.
Even while accepting the contradiction between the sentence and the indicative mark (*liṅga*), he justifies the sublation of the indicative mark with the words: "even though that is so."
"Even though it has another deity," so [it is said].

Indeed, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of a mantra is not more powerful than the statement of a Brāhmaṇa, because the mantra is dependent upon it as it serves to illuminate the matter prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, just as in the case of the *manotā* mantra—which, though incapable of manifesting two deities [simultaneously], [is applied] according to the rule: "Even if it belongs to another deity... [and so forth].

Thus, by the force of syntactical application (*vākyīya-viniyoga*), one postulates the capacity [of the mantra] through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth, whereby its status as an auxiliary to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice is established; likewise here too, its status as an auxiliary to the *gārhapatya* fire is established by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*).

Furthermore, it is not possible for the statement "even if [the animal] belongs to another deity" to exclude animals dedicated to Vāyu and others that were never applicable because they function as the *avāyavya*-recitation in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, the meaning is that it serves only to indicate subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) within the archetype by way of preventing their displacement (*utkarṣa*).

By this very same method, even in the view of those who maintain that there is syntactical application (*vākyīyaviniyoga*) in the case of "thus he takes the horse's halter," the sublation of indicative power (*liṅgabādha*) must be explained.
Regarding the phrase "of the two genders":

The meaning is that when it would follow—on the basis of secondary capability—that mantras such as "barhir devasadanaṃ" have a subordinate relationship to a secondary meaning, they are instead sublated by their primary capability, because they have a subordinate relationship to the primary meaning.
[This applies to the mantra] "syonaṃ te."
“I prepare for you a pleasant seat; with a stream of clarified butter I fashion it so that it is very gracious.

Sit upon it, O immortal one, and take your stand, being well-disposed, O essence of rice. This mantra is employed when placing the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) into the vessel that has been sprinkled with clarified butter.
Its meaning is as follows: “O essence of rice!”

O *puroḍāśa*, the sacrificial material made from rice, I prepare for you a pleasant (*syona*)— that is, smooth— seat (*sadana*), a place, by means of a stream of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Since I thus fashion it as a very comfortable (*suśeva*) place fit for a peaceful rest, upon that very seat, being well-disposed and delighted, you [should sit] in that which is immortal (*amṛta*) and free from death (*mṛta*), such as the burning and other forms of mortality.

"Be established, be firm. Here, regarding the performance of the act of seating (*sadanakaraṇa*) by means of the sentence consisting of the co-occurrence of the first half and the second half, it must be stated that the application [of both halves] as subordinate elements (*aṅga*) to the act of seating is set aside by *liṅga* (indicative power). How is this so? Because, despite the difference in the verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), there is an absence of "unity of purpose" (*ekārthya*)—defined here as the lack of multiple principal subjects (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) within distinct cognitive domains.

Since the status of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) has not yet been established, how could it be that both [properties] do not apply to either one of them alone, such that their contradiction could be determined? To this end, he establishes their syntactic unity with the words: "In which one of those... (*tasminkasmin*).

Even though there is no identity of meaning based on common cognition, because that word (*tacchabda*) is dependent on what precedes it— just as in the case of the word *ya* in "those who shall increase the lord of the sacrifice" (*ye yajñapatiṃ vardhānī*) and so forth— it possesses expectancy when being divided; therefore, by that alone, just like in those cases, one may assume a unity of meaning and thus the validity of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) is established.

For it is indeed possible that even the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) denoted by a verbal suffix may have a requirement for further specification and thus connect as a qualifier (*prakāra*) with another *bhāvanā*, as in the case of "Look, the deer runs.

Therefore, the meaning is that there is no harm even if the status of being the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyatva*) of the verbal suffix's meaning is sublated by the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

Although, because [the latter] has not yet arisen in conflict and because there is no hearing of the word that would trigger such an expectancy, one cannot assume that the preceding verbal suffix conveys its own meaning as a qualifier; [nevertheless, the point remains as stated].

Furthermore, since the preparation of the seat (*sadanakaraṇa*) is that for which the installation of you [the deity] is to be accomplished, by thus conceiving the latter mantra as the means (*prakāra*), it follows that it belongs to the latter mantra alone. Thus,

even though the first half-verse is enjoined for the preparation of the seat by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*), the second half-verse— consisting of the words "devasya tvā" and so forth— is, like the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*), connected with the first half-verse through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the words "pouring out" and so forth.

The sense is that since the attainment occurs only at the very moment of making the seat, the statement that it occurs "either in one of the two— namely, the making of the seat and the placing [of the oblation]— or in both, specifically in the act of establishing" must be interpreted in some way as being merely possible.
Having assumed the unity of meaning on the strength of that word, it is stated that there is syntactic unity; [the author] refutes this with the words "of that word" (*tacchabdasya*).

Even though it is observed that the word *yat*— which, by its own sentence, implies a restriction projected by the word *tat*— has its grammatical derivation established in instances such as "one should sacrifice with the Jaya-rites with whatever rite one desires to prosper" (*yena karmaṇertset taj jayābhiḥ*), there is nonetheless no observed rule that the word *tat* refers exclusively to what is presented by the [same] sentence.

Consequently, since there is no such rule here either that it refers exclusively to what is presented by its own sentence, the requirement of syntactic expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) would be unaccounted for if it were otherwise.

Since it is impossible to assume a single purpose, the application must be divided according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*): the first half is for preparing the seat, and the second half is for placing [the vessel] upon it.
This being the case, if there were meaninglessness in its separate application— as there is, for example, in the phrase "devasya tvā" and so forth—
then such an application would not occur; however,
by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*), it possesses the capacity to serve the purpose of placing [the oblation] as a means to the unmanifested transcendental result (*apūrva*).
Therefore, the meaning is that a split of the sentence (vākyabheda) based on indicative power (liṅga) is logical.
Regarding the relative strength and weakness when indicative power conflicts with context (prakaraṇa), order (krama), and number (saṅkhyā), the examples should be consulted in the Kaustubha.
This is the contradiction between the two statements.
"Separated."

In the sentence, "This is indeed the end of the sacrifice; therefore, whatever is prior [to it]," the meaning is that the word *yajña* (sacrifice) is separated [from its referent] because of the intervention of the pronoun *tat* and the word *yatkiñcit* between it and the word *prācīna*.
This is the contradiction between the syntactical connection and the context.

Although the word *paurṇamāsī* does not serve to present the subject matter (*uddeśya*) because it is construed as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) with respect to the ritual completion (*saṃsthā*), nevertheless, since it is already present [in the mind], its function is fulfilled by the assumption of another word denoting that same object; thus it is said to be "understood from the sentence" (*vākyāvagata*).
And so, even though the context (*prakaraṇa*) exists, it is merely a restatement of what has already been obtained through the portion concerning the *paurṇamāsī*; this is the meaning.
As for the phrase "yattu" (but as for that which...).

In the statement, “He throws the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*,” the distribution of the *sūktavāka* recitation—already enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)—into the two sacrificial sessions (*parvan*) according to the respective deities was determined in the preceding section (*pūrvapāda*).

Therein, the following is recited: “O Agni and Soma, may you enjoy this oblation; may you cause it to increase; may you achieve greater greatness. O Indra and Agni, may you enjoy this oblation,” and so forth.
In that context, although the terms for Agni-Soma and Indra-Agni are to be distributed separately, the remaining portions, such as “this oblation” (*idaṃ haviḥ*), and so on, apply to both sessions.

When words that have been recited possess both meanings due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), they are sublated by a sentence (*vākya*)—in the form of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the words "Agni" and "Indra" alone, such as "May Agni and Soma enjoy this oblation; may they cause it to increase; may they achieve greatness and further excellence"—by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the words that reveal those respective deities.
Therefore, the meaning is that, just like that case, there is a distribution of application (*viniyoga*) by means of division.

Considering it improper—according to the method established by himself in the section on *prakaraṇa* (context)—that context (*prakaraṇa*) is not at all a means of application for those [mantras] that are *sannipātin* (directly contributive), he provides another justification, beginning with the words "tacchruti" (that direct statement).

The meaning is that it is precisely the sentence—consisting of the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words denoting those respective deities—that serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), namely the characterization [of the grains] as the means to those respective *apūrvas*, and not the qualification (*adhikāra*) itself; this is said with the intention of refuting that [position].

As for what was stated here by the authors of the *Prakāśa*—namely, that since there would be purposelessness (*ānarthakya*) if the [grains] were for the sake of the Vedic *vrīhi* [grains], and because the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) would remain unfulfilled, even the *saṃnipātin* acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*) must be applied through the context (*prakaraṇa*)—that is not correct; for the purposelessness is avoided by the context known as "qualification" (*adhikāra*) through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the *apūrva*.

If [the threshing] has rice as its purpose by virtue of being of that nature, then—since the requirement for expectation is satisfied by the direct statement (*śruti*) and since application by context (*prakaraṇa*) is untenable due to the superior strength of the direct statement over context—the inclusion [of threshing] by context would be impossible.

By this [it is shown that] if there is no initial connection as a constituent of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the desire to avoid the futility of threshing—which is not connected to the primary rite—does not even arise; therefore, [its] inclusion by context [is untenable].
The statement of Somanātha is refuted;

for when threshing and other such acts are connected to the *prakaraṇa* (context) as constituent parts of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), just like the *prayāja* offerings, they are understood through that context to be related to the *apūrva*. Since they already serve the purpose of the *apūrva*, there is no possibility of their becoming meaningless if they were further understood as being for the sake of the rice (*vrīhi*). Therefore, in order to avoid that [meaninglessness], the status of being a means to the *apūrva* [is attributed] to the words "rice" and so forth.

Since [the application] is established by those very specific injunctions, the assumption of application through context (*prakaraṇa*) is useless; this should have been stated in the very section on context (*prakaraṇādhikaraṇa*), but it has been brought forward here as an incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*).
There is a contradiction between the two contexts.

The meaning is that, although there is an initial implication that the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices due to the context of the main section (*mahāprakaraṇa*), this is set aside by the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), and it is thus established as an auxiliary of the *prayāja* offerings.
Regarding the sequence of the topical sections (prakaraṇa).
"Such as 'he plays with dice,' and so forth."

In the context of the Rājasūya sacrifice—which consists of numerous *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, and *soma* offerings—in proximity to the *Soma* sacrifice known as the Abhiṣecanīya, certain duties such as gambling and others are prescribed by the texts: "He plays with dice, he defeats a Kṣatriya, he causes the Śunaḥśepa legend to be recited," and so forth. The phrase "he defeats" means that he causes [the opponent] to be conquered.
