The narrative concerning Śunaḥśepa, as recorded in the *Bahvṛca-brāhmaṇa*, refers to the *Śaunaḥśepa-upākhyāna*. Since these [subsidiary rites] are not independent *āgamas* (independent sacrifices) and thus lack the status of being directly denoted by the term *rājasūya*, and since their status as subsidiaries is beyond dispute by virtue of their proximity to the fruit-bearing *rājasūya* according to the principle established in the fourth book [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*], it would follow that—on account of their proximity—they are subsidiaries of the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice; however, this is set aside by the great context (*mahā-prakaraṇa*) of the *rājasūya*.
The meaning is that it is an auxiliary element (aṅga) of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
"Of prepared assistance."

Although, because the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries lack expectancy since they already assist their archetype, their connection with the ectype (*vikṛti*) arises from *sthāna*— which consists of the mutual expectancy between the ectype and one of those subsidiaries— and although, when the connection of the ectypal subsidiaries occurs through mutual expectancy, the stronger *prakaraṇa* (context) would result in the ectype’s adoption of only the new (*apūrva*) subsidiaries; nevertheless, in consideration of the relative strength of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) rather than the relative strength of the means of proof (*pramāṇa*), it is more appropriate to adopt the archetypal subsidiaries first, as they possess established auxiliary efficacy (*klṛptopakārakatva*).

For it is not the modification (*vikṛti*) that requires the constituent elements (*padārtha*), but rather the benefits (*anupakāra*) produced by them; and since the constituent elements follow in the wake of those benefits, the expectancy for the "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*) persists as long as the connection with the constituent elements continues. Therefore, by that very [expectancy], the constituent elements are first [connected].

Because the modified (vaikṛta) auxiliaries are grasped through the very requirement of what is to be raised [for performance], there is no "context" (*prakaraṇa*)—defined by the mutual requirement between two elements—in the case of the modification; this is indicated by the phrase "whose assistance is already established" (*kḷptopakāra*).
This is as in the case of the speckled [animal] and so forth.

By the injunction contained in the Cāturmāsya [section], namely, “He performs the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*),” the quality of being speckled is enjoined with reference to the after-offerings.

In that context, the modified sacrifice’s expectancy regarding the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) persists as long as it follows the sequence of assistance (*upakāra*) until its connection with the after-offerings is established.

As long as this connection with the after-offerings exists, because it is impossible for them to be connected without a relation to their own constituent parts (*aṅga*), [the quality] falls within that interval.

Since it is grasped precisely while the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the *pṛṣadājya* has not yet ceased— being grasped through mutual expectation— it is grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself; that is, the subsidiary (*aṅga*) situated between two such [expectations],
as in the case of the *āmanahomas* and so forth prescribed in the interval between the properties of the *prayājas* and *anuyājas* mentioned in the *Sāṃgrahaṇī-īṣṭi*.

Likewise, that which is not "clipped" by a subsidiary part connected to an ordinary (prākṛta) member—meaning it is grasped by the context (prakaraṇa)—is so because its expectancy is not yet satisfied; for, due to its priority over the connection with the subsidiary parts linked to the ordinary members, its expectancy remains unfulfilled until its connection with the primary rite's subsequent subsidiaries has been established.
This is the meaning of being "grasped by the context."
In reality, however, it will be stated in the fourth [book] itself that the *āmana-homas* are not grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*) because their expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) has not been satisfied.

And so, in the present case, when the sentence "He is consecrated in relation to the *māhendra-stotra*" grasps the archetypal *māhendra-stotra* as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the purpose of enjoining the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) as a subordinate element of the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice— since its expectancy has not been satisfied— and since [the consecration] occurs prior to that [stotra],...

Since the acts such as gambling (*videvana*), which are prescribed subsequent to the *abhiṣecanīya* rite, can also be taken up by the sacrifice because their expectancy has not been satisfied—just as the *sāptadaśya* (the rule of seventeen verses) prescribed for the *sāmidhenī* verses applies to animal sacrifices and so forth—it would follow that they are subsidiary to the *abhiṣecanīya* by virtue of context (*prakaraṇa*) alone;
therefore, he says: "And [this is true] of gambling and the rest."

To the extent that an auxiliary (*aṅga*) possesses a pre-established capacity to provide assistance (*kḷptopakārakatva*) through its own constituent parts (*svāṅga*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), to that same extent the auxiliary, together with its own constituent parts, is adopted by the modified rite (*vikṛti*) due to its need for assistance; for by that much alone, the latter's requirement is satisfied. As for the case where a non-archetypal auxiliary is prescribed in reference to an archetypal auxiliary, since it is observed in the archetype that the archetypal auxiliary provides assistance even without that [non-archetypal one], so it is here as well.

Because it is grasped precisely through the desire for modification (*vikṛti*), once that desire is satisfied there is no further grasping; for as long as the desire is not satisfied, there is no grasping. Just as in the case of the *upahoma* offerings, grasping occurs solely through the mutual desire (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*) [between the primary and the subordinate], and thus there is no "context" (*prakaraṇa*). By this same reasoning, neither that which is interposed within it (*tatsandaṣṭa*), nor a subordinate element connected to a primary element already related to another subordinate element, nor even a new subordinate element occurring after the primary rite, can ever be grasped by means of context.

And so, even though the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) in the present case is something not previously established (*apūrva*), since it is grasped precisely because its expectancy has been satisfied, the context of the *Abhiṣecanīya* does not apply; with this intention, he dispels the doubt by stating "by way of restating the archetypal subsidiaries" (*prākṛtāṅgānuvādena*).
To the question, "Where then is there subsidiariness to a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by means of context? he replies: "For that which... (*yasya hi*).

Regarding the *audumbara* quality enjoined by the sentence concerning the *audumbara* wood, when the expectancy arises as to "what should one effect by means of it," there remains indeed an expectancy for an end-result (*bhāvya*). This is because, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), that quality—being for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) alone, whether in its visible or invisible form—does not avoid pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) since the rite is accomplished even without it; thus, it is not set aside. Likewise, the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) also possesses an expectancy for the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāva*).

And that expectancy is pacified only when the substances are construed as being for the sake of the benefit (upakāra) and as following upon it, but not by the mere construing of the benefit itself. Therefore,

just as the expectancy of the sense-organ’s cultivation (*indriyabhāvanā*) for an instrument persists until the oblation (*homa*) is construed as its substratum— since once curd is construed as the instrument, it is impossible for that which is already established [as a substance] to function as an instrument [without a further action]— so too does this case proceed.
However, it does not cease [to require an object] merely by the connection with curd.

And it is said that the oblation (*homa*), being apprehended as the substratum (*āśraya*), is apprehended precisely by the requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*); there is no such thing as a fourth requirement called the "requirement for a substratum" (*āśrayākāṅkṣā*).
Thus, the requirement for the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is not satisfied merely by the connection with a benefit (*upakāra*).
The constituent elements (*padārtha*) that are grasped following upon the benefit are themselves grasped precisely by the requirement for the "how-to.

In that regard, although the archetypal elements (*prākṛta-padārtha*) are grasped by it, they are not grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*), because they have no further requirement since their purpose is fulfilled by being beneficial to the archetype.

However, those non-original elements such as the *audumbara* wood and so forth, which have taken the place of original ones, do not possess expectancy because they lack the capacity to assist other parts and thus their own requirements are already satisfied.
Nevertheless, they are enjoined by virtue of the subsequent state of the animal-tethering post (*paśuniyojana-yūpa*), as long as the requirement for *khadira* wood has not yet been met;
since they are grasped through this mutual expectancy, they are included by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, in that modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the context does exist.
The meaning is that this should be understood to apply to arrows as well.
He shows the distinction in the present case with the words: "But as for the consecration..."

By this, the following [argument] is refuted: "Because the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is enjoined as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *Māhendra* hymn, which itself is a subordinate part of the *Abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, there exists a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) for the *Abhiṣecanīya*. For if the *Abhiṣecanīya*, which is claimed to constitute that subordinate context, were still expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) at the time of the recitation of the *Śaunaḥśepa* episode, then—despite the fact that the *Śaunaḥśepa* narrative and so forth, being recited in its proximity, fulfill the requirements of their own syntactical meaning—the definition of a subordinate context would indeed apply. [But it is not so.]

The meaning is as follows: one might assume a syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*) [between the Abhiṣecanīya and the Videvana, etc.], but since that Abhiṣecanīya is already satisfied by its own archetypal subsidiaries (*prākṛta-aṅga*) even before the Videvana and so forth, one would have to postulate a lack of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for it only after [the subsidiaries have been supplied]. However, since the application is already established by the requirement of "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*) within the Rājasūya itself, it is impossible for there to be an intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*).

Having thus established that the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) cannot be grasped through the context (*prakaraṇa*), even while accepting its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *Māhendra* hymn, he now states that its being a subordinate element of that hymn is actually untenable: "In reality...

[He explains: after the recitation of the Śaunaḥśepa narrative, it is said, "he is consecrated. Thus, among the rites beginning with the dice-play (*videvana*) and ending with the consecration, which have arisen independently, the *Māhendra* hymn is mentioned in the phrase "he is consecrated" merely as a rule for the time of the *Māhendra* hymn.

Since the consecration (abhiṣeka) is not a subordinate element of the Māhendra-stotra, there can be no injunction for the consecration by way of a reference to the archetypal (prākṛta) subordinate elements. Therefore, because it is impossible to grasp the "how-to" (kathaṃbhāva) even through the medium of the stotra—as it would otherwise be an unprecedented (apūrva) injunction—the operation of the context (prakaraṇa) is not possible. Consequently, once it is understood that the rite must be performed through displacement (utkarṣa) or non-displacement (apakarṣa), there is no further need for an expectation of a purpose; thus, it should be performed precisely where its original production (utpatti) occurs.

The meaning is that if one assumes those [rites] based on a specific purpose, they belong to the *rājasūya* as a whole because of its being the primary context (*mahāprakaraṇa*), and not to the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice merely due to proximity (*sannidhāna*).
An objection is raised: "Is it not the case that what is called the *rājasūya* is not a separate ritual entity, but rather merely the *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, and *soma* sacrifices?

And since all of these are individual *vikṛti*s (modified sacrifices) and are thus self-sufficient (*nirākāṅkṣa*), how can there be a great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) for the *rājasūya*? This is the doubt expressed by the words "na ca" [and not].
He composes [the following], beginning with "starting from the purifier" (pavitra).

Starting from the Soma sacrifice known as the Pavitra, up until the Kṣatrasya Dhṛti— a Soma sacrifice prescribed by the injunction "one should finally sacrifice with the Triṣṭomāgniṣṭoma for the support of the Kṣatriyas"— these are treated as constituting the Rājasūya, because the ritual manuals begin with "he purifies these for the Rājasūya" and conclude with "one who sacrifices with the Rājasūya attains a full lifespan," thus presenting them under the designation of the Rājasūya.

The meaning is that because the procedure is recognized through the instruction of the constituent parts (aṅga) as prescribed by the text, and because the expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) of all [parts] is stimulated by their being included within the form of the Rājasūya, the expectancy persists until that point; therefore, it is logical that even those elements falling within that "sandwich" (saṃdaṃśa) are indeed to be grasped by that context (prakaraṇa).
And this fact—that the acts of gambling and so forth fall within the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the Rājasūya—is stated following another Vedic branch (*śākhā*).

In reality, however— in the *Taittirīyabrāhmaṇa*, within the section concerning the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) involving sixteen cups (*ṣoḍaśagṛha*), after enjoining the purification (*utpavana*) by means of gold through the injunction, "For he purifies these for the sake of the *Rājasūya*," and after enjoining many subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) in between such as ascending the throne-seat (*āsandi*), [the text prescribes] the *Āveṣṭi* offerings occurring before and after the consecration by means of an injunction accompanied by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "One who sacrifices with the *Rājasūya*..."

Having prescribed the consecration by means of the injunction, "He is consecrated after the *māhendra* stotra," and having prescribed gambling (*videvana*) and the narrative of Śunaḥśepa at the end of many subsidiary rites through the scriptural injunctions beginning with, "The quarters became the king's [stake]," there is no mention of these as being part of the *Rājasūya* until the conclusion of the *Kṣatrasya Dhṛti*, nor do gambling and the other rites fall within the category of duties prescribed under the heading of the *Rājasūya*.

Therefore, the *Vārttika* states: "For its *kathaṃbhāva* (the requirement of 'how' it is to be performed), following from the *pavitra* rite up to the *kṣatrasya dhṛti*, is capable of enquiring into the *videvana* and other such acts. This is because, although the *kathaṃbhāva* is satisfied by the archetypal (*prakṛta*) elements for the sake of establishing the individual *apūrva* (transcendental result), it persists from the *pavitra* onwards for the sake of establishing the *apūrva* of the entire composite result to be accomplished.

In the *Nyāyasudhā*, this passage is explained as referring to the inclusion [of the acts] within the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*) expectation— that is, their falling within the interval of the expectancy for the procedure— because they persist from the beginning of the *Soma* sacrifice up to the *Kṣatradhṛti* Soma sacrifice, and thus come into contact with the gambling (*videvana*) and other acts occurring in that interval; however,
it is not explained as referring to their falling within the "clamping" (*saṃdaṃśa*) of the properties prescribed by virtue of being designated as part of the *Rājasūya*.

In the *Śāstradīpikā* as well, since certain ancillaries (*aṅga*) are heard to be for the sake of the Rājasūya, the expectancy regarding the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) is established by virtue of its being the Rājasūya; thus, their status as its ancillaries is stated on the basis of the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*), and not from a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

For when the *bhāṣya*, *vārtika*, and other such works have not shown that the *videvana* (shaking the dice) and other elements fall within the context of enjoined subsidiaries (*vācanikāṅga-sandaṃśa*), it is impossible to assume they belong to a different recensional branch (*śākhāntarīya*).
Therefore, the claim by all these modern authors that these are recited within the context of enjoined subsidiaries is nothing but an error.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), however, even the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that [the *videvana* and other rites] are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) of the *rājasūya*—derived from the context of the major section (*mahāprakaraṇa*)—is appropriate here only as a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*).

This is because, in the Taittirīya recension, many subsidiaries of the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, such as the *videvana*, are recorded within the procedure of the *abhiṣecanīya* itself, following the consecration (*abhiṣeka*): "He gives five dice with the formula ‘The king has become the overlord of the quarters’" and "He causes the *Śaunaḥśepa* story to be recited. Thus, they are situated in the midst of the *abhiṣecanīya*.
“*Apāṃ naptre svāhā*, *ūrje naptre svāhā*, *agnaye gṛhapataye svāhā*—thus he offers three oblations,” and so forth, as these have been recited.

Since these [oblations] are raised according to the principle of subsidiary offerings (*upahoma-nyāya*) and, being connected with the *Abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice due to its expectancy, they would necessarily result in being subsidiaries of the *Abhiṣecanīya* itself within that interval.
This is likewise the case in the *Āpastamba* and other *Kalpasūtras*, in the section concerning the distinction of purposes such as piercing (*vedha*) in the *Parimala*.

As for the Pāñcamika (fifth-book) statement— which, taking up the sequence of rites beginning with the dice-game and ending with the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) that is prescribed after the *Abhiṣecanīya* and before the *Daśapeya*, asserts the displacement of the dice-game and other rites based on the displacement of the consecration according to the principle of "displacement of what follows" (*tadantāpakarṣanyāya*)— let it be considered authoritative because it was recorded by the author of the Bhāṣya, provided one assumes a recension from another Śākhā.
However, their status as subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) of the *Abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice cannot be precluded by the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) observed in the Taittirīya recension;

for there is no need to arouse an expectancy for the *Abhiṣecanīya* in order to connect the oblations such as "Svāhā to the grandson of the waters" (*apāṃ naptre svāhā*) with it, nor is it accepted by anyone that these [oblations] are subsidiary to the *Rājasūya*.

Thus, although the word "Rājasūya" is heard in the sentences concerning the *utpavana* (purification) and other rites, it refers specifically to the particular sacrifice within the Rājasūya known as the *Abhiṣecanīya*, due to the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*); enough with this elaboration.

Furthermore, in this case of proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhānasādeśya*), there is an absolute absence of even the possibility of a context (*prakaraṇa*); and even if it were occasionally possible, since the sublation of context by that [proximity] will be stated later in the section concerning the general injunction for animals (*paśu-sāmānya-vidhy-adhikaraṇa*), this is not an example of the superior strength of context, as it is an exception to that.

Likewise, in the case of sequential recitation (*yathākramapāṭha*), regarding pairs of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras which have the same sequence as rites such as those dedicated to Indra-Agni (*aindrāgna*), etc., [the same principle applies].

Because neither the *dabdhi-mantra* nor the *śundhana-mantra*— though both are recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa— is mentioned in the context of any specific [subordinate] act,

and because the *dabdhi-mantra* would contradict the indicative power (*liṅga*) consisting of the second-person plural ending in the mantra "asi śundhadhvam" (which, though recited in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, refers to the "you" addressed by the nearby concluding passage), and because the *dabdhi-mantra* cannot be applied by context even though its indicative power is not explicit, [the application occurs] according to the order characterized by numerical sequence (*yathāsaṅkhya*).

Because the *sannidhi* (proximity) [of the mantra] is already assigned to the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice and to the cleansing of the *sānnāyya* vessels, it cannot serve as an example [for the power of position].

Likewise, since those mantras situated in proximity to a modification (*vikṛti*) that is itself devoid of expectancy lack a context (*prakaraṇa*) within that modification, they become auxiliaries to it through *sthāna* (position) alone; thus, because the coexistence of context and position is impossible, they cannot serve as examples. With this intention, he says:
"Thus, of context... (*evaṃ prakaraṇasyeti*).

The purpose [of this discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is an expiation for the omission of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *soma* sacrifice due to intervening gambling and so forth;

whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is an expiation for the omission of an auxiliary of the *iṣṭi* within the *soma* sacrifice by way of their combination (*samuccaya*). This has not been stated because it is obvious.

As for the statement made by the authors of the *Prakāśa*—namely, that in their own established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the two expiations for the omission of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) in the Soma sacrifice are to be treated as optional (*vikalpa*)—that is improper, because it is impossible to avoid the deficiency of one through the performance of the other; thus, it should be disregarded.
Another purpose [of this discussion] is to be seen in the *Kaustubha*.
Regarding the two, namely sequence and designation.

Regarding a mantra recited in the *Pauroḍāśika* section, which—by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*) and its inclusion within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-adhikāra*)—is generally understood to serve the purpose of purifying the vessels used in those sacrifices; when a desire for specific application arises, it is initially suggested by the name (*samākhyā*) that it is an auxiliary to the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*), and thus an auxiliary to the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the mortars, pestles, ladles, and other vessels belonging to the Āgneya and other sacrifices performed therein.
However, due to proximity (*sannidhāna*), it is established as an auxiliary specifically to the purification of the vessels for the *sānnāyya* offering.

In this context, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* has derived the word *pauroḍāśika* as ending in the suffix *ṭhak*, based on the rule "puroḍāśāt ṭhak" while the rule "adhikṛtya kṛte granthe" is in force; however, that is incorrect,
because such a traditional rule (*smṛti*) is not found under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "adhikṛtya."

Therefore, being dissatisfied with this [explanation], Somanātha has provided the following derivation—which is more appropriate—under the governing rule *tasya vyākhyāna iti vyākhyātavyanāmnaḥ*: he explains it as being formed by the suffix *ṭhan*, prescribed by the sūtra *pauroḍāśapuroḍāśāt ṣṭhan* (Pāṇini 4.3.70).
And in the case of the expression *tasya vyākhyāna*, the meaning "that by which something is explained" (*vyākhyāyate anena*) is indeed possible.

Likewise, in the second Sūtra, the term *pāuroḍāśika* is explained as follows: *pauroḍāśa* refers to the flour-balls (*piṣṭapiṇḍa*) used for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and the *mantra* that consecrates them is also called *pauroḍāśa*; the word *pāuroḍāśika* means "that which exists in the exposition (*vyākhyāna*) thereof. Since this meaning is shown in the *Kāśikāvṛtti*, and since it is understood that the word *vyākhyāna* (exposition) has the sense of "presentation," the exposition in the form of such a presentation is [the subject] by which chapter or section (*kāṇḍa*).

Therefore, even though this section (kāṇḍa) sets forth mantras for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), its primary purpose is not that; rather, the meaning is that there is indeed a sublation of that [mantra].
"Of the mantra."

And thus, although the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) is stronger than proximity (*sannidhi*), nevertheless, because the intermediate proximity is stronger than that due to the stimulation of expectancy by the intermediate "sandwich" (*avāntarasaṃdaṃśa*), the meaning is that the former is sublated by the latter; however,
this does not constitute a formal application (*viniyoga*).
The remainder [of the argument] is that [the mantra] is to be applied solely by means of the *liṅga* (indicative power).

And thus, having perceived the name (*samākhyā*) and having inferred that there must indeed be a connection between these two— the *puroḍāśa-kāṇḍa* as expressed by the stem and the suffix— having postulated a connection between the mantra contained within that *kāṇḍa* and the *puroḍāśa*, and through that medium...

By means of another *śruti* that postulates the requirement for the *āgneya*, one first infers a *śruti* [itself], and having understood the connection with the *āgneya-āpūrva*, one then— through *lakṣaṇā*—
postulates its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the cleansing of the vessels that serve as the means (*sādhana*) for that *āpūrva*.

Meanwhile, the location situated between the preparation of the *idhma* and *barhis* and the pouring out of the handfuls [of grain] belongs to the injunction for the cleansing of the *sānnāyya* vessels.

Because it is recited in the middle section of the *anuvāka* containing the mantras for the faggot (*idhma*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and the pouring out (*nirvāpa*)— and thus possesses an established proximity— it brings to mind the vessels for the *sānnāyya* offering.

Through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means for the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of those vessels, and through the sequence of requirements (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, the assumption of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) leads, by means of indicative power (*liṅga*), to its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the cleansing of those very vessels.
Nor is the designation (samākhyā) without a basis even in the absence of its being for the purpose of cleansing the vessels used for the cake-offering (pauroḍāśika);

for just as there is a connection with the cake-offering for the Sānnāyya-yājyā and so forth contained in that section, here too, such a designation is appropriate for the entire section on account of its abundance—this is the sense.

In reality, however, because these [mantras] are directly enjoined by the sentence in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa itself—“He purifies them for the sake of the sacrifice to the gods”—neither proximity nor name functions as the means of application here; this should be observed in the Kaustubha.
For fear of prolixity, those [arguments] are not stated here either.
However, at the root [of the system], because the weakness of that which is sublated by what it sublates is easily understood, these [points] were not explicitly stated.

Thus, among the means of proof for application—*śruti* and the rest—the relationship of sublation and sublated is established according to the method stated in the *Vārttika*: "Direct statement (*śruti*) is always the sublater, while name (*samākhyā*) is always the sublated; as for the intermediate ones, their status as either sublated or sublater depends on their relative position. Now, since indirect indication (*liṅga*) and the others function more slowly, it follows that when a direct statement exists, it is impossible for them to convey the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅgatva*).

To dispel the doubt as to how there can be a sublation (*bādha*) of a connection that has not been established, and indicating that there is no single uniform nature to sublation in all cases, he demonstrates the essential nature of the sublation already explained with the words: "And this [sublation]... (*sacāyam iti*).
By means of each preceding valid cognition.
Consequently, the status of being a limb of Indra is sublated even before it has been attained;
the meaning is that this occurs because the very root of the conceptual construction has been destroyed.

To the objection, "In that case, how is it that the determination of sublation of what has not been reached (*aprāptabādha*) is discussed even in the tenth [book]?"—he refutes this by showing that there is no evidence for such a fixed rule (*kuladharma*). He does so by stating "In this way" (*evam*): while the determination of sublation of what has been reached (*prāptabādha*) is the primary subject there [in the tenth book], the determination of sublation of what has not been reached occurs only incidentally (*prasaṅgataḥ*) in certain instances; yet, this does not mean that only sublation of what has been reached is determined in the tenth book, nor that only sublation of what has not been reached is determined here [in the sixth]. Thus, he rejects the claim of a fixed rule based on a lack of proof.

The sense is that, because the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice has its requirements satisfied by the two *ājyabhāga* offerings themselves— whose assistance is already established by the rule prescribing them again— the *gṛhamedhīya* does not require the assistance produced by the *prayāja*s and other elements. Consequently, there is an obstruction to the extended application (*atideśa*) that would bring those elements, and thus the *gṛhamedhīya* constitutes a case of "sublation of what was not otherwise obtained" (*aprāptabādha*).
"But in other cases," however.
Just as the *āhavanīya* fire, obtained through a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*), is set aside by a specific injunction (*viśeṣa-śāstra*),
or as the constant fifteen-fold recitation (*pāñcadaśya*) is set aside by the seventeen-fold recitation (*sāptadaśya*) occasioned by a Vaiśya;

and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the sublation of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) *kuśa* grass by the modified (*vaikṛta*) *śara* grass through the principle of "occupying the place" (*sthānāpatti*) and so forth— all such forms of sublation other than those mentioned in the Vārttika are included.
In this context, the meaning is "sublation of what has been attained."
Now, one might ask: how can there be a sublation of that which has been established by a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) and so forth?
For in this case, a sublation in the form of falsity—as in "this is not silver"—is not possible;
because the general rule is itself free from defects, the cognition produced by it cannot be false, as it is not generated by any defect.

If it is argued that even in the absence of a defect residing in the instrument (*karaṇa*), since the instrument actually possesses a cognition whose object exceeds the particularity (*viśeṣa*), the cognizer’s erroneous apprehension of that object as having such a nature can arise due to a defect of the cognizer consisting in negligence caused by the non-perception of the particularity; and thus, through the perception of the particularity, the falsity of that [erroneous cognition] is established.

Then, even in cases such as those involving *śruti* and *liṅga*, since no specific indication of being an auxiliary to the *gārhapatya* fire is perceived by the cognizer, there arises the possibility of a delusion regarding its being an auxiliary to Indra—this being mediated by the postulation of a *śruti* based on the mere observation of *liṅga*. Consequently, it might be argued that in all such instances there would result only a sublation of what has already been established (*prāptabādha*).
To dispel this doubt as to how there can be a sublation of what has not yet been established (*aprāptabādha*), he says: "And its true nature... (*tattvaṃ ca*).
Because that [nature] has been established.
For among the means of proof such as direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, a direct statement is not to be inferred from an indicative mark and the like;

because when there is a contradiction with a perceptible direct statement, such an inference is necessarily not postulated, and even if it were sometimes postulated, its falsity would simply be inferred by the perceptible direct statement.

The meaning is as follows: since the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) and so forth are already established, they cannot be newly postulated; furthermore, if one were to postulate their falsity, it would follow that there would be no *āhavanīya* fire in other *homa* offerings, making such a postulation impossible.

Therefore, because the general rule is merely restricted in its scope by the specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) and the like, it is logical that it constitutes a sublation of what was previously obtained (*prāpta-bādha*), due to the disparity between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*).
"It is being oppressed."

Furthermore, for one who has first perceived only the *pada-śāstra* (the science of word-formation), there can be no error regarding it through the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) that prescribes the formation of words; thus, its cessation does not occur upon the perception of a particular [exception], because the absence of the perception of a particular [exception] means the absence of the cause of error.
For this very reason, at that time, the general rule immediately realizes that its scope is restricted to objects other than those [exceptions].

In this regard, for one who has previously apprehended a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*), once an error has arisen due to the presence of its causal conditions (*sāmagrī*), that error ceases upon the perception of a particularity (*viśeṣa-darśana*).

Subsequently, it is only then that the [subsequent cognition] is understood to have a different object from that [previous one]. Therefore, the meaning is that the sublation (*bādha*) of the former results effectively as a consequence.

[Objection: But surely—then, in a case such as "He does not perform those two at the animal sacrifice," where the very purpose of the scripture is sublation (*bādha*), it would follow that when there is first an observation of the extended rule (*atideśa-śāstra*), one observes through the obtaining scripture (*prāpaka-śāstra*)—aided by the non-perception of specific qualifications—the erroneous application of even the *ājyabhāga* offerings;

and since the understanding of the prohibitory scripture (*niṣedha-śāstra*) is thus established, [the prohibition] would subsequently remain effective even when the specific qualifications are perceived. Thus, for the obtaining scripture...

Even though sublation (*bādha*), consisting in the conceptualization of an object distinct from that [prohibition], is possible, when the prohibitory scripture itself is first perceived, then— following the perception of its meaning and prior to the requirement for the attainment of the prohibited act— the general scripture is perceived; and because the specific [prohibitory] cognition exists at that time, it is impossible for a delusion regarding the *ājyabhāga* to arise, which would otherwise render the final determination of the prohibition untenable.
One must necessarily accept that the scripture which brings about [the performance] lacks the capacity to produce valid knowledge regarding the *ājyabhāga* offerings for the sake of prohibition.

Therefore, since in the case of a prohibition of what is established by scripture, it must be admitted that the "attainment" (*prāpti*) is of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*), for this very reason, in such instances, the Mīmāṃsakas accept an option (*vikalpa*). How then could there be sublation of the enjoining scripture by the sublatting scripture, given that the sublation is delimited by the status of being a sublation of what was already attained?
To dispel the doubt that the definition might still be possible due to the obstruction of its having itself as its object, he says: "In the same way, even where... and so forth.
He provides the answer: "Nevertheless... (tathāpi).

Since here attainment (*prāpti*) consists solely of the form of valid cognition (*pramā*), for this very reason, because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is admitted, even though in that alternative where the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are absent it is impossible for the prohibitory scripture to act as an obstacle by depending upon them, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the definition, because the general scripture is obstructed from applying to that specific case. This is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Even if there is sublation by a specific rule (viśeṣa-śāstra) according to this method, since the status of being a valid cognition (pramā) is still obtained from the general rule (sāmānya-śāstra), does this not lead to the contingency of an option (vikalpa)? To this, he says: "And as... (yathāca).
And this has already been established previously.

First of all, passion (*rāga*) does not possess the capacity to produce a valid cognition (*pramā*) that [the action] is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*).

This is because the occurrence of activity is accounted for by the assumption that the absence of the knowledge that [an action] is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence acts as an obstacle to activity, and thus it is the absence of that [knowledge] itself which is assumed to be the cause of activity; therefore, [the production of such a cognition by passion] is impossible.

However, where there is the production of a valid cognition regarding the aspect of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), there can be no contradiction with the understanding of it as a means to an undesired end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*) derived from a prohibition; therefore, the prohibition does not sublate that aspect.

As for the activity that occurs when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, that simply does not arise when the causal complex is absent; thus, the sublation by the prohibition in cases where a prohibition applies to what is prompted by desire (*rāga*) is merely a matter of chance (*daivavaśa*), and there is no option (*vikalpa*).

Likewise, here too, since the erroneous cognition that "the foot-offering (pada-homa) is a means to the desired end"—which was produced by the non-perception of a distinguishing feature—is removed by the perception of that distinguishing feature, it follows by implication that the cognition of the foot-offering as a means to the desired end in the Āhavanīya fire is also removed. Consequently, due to the absence of the causal complex [for action], there is no inclination toward the Āhavanīya fire; rather, the inclination occurs toward the foot-offering. Thus, by bringing about the absence of the causal complex, [the knowledge of the distinction] functions as an obstacle to an inclination that would otherwise have occurred spontaneously.
The meaning is that, regarding the negation, since it depends upon [the prior] attainment, it cannot be an error; thus, there is an option (vikalpa).
Thus, there is weakness of the subsequent and strength of the preceding among the means of knowledge, such as direct revelation (*śruti*) and the rest;
likewise when the subsequent is perceptual while the preceding is inferential, or when the subsequent is absolutely meaningless.

In that regard, "where, however, the direct revelation is inferential and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is perceptual, how is it [resolved]? As in the case of a conflict between a traditional rule (*smṛti*) and a Vedic indicative mark."
In this regard, while another basis for *smṛti* may be possible, such is not the case for *liṅga*; therefore, it is that [the *liṅga*] alone which must be followed as being stronger.

Following the method stated in the Vārttika—"Even if a weaker means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has some purpose that is contrary [to what is established], a sublation (*bādha*) should be applied"—it is intended that even when the other [the *liṅga*] is stronger, there is only "sublation of the unobtained" (*aprāptabādha*). With this in mind, he concludes the two-fold nature of sublation by saying: "Therefore, it is established."

In this context, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* has cited the marriage to a maternal uncle’s daughter as an example of scriptural inference (*ānumānika-śruti*) being sublated by perceptible evidence (*acapratyakṣa-liṅga*).
The refutation of that [position] is to be found in the *Kaustubha* itself within the section on Smṛti;
however, another example must be sought.
The examples of futility (*ānarthakya*), causality (*hetuka*), and the predominance of the contrary (*viparītaprābalya*) are to be seen in the *Vārttika* and the *Kaustubha*.
The purpose (*prayojana*) has not been stated here because it is obvious.
For the sake of preserving the tradition, as far as the power of one's intellect extends,
the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* has been explained, culminating in the investigation of strengths and weaknesses.
Thus ends the seventh section, on the relative strength and weakness [of arguments].

— — — — — — (B1) (Section 8 / [a.3 pā.3 adhi.8]) "Or rather, it is *ahīna* because of the context; it is secondary. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.15). Having thus determined the relative strength of conflicting authorities, the subsequent detailed exposition, extending until the end of the chapter, is intended to investigate where such conflict exists and where it does not.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, after prescribing the Upasad rites, it is heard in scripture: "There are exactly three Upasads for the Sāhna [one-day sacrifice], but twelve for the Ahīna [multi-day sacrifice].
Regarding this, there arises a deliberation as to whether the number twelve is to be incorporated into the Dvādaśāha (the twelve-day sacrifice) or into the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself.

First, regarding the number three, since it is enjoined by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *upasad* offerings, it serves the purpose of the *upasad* which is a means to its own transcendental result (*apūrva*), according to the principle of vocal restraint (*vāṅniyama*).

Furthermore, because the *upasad* offerings are understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) to be subsidiaries of the Jyotiṣṭoma alone, the word "sāhnā" is merely a restatement [of the fact] that they are completed in a single day; it is not a qualifying attribute of the thing being referred to (*uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa*).

Because it would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and because it would be redundant (*vaiyarthyāt*), the number twelve— being enjoined by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to that very same thing— is for the sake of the *upasad* offerings alone. Nor is there an injunction of it with respect to the *ahīna* sacrifice as its subject.
Because that [number] is heard as being subordinate to the *upasads*, its connection with the *ahīna* sacrifice is untenable;
furthermore, because the number twelve is established through its repetition,
and because it is already obtained there by another statement read within the context of the *dvādaśāha*.
Therefore, this [term] is also optionally interpreted as a triad.

Furthermore, the term *ahīna*—accepting it as a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) based on etymologies such as "that which is not deficient" (*na hīyate*)—is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma;
for all other sacrifices, being modifications (*vikṛti*), do not abandon it, as they depend upon it.

Now, this is not a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*); for if it were so, it would be a *tatpuruṣa*, and by the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa*, the first member retains its original accent when it is a word meaning 'equal,' a third-case word, a seventh-case word, a comparative, an indeclinable, a second-case word, or a gerundive" (Pāṇini 6.2.2), together with the continued application of the rule "the first member [retains its] original form," the negative particle *nañ*—being an indeclinable as the first member—would necessarily result in being acute-accented on the first syllable.

Rather, because it has the middle syllable acute, [it must be a different formation], according to the rule "The suffix *kha* is added after *ahan* in the sense of a sacrifice" (Pāṇini 5.1.107), together with the continued application of the rule "a collection thereof" (Pāṇini 4.2.37).

Since the word *ahaḥ*— which denotes a collection of sacrifices— is prescribed to have the suffix *khap* [added to it], and since that suffix is subject to the substitution rule of the traditional grammar (*smṛti*) stating, “*āyan*, *enī*, *īy*, and *īyi* are the substitutes for the initial sounds of suffixes beginning with *pha*, *ḍha*, *kha*, *cha*, and *gha*,” this word ends in the suffix *khap*. Consequently, by the rule “and [the suffix] is udātta-accented on its first syllable” (*ādyudāttaśca*), the high-pitched accent (*udātta-svara*) is established for the vowel *ī* at the beginning of the suffix.
If it is argued that this cannot be a *nañ*-compound because the substitute *in*— being a constituent of the *ādeśa*— cannot be a constituent of the suffix *kha*,

since the traditional rule (*smṛti*) states, "The mention of 'as if taught' (*upadeśivad-vacanam*) regarding forms like *āyana* is for the sake of establishing the accent," and thus the substitute *in* is also treated as being "as if taught" at the time of the suffix's teaching in order to establish the accent of the suffix;
therefore, this is not a *nañ*-compound.
Nevertheless, in accordance with the context, the term *ahīna* is justified as being used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*) for the Jyotiṣṭoma on account of its similarity in having multiple days.

However, in reality, since the property of being a collection of sacrifices accomplished over days—which serves as the delimiting factor of the primary meaning (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—exists in the Jyotiṣṭoma as well, insofar as it consists of a series of repetitions, the term *ahīna* can be understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*) in its primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*). This being the position reached: let us set aside the word *ahīna* for a moment.

The particle *eva* (only/just) itself, by reiterating that numbers other than three lack the status of being the means [of accomplishment], does not tolerate an option with respect to the number twelve.

Furthermore, since the connection of both the triad and the dodecad with the Jyotiṣṭoma would be established through the context (*prakaraṇa*) alone in this way, it would follow that both the words *sāhna* and *ahīna* are redundant.

However, in this view, because a rite completed in a single day is a small action, a small number alone is appropriate; thus, the word *sāhna* is not redundant, as it serves as a praise based on such appropriateness.
Furthermore, since two numbers cannot have the same referent, a difference in words is not appropriate within a single injunction;
therefore, there is no dispute that the word *ahīna* refers to something other than the *sāhna*.

And this is logical, because of the traditional rule (smṛti): "The suffix *kha* is applied after *ahan* [to form a compound] when denoting a sacrifice," in conjunction with the continued application (anuvṛtti) of the rule "the suffix *ka* is applied after a word meaning a collection thereof."

Furthermore, because of Vedic usage, the term *ahīna*—through its etymological-technical (*yogarūḍhi*) meaning—is understood to have as its delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) the very nature of being a specific sacrifice accomplished by a collection of days, which excludes the *satra* and others, and which consists of a collection of *sutyā* rites enjoined by the injunction of the root *yajati*. Therefore, it is impossible for the number twelve to be applied to the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
Consequently, there is an injunction of the number twelve with reference to the *upasads* connected with the *ahīna*.

Furthermore, since in the case of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) the ancient masters maintain that mutual relationship is grammatically established (*vyutpanna*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) when referring to a qualified object. In reality, however, because the twelve-fold number of *upasads* is already obtained through extension (*atideśa*) by reference to the *ahīna* sacrifice, this sentence— preceding [the application of the rule]— prescribes the twelve-fold number itself as the result of obtaining that [number], just as in the injunction "that [cup] with four [verses]."

The intention of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) is that another statement found in the section on the *dvādaśāha* is not contradictory, either because it belongs to a different recension (*śākhāntarīya*) or because it pertains to the *satra* sacrifice in general.

In reality, however, since the statement in the *dvādaśāha* section applies commonly to both the *satra* and the *ahīna*, the attainment of the number twelve is established even for the *ahīna*. Therefore, for the sake of achieving syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) and for the meaningfulness of its placement within the context (*prakaraṇapāṭha*), it is appropriate [to interpret it accordingly].
This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) specifically for the injunction regarding the number three;
it is a praise stating that a large number is appropriate for a great rite, but not for the one under discussion (the *prakṛti*).

Therefore, since the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the syntactical connection (*vākya*), and the number twelve is understood as being connected with the *ahīna* sacrifice, the number twelve does not apply to the *jyotiṣṭoma* by virtue of that context.

However, it should be understood that in the root [text], the objection regarding the contradiction between direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) is raised by taking recourse to the figurative nature of the genitive case. // 3.42 //
Thus ends the eighth section concerning the deficiency of the earth.
(B2) (B1) (Section 9 / [a.3 pā.3 adhi.9]) Duality and Plurality.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, having prescribed the obligatory *pratipad* with the verse "Sing forth to him, O men" (*upāsmai gāyatā nara*), the scripture states: "One should use 'For you two are the lords of heaven' (*yuvaṃ hi sthaḥ svarpatī*) as the *pratipad* for two sacrificers,
and 'These drops have been poured forth' (*ete asṛgram indavaḥ*) for many sacrificers."
In that regard, if in the first sentence the phrase "of two sacrificers" (*yajamānayoḥ*) contains a locative case ending, then it refers to them as a causal condition (*nimitta*);
even though there is the hearing of a separate case-ending.

Nevertheless, according to the principle of the *Havirārti* section, since there is no possibility of being merely optional, the status of being a cause does not terminate with each [condition] individually; rather, in accordance with the requirement that the primary cause must be present, it is established that the status of being a cause belongs only to the two combined as delimited by duality and delimited by the state of being the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
However, if it were a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*),...

Being a restatement of the relationship known as "eligibility" (*adhikāritva*), and in order to avoid its own redundancy, it accepts figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in both terms. Due to parsimony (*lāghava*), there is a single basis for the co-occurrence (*vyāsajyavṛtti-nimittatva*) of duality and the state of being the sacrificer (*yajamānatva*), because there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanā-viraha*) to determine which is the qualifier and which is the qualified. Similarly, in the expression "for many sacrificers," the dative case (*tādarthya-caturthī*)—which likewise restates the relationship of eligibility—also possesses figurative indication with respect to the aforementioned basis.
Consequently, there is no contingency of either [the *pratipad* or the *mantra*] being unintended.

Furthermore, even though the mantra is prescribed with reference to the *pratipad* as its specific occasion (*nimitta*), because they are of different classes (*vijātīyatva*), there is no plurality of intended objects.
Thus, there is no dispute regarding both positions: that the connection with the *pratipad* is obtained either through explicit mention or through the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Thus, when considering whether these two mantras are to be inserted into the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, or into sacrifices such as the Kulāya and Ahīna which have two or more sacrificers, the conclusion is that they are inserted into the archetype (prakṛti) alone, because there is no contradiction with the context (prakaraṇa).

Nor is there an absence of a causal condition (nimitta) there; for by the verbal form in "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring," the [number of] agents is mentioned as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (upādeya).

Even if there is an intention [to use the singular], since it will be stated later that the application of "according to one's ability" (*yathāśakti*) applies to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* by virtue of its being a permanent rite (*nitya*), if one person is unable [to perform it alone], then two or more sacrificers would be obtained; thus, the prescription of the *pratipad* (introductory verse) is possible.

Alternatively, since the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) denotes anyone who performs a sacrifice and can therefore apply to the wife as well, there is no obstacle to its feminine gender in the first sentence; hence, when there are two wives, that mantra [is used].

Regarding the second sentence as well, since it is impossible for the context (*prakaraṇa*) to be set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) according to the principle of the *pāśādhikaraṇa*, the grammatical instruction for the substitution of genders (*vyatyayānuśāsana*) indicates that the masculine gender refers to the feminine; thus, the second mantra applies when there is a plurality of wives. However, it is argued that the first mantra is obligatory (*nityā*) when there is only one wife. To this, we reply: even though the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is obligatory, the rule of acting according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti-nyāya*) does not apply to the number [of wives], which is fixed at one.

In the sentences concerning the origin [of the sacrifice] and so forth, that [number] is connected to the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) by virtue of the scriptural indication of co-referentiality (*samānābhidhāna-śruti*). Because it is internal to the *bhāvanā*, when there is an incapacity [to perform the whole], it is this very [number] that must be accommodated by subverting other subsidiaries such as the measure of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

Furthermore, the application of "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśakti*) attaches only to that which is enjoined as something to be performed because it is achievable through human effort (*kṛti-sādhya*), and not to things like time which are not to be performed.
Therefore, just like that [time], this [number] also does not fall within the scope of that principle; thus, duality and plurality do not apply to the sacrifice under discussion.

Furthermore, the word *yajamāna* does not refer to the wife (*patnī*); for since its primary usage is restricted to males, its denotative power (*śakti*) is understood as such, and there is no evidence for resorting to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Moreover, it is untenable to accept a grammatical rule for a deviation from the norm (*vyatyaya*)—which is only permissible when there is no other recourse—since the masculine form *yajamānebhyaḥ* and the pronoun *prāsmāi* (in *prāsmāi agnim bharata*) are prohibited in the case of the ewe (*meṣī*), just as they are in the case of the *maitrāvaruṇī* cow.

And therefore, since there is sublation of the context by the sentence, its displacement occurs only in those cases where the dual or plural number is explicitly prescribed for the *kulāya*, *ahīna*, and other sacrifices—such as in the statement: "The king and the domestic priest, desiring union, should sacrifice with this [rite]; one, two, or many should sacrifice. Nor is there an absence here of anything that brings that specific sacrifice to mind.

Since the general connection with the sacrifice is understood through the very connection with the *pratipad*, there is no obstacle to the specific [connection] being established by the force of the occasion (*nimitta*). // 3 // 43 //
Thus ends the ninth section, concerning the superiority of the first lunar day.
(10th Topic / [A.3 Pā.3 Adh.10]) And the tail [is subsidiary], because it is a part [of the animal]. Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.20.
In the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings within the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, [the tail is mentioned].
It is heard in the scripture: "One should perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with the tail.

In this regard, does this sentence enjoin the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings by referring to the tail produced as a by-product of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice? And consequently, is there a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of this injunction from its context (*prakaraṇa*)?

Furthermore, in the deliberation as to whether the substance is enjoined as the tail (*jāghanī*) with reference to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, [the conclusion is as follows]: Since the word *jāghanī*, like the words "upper half" (*uttarārdha*) and so forth, denotes a substance that is a single part [of a larger whole], it is understood that the tail is already employed for another purpose; and since its utility is thus established, it is understood to be the object of reference (*uddeśya*), similar to the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings. Therefore, even by accepting an indication of the accusative case-meaning by the instrumental suffix (*tṛtīyā*), the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings themselves are enjoined with reference to that [tail].
And thus, by accepting the second type of injunction (*vidhi*), there is parsimony (*lāghava*);
otherwise, there would be the contingency of falling into the third type of injunction.

And so, since the syntactical connection (*vākya*) sublates the context (*prakaraṇa*), even though only the status of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings as subsidiary to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) is understood, [the text continues] with "by means of clarified butter (*ājyena*)..."
Since the injunction "one should perform the *saṃyājya* offerings for the wives" would otherwise be rendered meaningless, it cannot be set aside by the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore,

although the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice is understood to be a subsidiary part of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices by virtue of being a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), the injunction of this [offering] as a direct auxiliary (*sannipatyopakāraka*) and a subsidiary of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice through this specific statement is not untenable.

And since it is possible even in common worldly experience for the tail (*jāghanī*) to be produced as a byproduct of an animal employed for another purpose, how can its connection to a sacrifice be established—given the absence of an invariable relationship with a *kratu* (sacrifice)—through the sentence "They perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with the tail" (*jāghanyā patnīḥ saṃyājayanti*), which is heard within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] and prescribes the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with reference to the tail that serves as a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the rite under discussion? [The answer is: Just as in the case of the statement "He takes the *aṃśu* [cup]," even though this [sentence regarding the tail] is studied outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), its connection to a sacrifice is established through that other sentence.
This is because the understanding of a connection with the sacrifice (*kratu*) is logically established.

As for the claim made by some—that since the connection of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*) is understood through extension (*atideśa*) alone, the contextual sentence must, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), enjoin a separate ritual action possessing those same characteristics—that is incorrect;

for even if the connection of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with the animal sacrifice is understood through extension as being an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), there is an absence of anything that indicates such a specific intention (*tātparya*).

In the case of this sentence studied as an independent statement (*anārabhyādhīta*), since there is no means of proof for the presentation of the *jāghanī* (tail) as belonging to that [sacrifice], and because its proximity is established through extension (*atideśa*), it is impossible for it to be a separate rite due to the absence of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*); thus, it has been set aside.
Therefore, since the context is sublated by the sentence, this injunction is transferred to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Although the word *jāghanī* denotes a part of an animal, it lacks a correlative relationship like words such as "the upper half" (*uttarārdha*).

Therefore, since it is possible to enjoin the *jāghanī* established in common worldly usage— such as that found in a marketplace— for the purpose of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, just like clarified butter (*ājya*),
there is no justification for accepting a metaphorical sense (*lakṣaṇā*) for the instrumental case-ending.

Furthermore, since the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), their status as remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) would be set aside by the sentence situated within the context of the animal sacrifice (*paśu-prakaraṇa*), thereby resulting in the attainment of their status as direct auxiliaries (*sannipatyopakāraka*). Consequently, the sentence situated within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-prakaraṇa*) would become redundant. Therefore, the injunction for the tail (*jāghanī*) is indeed made with reference to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings themselves. Nor should it be argued: "If, by way of restating an already established action, one were to enjoin the wives (*patnī*) as well, then even if the attainment [of the wives] as deities (*devatā*) is raised, there would still be the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the injunction of a qualified object. This is because [the wives] are not enjoined as deities, but rather as those who are to be honored. Thus, there is no syntactical split. Furthermore, the word "wives" (*patnī*) is used here in its primary sense (*mukhya-vṛtti*), whereas in the original injunction, it is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa-vṛtti*). Therefore, the injunction is valid. It is not the case that the word "wives" is used in a secondary sense here, while in the original injunction it is used in its primary sense; rather, the opposite is true. Hence, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the word "wives" is used in its primary sense in both the original injunction and this [present] injunction. Consequently, the injunction of the tail with reference to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings is established. Thus, the view of the *Tantravārttika* is correct. This concludes the discussion on the tail. Since the specific ritual action can be understood through the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) itself, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*);
