(11th Adhikaraṇa / [A.3 Pā.3 Adhi.11]) Santardana (joining together) should exist in the archetype, as in the case of the purchase, because there is no loss of purpose.

Regarding the two pressing-boards (*abhiṣavaṇaphalaka*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma, after prescribing non-joining with the statement, "He does not join them together," the text then prescribes joining with the statement, "But indeed, in a long Soma sacrifice, they should be joined together for the sake of stability."
It has been prescribed.
"Santardana" (joining) means the joining of one plank upon another by thinning them at the point of contact between the two planks.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether this *santardana* pertains solely to the context (*prakaraṇa*) or is displaced (*utkṛṣyate*) to all sacrifices other than the *agniṣṭoma*: [the conclusion is that] because it favors the context, there is no displacement.
Nor is there a contradiction of the scriptural statement;
for even the Jyotiṣṭoma, in comparison with the iṣṭis and other sacrifices, possesses length, and because its substance is Soma, the designation "long-Soma" (dīrghasoma) is appropriate.
Consequently, in that very context, there is an option between tightening and not tightening the joints, just as in the case of rice and barley.

As for the example of "buying" (*kraya*) given here in the Sūtra regarding the alternative (*vikalpa*), it should be understood as being based on the absence of a scriptural statement, since a combination (*samuccaya*) will be stated in the twelfth [book] by the injunction, "He buys with ten. Alternatively, since the *iṣṭi* and other rites are not mentioned here, and since length is constant with respect to them, the term "long *soma*" (*dīrghasoma*) would result in redundancy; thus, the alternative (*vikalpa*) is vitiated by the eight defects.

Furthermore, because a long [duration] for the sacrificer is illogical, one may accept even a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound—namely, "the Soma of the long sacrificer" (*dīrghasoma*)—in accordance with the context; thus, the rule for splitting the sacrificial post (*santardana*) is prescribed on the basis of the sacrificer's length as the occasion.
However, if, according to the principle of the section on the *niṣādasthapati*, a *karmadhāraya* compound alone is more logical, then [it would be] by the length of the sacrificer...

Furthermore, since there is a risk of the wooden boards splitting, it is impossible for the praise of *santardana* (the joining together) to function as a means to that end; thus, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "for support" would be untenable. Therefore, the term *dīrghasoma* is accepted as a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "a long soma. Nevertheless, because the increase in the quantity of soma to be offered is necessary due to the increase in the number of offerings when the Jyotiṣṭoma itself is joined with other terminuses (*saṃsthā*) such as the *ukthya*, the status of being a "long soma" is established. Consequently, the injunction finds its place [in the Jyotiṣṭoma] because there is no conflict between the syntactical connection (*vākya*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Nor can the increase in the quantity of the gift be accomplished by means of water and so forth;
for, in the absence of an explicit scriptural statement, it is impossible to perform a sacrifice whose substance is Soma using Soma mixed with another substance.
Furthermore, there is no sublation of the prescribed measure of Soma, characterized as consisting of three joints and ten handfuls.

Because there is no sublation [of the general rule] by the grasping of thick and long *soma* stalks, for this very reason, since there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a sacrifice by the word *soma*, it can also be said that the state of having thick and long *soma* stalks is itself the occasion (*nimitta*) for the joining together (*santardana*). In reality, however, after the grasping of the *soma* measured as three joints and ten handfuls, [the text says]: "He gathers the remaining stalks together."

Because of the injunction for collecting [the remains] there, and because in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"If the Soma were only as much as he measures out, it would belong to the sacrificer alone and not to the members of the assembly"—the previously mentioned measure is censured; and since, like the subsequent milking, it is understood to refer to whatever is required, the rule of the *kapiñjala* section does not apply. Thus, due to the absence of a fixed limit, an increase in the quantity of the offering is easily established.

And even so, since the *agniṣṭoma* termination is a subsidiary (*aṅga*), while the other three optional terminations are modifications (*vikṛti*), they lack an inherent context (*prakaraṇa*) of their own; furthermore, because there is no increase in the number of offerings (*pradāna*) in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, there is no increase in the quantity of the substance to be offered (*pradeya*).
How, then, can there be no contradiction between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*)?

It must be stated that in the case of the optional *saṃsthās*, because an increase in the number of extractions (*graha*) necessitates an increase in the performance (*abhyāsa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma which serves as their substrate, and because—even though the four *saṃsthās* themselves lack an independent context (*prakaraṇa*)—the Jyotiṣṭoma is woven through all of them, it is logical that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is upheld by the injunction for *santardana* (joining) within the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma when it takes on an optional *saṃsthā*.

For this very reason, in the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma with the *agniṣṭoma* *saṃsthā*, there is no *asantardana* (non-joining), since there is no increase in the offering; thus, there is no optionality (*vikalpa*) either.

For this very reason, there is extreme simplicity, since the long-form Jyotiṣṭoma—the correlate (*anuyogin*)—and the short-form Jyotiṣṭoma—the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—are both obtained from the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself.
Nor is it the case that, if the other forms of the Jyotiṣṭoma were likewise accepted as being within the context, [the following scriptural statement would be contradicted]:
"This indeed is the first of sacrifices, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma; he who, having not sacrificed with this, sacrifices with another, falls into a pit."

It should not be argued that even in the phrase "it becomes that" (*tadbhavati*), because the word "this" (*etad*) would result in the inclusion of the Jyotiṣṭoma with other terminuses (*saṃsthā*), it would contradict the statement to be made later— that only the Agniṣṭoma-terminus is to be understood due to the context (*prakaraṇa*).
This is because the context is accepted precisely on the grounds that [the fruit] belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma as such, without being restricted by any specific terminus.

Furthermore, it is because it is untenable for [the other *saṃsthās*] to be delimited by the context as subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) of the *agniṣṭoma* *saṃsthā*, just like the other subsidiary elements. For even though the word "this" (*etad*) denotes that which is delimited by the nature of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the word "other" (*anya*), which denotes all its modifications (*vikṛti*), also denotes the *saṃsthās*; thus, since there is an understanding of an injunction for those [modifications] to occur after the *jyotiṣṭoma*, it follows by implication that [the rule applies] specifically to that which has the *agniṣṭoma* *saṃsthā*.

Since the performance [of the act] is possible for the first time [only in this context], and because there is thus no contradiction between the syntactical connection (*vākya*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), it follows that the *santardana* (the joining together) should find its place within the context itself—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). However, the author of the Bhāṣya has established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by simply accepting this very position as the desired outcome; and the prima facie argument was formulated according to the first two methods mentioned above.

The author of the Vārttika, however, has stated that [the term *dīrghasoma*] applies only to modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) in which there is an increase in Soma. His intention is as follows: first of all, you yourself have no dispute that "length" (*dīrghatva*) is produced by an increase in Soma resulting from an increase in the number of vessels (*graha*). Furthermore, these increased vessels are subsidiaries of the *saṃsthās* (sacrificial forms) due to specific scriptural injunctions, and not subsidiaries of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself.
Therefore, because the state of being a *dīrghasoma* lacks a direct connection with the *jyotiṣṭoma*, it refers exclusively to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

Nor can it be argued that even if the aforementioned cups lack the status of being limbs of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, they are connected to it by way of the sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthā*), and thus the state of being a *dīrghasoma* is established for that [sacrifice];

for in cases such as the *sarvatomukha*, where there are various terminuses like the *agniṣṭoma* in the eastern and other directions, the state of being a *dīrghasoma* would apply to the other direction.

Because of its existence, even in the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice, there is the attainment of *santardana* (joining together); for wherever there is an increase in the quantity of the offering material (*pradeya*) necessitated by an increase in the number of vessels (*aṅga-grahaṇa*), or wherever there is an increase in the offering material necessitated by that [increase], there the injunction for *santardana* is understood as being for the purpose of purifying the substance that serves as the means to the *apūrva*. And since such an increase is necessitated by the specific sacrificial form (*saṃsthā*) rather than by the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself, it does not pertain to the *jyotiṣṭoma* as a subordinate part (*aṅga*).

Alternatively, because the injunction for *santardana* (separating the two poles) would otherwise be untenable, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the direct statement (*vākya*), and thus it finds application only in all modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) of the aforementioned type,
and not in the *saṃsthās* alone; for since those are themselves modifications, they lack a distinct context.

Therefore, since the root *saṃtṛd* (to pierce) is transitive, it is understood from the immediately following accusative case-ending that the *phalaka* (wooden board) alone is the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*). Consequently, because it is impossible for "one who has performed a long *soma*-sacrifice" (*dīrghasoma*) to be either the objective referent (*uddeśya*) or a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it can only function as a conditional cause (*nimitta*).

For this very reason, this is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound, nor is it a *tatpuruṣa* compound—even one where the word *soma* would metaphorically indicate the sacrifice (*yāga*)—whereby the accent would fall on the first member.

Rather, having spoken of the creeper itself by means of that [word], it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound; and because it is a compound, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) even though there is a specific qualification regarding the cause or the intended object. // 3 / 45 //
Thus ends the eleventh section concerning the *santardana* (joining together).

(Section 12 / [A.3 Pā.3 Adhi.12]) That which is associated with a number should belong to the sacrifice because of the context. Jaimini 3.3.32. The *Pravargya* rite, studied as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), is heard in the scripture: "When they perform the *Pravargya*."
And regarding that [Pravargya], there is an application as a subsidiary of the Jyotiṣṭoma in the statement: "One performs the Pravargya before the Upasads";
for its presence [in the context] is established by the principle of non-redundancy (*dviruktatva*), assisted by the fact that it has an invariable connection with the sacrifice.
Nor should it be argued: "Why could it not rather be a subsidiary of the Upasads?"—because...

Furthermore, because the word *upasad*—which presents its own meaning as being correlative to time—cannot serve to provide the subject (*uddeśya*), and because it is already present [in the context], one might argue that a separate word denoting it must be assumed to accept it as the subject. However, since the presence of the *jyotiṣṭoma* is necessary for the purpose of knowing that the *upasads* possess a result, it is more parsimonious (lāghava) to conclude that [the mention of the *jyotiṣṭoma*] is for that very purpose;
moreover, the *pravargya* is mentioned within the very context of the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa.
And in that regard, it is heard in the Śruti: "One should not renounce [the world] at the first sacrifice.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether the term "first sacrifice" (prathamayajña) denotes the Jyotiṣṭoma in all its forms and stages, or merely its very first performance: the word "first sacrifice" refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma because of its grammatical coordination [with the word "sacrifice"] in the passage, "This indeed is the first of sacrifices, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma."
This is because it is performed first and because its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) exists.

Although—since the various sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthā*) are denoted by other terms and the injunction regarding them specifies that they follow the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—the *Jyotiṣṭoma* as a whole, comprising all its terminuses, is not necessarily performed first;

nevertheless, since that [status of being performed first] exists insofar as it is co-referential with the generic property of being a *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there is no obstruction to its status as the basis for application.
Therefore, based on this statement and the context, this prohibition— or rather, this exclusion (*paryudāsa*)— applies specifically to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice,
meaning that one performs the *pravargya* rite in a sacrifice other than the Jyotiṣṭoma;
otherwise, an option (*vikalpa*) would result.
As for the statement, "One chooses the priests at the Agniṣṭoma," it serves as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to what has been excluded.
Furthermore, that [rule] is restricted by the passage, "But one who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) and a *śrotriya* may, at his pleasure, choose them.
Therefore, for one who is both learned in the Vedas and a *śrotriya*, the performance [of choosing the priests] is obligatory in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice when it concludes with the Agniṣṭoma form.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, however, there is non-performance [of the *prathamayajña*] as a rule; whereas in the *vikṛtis*, its performance is mandatory. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the following is established]: since the comprehension of the meaning is possible through the individual capacities [of the words], there is no evidence for postulating an additional capacity. Furthermore, because the word *prathama* denotes that which prompts what has not yet been performed, it is understood to refer to the first performance; thus, the word *yajña* [in *prathamayajña*] refers to that initial performance.

And by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), having accepted that the word is directed toward the performance due to the context— or rather, that it is directed specifically toward the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice—

the term "first sacrifice" denotes the first performance of the *jyotiṣṭoma*. And that [first performance] belongs to the *jyotiṣṭoma* which has the *agniṣṭoma* as its final form (*saṃsthā*), according to the principle of the fifth book (*pāñcamika-nyāya*).
Because of the statement, "The sacrificer should first sacrifice with the Atirātra," and because [the Pravargya] belongs to that which has the Atirātra as its concluding form,
this statement effects either a prohibition or an exclusion of the Pravargya in both cases,
but not in other modified forms (vikṛti).
In that regard, [the rule] does not apply there because it is not obtained through either direct instruction (*upadeśa*) or extended application (*atideśa*).

Nor should it be argued: "Since 'firstness' (*prāthamya*) is intended with reference to the first performance in relation to the second and subsequent performances in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and since such 'firstness' exists in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) as well in relation to its second and subsequent performances, how is it that [the rule] is not obtained there?"—this must not be said.
Since the requirement for a referent of "primacy" (prāthamya) cannot be satisfied by imagining the second or subsequent performances as its referents—
and because the scriptural statement, "This indeed is the first of sacrifices," restricts that primacy to the *jyotiṣṭoma* and its modifications alone—
it must be understood that the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself is the subject of the first performance.

And thus, by means of conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*)— supported both by the remainder of the sentence and by Vedic usage— the term *prathamayajña* (first sacrifice) denotes specifically the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice as characterized by primacy relative to other Soma sacrifices.

Otherwise, if it were to denote any sacrifice whatsoever that is characterized by primacy relative to its own second or subsequent performances, there would result the undesirable consequence that in such injunctions as "Those who have established the sacred fires and have performed their first sacrifice should perform a sacrificial session (*satra*) with seventeen householders," the mere sacrifice [in general] would follow immediately after [the first performance].
Therefore, the prohibition of the *pravargya* rite applies only to the first performance of the two aforementioned types of *jyotiṣṭoma*.

In reality, however, this is not a prohibition; for if it were, then—just as in the case of the statement "one does not perform those two at the animal sacrifice"—there would result an option (*vikalpa*) even regarding the first day of the *atirātra* sacrifice.
Nor is there an option in cases such as those mentioned, where there is a prohibition of an action either in its own form or in its relation to a specific objective.

However, in cases where there is a prohibition of the *kāraka* (the factor of action), such as "One should not perform the *śrāddha* at night," since the prohibition pertains solely to the *kāraka* and does not pertain to the action itself, it is impossible for it to give rise to an option regarding an injunction whose object is the action;
and in the present case, the word "first sacrifice" (*prathamayajña*) does not have the sense of being the thing to be designated (*uddeśya*).
However, some have argued that this is a case of the locus as a grammatical factor (*kāraka*), just as in the expression "the *prātaḥsavana* [rite] is low-pitched" (*mandram prātaḥsavana*).
They claim that, consequently, there is no risk of falling into a logical dilemma (*vikalpa*). This must be rejected;

for even if the locus of the first performance were obtained through an injunction as a grammatical factor, by parity of reasoning, it would necessarily follow that the locus of the first performance itself would result in a dilemma.

For this very reason, since the attainment of some unspecified time through implication involves the optional adoption of night—which, being attained through desire, lacks the status of a mandatory rule—the prohibition thereof does not result in an option.
In the present case, however, the status of being the locus for the first performance is not optional, because the connection of the subordinate element with each primary is mandatory.
Therefore, even its prohibition necessarily results in an option.

In reality, however, since it is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* that the very object of the first performance is what is intended, this [objection] is of no consequence. Therefore, like the statement "not at the *anūyāja*s," this is merely an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) as a supplement to the unattached injunction (*anārabhyavāda*), meaning: "one should perform the *pravargya* in a case other than the aforementioned first performance.

Consequently, since there would otherwise be the contingency of non-performance during the first performance due to a lack of an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its application, the text states: "one performs the *pravargya* in the *agniṣṭoma*."

Although this statement, in reality, brings about what was absolutely unattained, it serves as a counter-exception (pratiprasava) for the purpose of prescribing the Pravargya rite as a mandatory rule even in the first performance, provided that the Agniṣṭoma is the concluding form (saṃsthā);
it is not, however, optional.
Because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
and because this [construction] does not have another object— since it is already established everywhere by the general rule— it has as its object only the subject matter of the first application.
And by this, the conclusion of the statement beginning with "kāmam" (if one so desires) is reached.
Therefore, in the first performance of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice, it must be performed as a constant duty by one who is *anūcāna*;
likewise, so too by one who is *śrotriya*.
An *anūcāna* is a teacher of the Veda.
By this, there is the exclusion of the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya.
A *śrotriya* is one who knows the Veda and its meaning with excellence;
for the word *kāmaṃ* denotes excellence.
Furthermore, because both agents are prescribed by the single word "tasya" (of him), there is no multiplicity of things to be enjoined (*vidheya*).
Consequently, for others, there is a permanent non-performance even when the first day of the *agniṣṭoma* is being undertaken.

As for what was stated in the Vārttika—that there is an option for those who have studied the Vedas (*anūcāna*) and others, while for others there is permanent non-performance—[that refers to a different context].
That is merely an overstatement.
For this very reason, Pārthasārathi stated that the application [of the term] for those who have studied the Vedas (*anūcāna*) and others is indeed constant.

However, if there is a persistent insistence that that very point must be justified, then one may certainly justify it by saying that since the option is expressed by the word itself and the *agniṣṭoma* sentence is restricted (*upasaṃhāra*) by that [word], there is an option (*vikalpa*) for those who have studied the Vedas and the rest.
In every case, since there is no counter-exception regarding the first performance of the Atirātra, its non-performance is indeed constant;
however, it is established that in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), its performance is constant during the first performance. // 3 // 46 //
Thus ends the twelfth section concerning the Pravargya rite.

(Thirteenth Adhikaraṇa / [A.3 Pā.3 Adhi.13]) The pounding for Pūṣan should be understood as applying to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because it is not enjoined in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Jaimini 3.3.34.
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in scripture: "Pūṣan has a portion of ground flour, for he is toothless."

In this regard, when considering whether there is an injunction for a separate ritual as an auxiliary to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves, or rather an injunction for mere grinding in a sacrifice dedicated to the deity Pūṣan— the former is not the case, because it would result in the violation of the principle of "single thrust" (*ekaprasaratā*) by taking the sacrifice indicated by the word *bhāga* (share) as the objective, and because it would also result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if [the sacrifice] were qualified by the term *pūṣan*.
Furthermore, it is because grinding—which has as its subordinate element the substance that is the referent of the *kta* suffix—is logically incapable of being connected with the sacrifice.

For this very reason, the word *pūṣan* alone cannot be intended to designate either its own primary meaning or a sacrifice dedicated to the deity Pūṣan (which is indicated by that primary meaning); for there is no evidence for the cognition of the sacrifice, since Pūṣan lacks an invariable connection with the ritual (*kratu*).
Therefore, since it might be argued that this is indeed an injunction for a different ritual action qualified by specific qualities, substances, and deities— [we reply]: By the term *prapiṣṭabhāga*,

through the etymological derivation meaning "that which has a portion (*bhāga*) to be partaken of or served (*bhajanīya*"), even though actual service is impossible, a mere relationship between the ground flour (*prapiṣṭa*) and Pūṣan is understood, as evidenced by common usage such as "the property of a deity" (*devasva*).
Both parties are in agreement on this much: that since that [result] is not possible without a sacrifice, it leads to the inference of a sacrifice.

Furthermore, it has already been understood from the outset that, given the possibility of the mere qualifier [being established], it is improper to postulate a qualified injunction and so forth; thus, due to the absence of evidence, there is no inference of another, unprecedented sacrifice.

Consequently, when a sacrifice is being inferred, the presentation of it as a sacrifice to the deity Pūṣan—well-known through its connection with the inferring factor, namely Pūṣan—is also easily attained.

And therefore, since it is precisely the inference of a specific sacrifice that serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the word *pūṣan* refers to the deity Pūṣan who is the means for producing a distinct type of transcendental result (*apūrva*).

And it is with reference to him alone that the state of having ground flour as the substance is enjoined—this being the meaning of the compound *prapiṣṭabhāga*—through its relationship of being the material for the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) produced by the sacrifice itself.

Furthermore, just as there can be an injunction of a deity with reference to a substance, so too there can be an injunction of a substance with reference to a deity through the aforementioned relationship, resulting in the injunction of the mere qualifier.
And although the application of the original substance might also be possible through extended application (atideśa),

nevertheless, because its prescription is accepted as occurring prior to that, there is no resulting violation of the principle of "single thrust" (ekaprasaratā). Furthermore, since the injunction is merely for the act of grinding and there is an absence of evidence for a distinct quality (guṇa) or other such factors, it does not constitute a separate ritual action (karmāntara).

By this, the view held by Prakāśa—that through the word *pūṣan* there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a rite having that deity as its object, and that for the sake of that [rite] there is an injunction of the act of grinding indicated by the term *prapiṣṭabhāga*—has been set aside.
This is because, according to the principle of the *niṣādasthapati* section, an injunction of a distinct rite (*karmāntaravidhi*) is more logical than an indication;
furthermore, such a view would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the rule to cases such as "the one who utters *vaṣaṭ* shall have the first draught."

In this regard, the method we have stated is impossible, because since the eating is already established by a direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*), it is untenable to accept that [the present rule] applies prior to that.
The ancient commentators maintain that all of this has already been proven and is merely being recalled here for the sake of what is to be said subsequently. // 3 // 47 //
Thus ends the thirteenth section concerning the fact that the grinding of the *pauṣṇa* [portion] is for the sake of a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

(B2) Regarding this, it has been stated that since the commentators and others previously established the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the terms *dīrghasoma* and *ahīna* from the context by overriding the general context (*prakaraṇa*), because those terms do not fit within the original ritual (*prakṛti*), the same logic applies to the term *pūṣan*. Since its displacement is likewise established due to its lack of fit within the context, there is no need to formulate a prior prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and a final conclusion (*siddhānta*) here; rather, the author of the Sūtras reminds us of this for the purpose of introducing what follows.

In this regard, since the meaning of the sentence would be untenable even if there were an excellence [of the deity] within the modification (*vikṛti*) by means of the arguments to be stated later, there can be no inclusion therein by subverting the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Rather, it is appropriate that the word *pūṣan* be included in the context in some way without contradicting it, even without resorting to a figurative sense (*gauṇī*); thus, with the intention that the commencement of the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) is indeed possible despite the difficulty of resolving the further objection, [the author proceeds].
He formulates the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) as follows: "Not, first of all... and so forth.

As for what was argued in the *Bhāṭṭadīnakara*— namely, that because there is an absence of a fourth-case ending or a taddhita suffix, the divinity (*devatātva*) is not presented [in the text], and thus it cannot be an injunction of a separate rite dedicated to that deity;

whereas in the case of an injunction of mere grinding (*peṣaṇa*), Pūṣan— who is already established as a deity— is merely restated (*anuvāda*), and thus his divinity is indeed presented, thereby establishing a disparity between the two cases— that is incorrect.

In the *Adhvarakalpanā*— because there would be the consequence that even the sacrifice enjoined by the rule "Sarasvatī shall have the *ājyabhāga*" would be prescribed as a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*), and likewise because that same consequence would not arise in the case of the rule "There are two [offerings] for Sarasvatī"—

if, however, it were argued that the status of being a deity is established somehow through its mention as a deity in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and through the employment of the word "portion" (*bhāga*).

Thus, here too, it is exactly the same because that [connection] is established by the supplementary statement regarding the absence of teeth (*adantakatva*), and because the word "portion" (*bhāga*) is employed;
[this is so] "by way of the connection with having the sacrificial pap (*caru*) as its material.
The employment of the word "pap" (*caru*) was made to indicate the connection, as seen upon considering the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*).
"And it is possible" refers to the sentence concerning the *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice; this is the ellipsis.
"Even though" (*yadyapi*) [is used] as well.

The meaning is as follows: just as in the sentence "The priests proceed wearing red turbans," because the extension (atideśa) applies only to those priests already denoted by the term "red-turbaned," it is accepted that this occurs first;
thus, [the rule] has the result of enjoining the state of wearing a red turban as a qualification of the injunction. It is the same here.
[Otherwise], there would be the consequence of an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

The meaning is that even in the sentence concerning priority (*prāthamya*), by indicating priority through the compound word (*samasta-pada*) and enjoining it as a qualification for the act of eating already established by the name (*samākhyā*), there is no resulting establishment of a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).

Now, one might raise the following objection: "Just as in this case, before the application of the extended injunction (*atideśa*), the injunction regarding the ground-substance being ground is accepted as having the mere act of grinding as its result, so too in that other case, before the occasional consumption (*naimittika-bhakṣa*) is obtained for the sake of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer, there is an injunction of the consumption qualified by priority; thus, [the second case] would not constitute a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*). To dispel this doubt:
He demonstrates the distinction [between the two cases] with the words: "In that case, our... and so forth.
In that regard, concerning the sentence on primacy (*prāthamya-vākya*):
"the manner stated by us" means the manner which has been explained by us here.

And thus, since the consumption (*bhakṣa*) of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer—which occurs on every occasion—is already enjoined by the respective direct injunctions (*pratyakṣa-vidhi*), it is not proper to assume a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*) based on the operation of the sentence on primacy prior to that.
This is the meaning.
Since such an investigation of the subject matter is possible, he repeats what was stated by the ancients—as if to mock them—saying: "All this... and so forth.
By the two words "tad etat" (this very thing) and by the phrase "prāñcaḥ" (the ancients), derision is indicated.
Thus ends the thirteenth section concerning the fact that the grinding of the *pūṣan* [portion] is for the sake of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
— — — — — — — (B1) (Adhikaraṇa 14 / [A.3 Pā.3 Adhi.14]) "That [grinding] is for all purposes, because there is no distinction" (Jaimini 3.3.35).

Regarding the consideration of whether that grinding should apply to the sacrificial cake (*caru*) dedicated to the deity Pūṣan, as well as to the animal victim and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), or only to the *caru*— the conclusion is as follows:

Since there is no distinction [between the sacrificial cakes] and because of the force of the reason for being toothless, it follows that [the grinding] applies everywhere; however, this being the case— first, regarding the *puroḍāśa*, the injunction of grinding prior to cooking would be redundant since it is already established by necessity,
whereas after that, there would be the consequence of destroying the form denoted by the word *puroḍāśa*.
The same applies to the heart of the sacrificial animal and other parts, since these terms also denote meat characterized by specific shapes.
Furthermore, in neither case is there an injunction for grinding after the portions have been cut off.
For if grinding were enjoined as something never previously obtained, it would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*);

however, there is simplicity (*lāghava*) if it is merely a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the grinding that was applicable by extension from the *caru* but was set aside due to a lack of purpose.

Indeed, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), since the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) to be offered cannot otherwise be accomplished, grinding—though already implied by the requirements—is endowed with its specific ritual properties (*sadharmaka*) for the sake of achieving purposes such as having the Adhvaryu priest as the performer.

It has been established that since the accomplishment of what is to be offered occurs even without that [grinding] in the case of the *caru*, grinding is not the cause with respect to that which is delimited as a *caru*; therefore, it is restated as it is being withdrawn.

For this very reason, a "reinstatement" (*pratiprasava*) is an injunction [that applies] when there is the possibility of withdrawal by some other cause of that which had been obtained through general application (*prasakta-prāpti*).

In that case, there is simplicity because the operation of the injunction (*vidhi*)—such as its connection with the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*), the applicatory injunction (*viniyoga-vidhi*), and the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*)—is absent as far as possible.

For this very reason, although a different transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭa-prayojana*) must be postulated here for grinding (*peṣaṇa*) due to the loss of its original purpose—which was the preparation of the material to be offered (*pradeya*)—there is no obstruction to its being a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).

However, since the grinding is not a separate rite (*karmāntara*), the properties (*dharma*) of the original grinding, which are obtained here by virtue of being subsidiaries to the original grinding according to the maxim "when the principal is carried away, it carries its subsidiaries along," must have their effects postulated here as another transcendental result (*adṛṣṭa-rūpa-kāryāntara*).
This is not a fault.

Furthermore, this point is accepted: when the fire-preparation rites such as churning—which are recited in the section on animal sacrifices—are applied as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices by virtue of a scriptural injunction, one may assume that their specific properties are employed for a different purpose;
however, in this actual case of grinding (*peṣaṇa*), there is no assumption of a different purpose whatsoever.
Precisely because [the grinding] is for the sake of accomplishing the object to be offered (*pradeya*).
For although grinding is not a cause with respect to that which is delimited by being a *caru* (cooked rice offering),
nevertheless, since the word *caru* is applied even to a *caru* made of flour, and by the force of the injunction for grinding in the passage "the *caru* for Pūṣan," [grinding is understood].

Although the word *caru* denotes a general category, it is determined here to refer specifically to a *caru* made of ground flour; since that substance to be offered cannot be accomplished without grinding, there is no need to postulate a different purpose for the grinding.
For this very reason, "being a *caru*" (*carutva*) consists in being composed of rice grains cooked internally by steam such that they have not been strained out.
In this context, the term "not leaked" (*anavastrāvita*) is used to exclude cooked rice mixed with sauce;
"inside" (*antar*) is used to exclude *maṇḍaka* cakes;
and "rice" (*taṇḍula*) is used to exclude soup, vegetables, and the like.

For this very reason, since that [result] is possible even in the case of a flour-filled vessel, grinding does not constitute an obstacle; therefore, the grinding takes place right there. // 3.4.48 //
Thus ends the fourteenth section concerning the placement of the grinding of the *pauṣṇa* [portion] specifically within the *caru*.

(B2) Since there is no established conclusion that grinding (*peṣaṇa*) applies only when there is a single deity, even sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and animal sacrifices (*paśu*) dedicated to two deities serve as examples here.

Thus, although sacrifices involving a sacrificial cake or an animal dedicated solely to Pūṣan are not well-known, [the rule applies] to the animal, the *caru*, and the sacrificial cake prescribed by such sentences as: "One should sacrifice a three-year-old goat to Soma and Pūṣan," "The sacrificial cake for Soma and Pūṣan consists of eleven potsherds," and "The *caru* is for Indra and Pūṣan."

The intention is that the deliberation as to whether grinding (peṣaṇa) occurs or not is indeed possible; or else— [considering] the cake (caru) and the animal (paśu) dedicated to Pūṣan, which are prescribed by the sentences "one should subsequently offer a cake to Pūṣan" and "one desiring food should sacrifice a dark-colored animal to Pūṣan," both having Pūṣan as their sole deity, and likewise [the cake] by the rule "having sacrificed the animal, one offers the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)" as being an auxiliary to the animal sacrifice whose deity is Pūṣan alone...

Intending to show that since the prescribed *puroḍāśa* cake is dedicated to the deity Pūṣan as part of the principal sacrifice, it is possible for there to be a *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Pūṣan alone, he begins the inquiry with the words "that grinding" (*tatpeṣaṇam*). [He states] "because of the consequence of prolixity" (*gauravāpatter iti*).

In the fifth [section], by means of the passage ending with "the offering of the portions" (*avadāna*), it is stated that these constitute a single ritual act (*ekapadārtha*) for the sake of accomplishing them in immediate succession; therefore, this [point] should also be understood as an illustration of the fact that if the grinding (*peṣaṇa*) were performed after the offering of the portions, the unity of the ritual act would be destroyed due to the intervention (*vyavadhāna*). He establishes this very point of parsimony (*lāghava*) with the words: "For in the archetype... (*prakṛtau hi*).

Furthermore, since the word *caru* is used even for a vessel of flour-cake, one might raise the objection that grinding—which is required only when that [flour-cake] is taken as the offering for the sacrifice dedicated to Pūṣan—is not excluded;

thus, it would follow that grinding must be prescribed as something not otherwise established (*aprāpta*) in order to accomplish that [offering]. To refute this doubt, [the author notes] that because the word *caru* is also used for boiled rice (*odana*) even without flour, its inclusion [in the sacrifice] is established, and therefore grinding [is not required].

Since there is indeed a cessation [of the action] due to the absence of a purpose, he demonstrates that grinding lacks causality with respect to that which is delimited by the state of being "caru" (the sacrificial rice), by means of the phrase "in its absence."

In order to indicate that the definition of *pratiprasava* (reinstatement) formulated by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* and others in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) is incorrect, he himself demonstrates the true nature of *pratiprasava*: "Of that which has been reached through [prior] application"—this is the formulation of its definition, and its refutation has already been stated.
Because of the absence of activity.
The meaning is that there is lightness because of the operation [of the mind] merely toward the act of re-creation.

Regarding this, there are two views. Among them, first, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* [states]: "The nature of *caru*—defined as being cooked rice (*odana*) characterized by the qualities of not having been strained out (*avastrāvita*), not having been strained out (*anavastrāvita*), being continuous (*anuvṛtta*), and being mutually unattached (*anyonyāsaṃlagna*)—is based on the quality of clarity (*vaiśadya*). However, in the case of *caru* prepared from flour (*piṣṭa*), the nature of being rice does not depend on clarity; rather, it depends solely on the fact that it has been cooked internally by steam (*antarūṣmapakvatva*) without being strained out. Thus, in the case of *caru*, the nature of being rice does not require clarity."

If it is asked: "How then, given that *caru* is not boiled rice (*odana*), can the word *caru* be said to denote boiled rice in the Siddhānta-sūtra of the tenth Adhikaraṇa, which states: ‘Or rather, it is boiled rice, because it is so employed’? The answer is: No. This is because, although the intention of the sūtra is to refute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the word *caru* denotes merely a cooking vessel—since the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), “Aditi with boiled rice,” indicates that the word *odana* (boiled rice) serves to specify a particular type of *caru* known as *vaiśadya*—nevertheless, the word *caru* denotes merely the state of being cooked internally by steam without being drained [of its liquid].

Furthermore, since even soup, vegetables, and the like would result in being classified as *caru*, and in order to exclude them, although the word "rice" (*odana*) may serve to indicate something distinct from soup and such,
there is no evidence that the word *caru* specifically denotes rice; moreover, the term *caru* is not applied to rice that has not been drained of its liquid.
Therefore, the status of being *caru* is established only for that which lacks clarity (*vaiśadya*);
likewise, the establishment of the status of *caru* is also achieved for a *taṇḍula-caru* (rice-porridge) only when it lacks clarity.
In some cases, the use of the word "food" (*odana*) for flour—as in "flour-food" (*piṣṭaka-odana*)—is merely figurative.

Pārthasārathi, however, in the tenth [book], in the section concerning the *trivṛt* and *caru* (Tarkapāda 10.2.63–69), establishes that the word *caru* denotes boiled rice (*odana*) alone; this is because of the etymological derivation from "that which is cooked by internal heat" (*anavasrāvitāntarūṣmapakva*) and because of the usage of the word *caru* by ritualists (*yājñika*) for such rice. For this very reason, since clarity (*vaiśadya*) is possible even in a *caru* made of flour, it is only when that [flour-based caru] possesses the form of boiled rice that clarity is present in it.

Since the application of the word *caru* is accepted as being primary [in its denotation], there is no difference in the performance of the rite whether one accepts it as denoting cooked rice (*odana*) or not; therefore, without showing any insistence on that point, he establishes that the grinding (*peṣaṇa*) is for the purpose of securing the substance to be offered (*pradeya*), by demonstrating the mere application of the word *caru* to a *caru* made of flour—
this is expressed in the words "In reality, however" (*vastutas tu*).

Even when the term *caru* is understood as referring to a flour-oblation (*piṣṭaka-caru*), since there is no contradiction with the meaning of the sentence "the *caru* for Pūṣan," it is appropriate to determine a specific meaning for the word *caru*, even though it is generally applicable, in order to ensure that the injunction for grinding serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Thus, the grinding is intended solely for the preparation of the flour *caru* to be offered;
the meaning is that one should not postulate any other effect of an invisible nature (*adṛṣṭa-rūpa*).

In this regard, the following should be noted: if, here, by the force of the injunction for grinding (*peṣaṇa*), the word *caru*, which denotes a general sense, were to be restricted to the specific meaning of a ground *caru*, then it would not be appropriate to laboriously accept its status as an injunction for grinding.

For, just as the statement “*nivītam manuṣyāṇām*” serves as a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the sentence concerning the *upavīta* in the Taittirīya recension, so too can it function here as a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*)—as in the case of “*aditim odanena”*—by being a supplementary part to the injunction regarding the taking of the *prāśitra* portion.

There is no rule that only that which is recited in close proximity can be an indicator (jñāpaka); for, in the absence of any contrary evidence, it is logical that something situated in another location—provided it is of such a nature—can also function as an indicator.
For this very reason, it is logical that even that which constitutes a supplementary portion (vākyaśeṣa) of the *ātithya* rite can serve as an indicator.

Indeed, it is accepted that the explanatory passage (arthavāda) located in another section— namely, “for there is no offering of after-sacrifices (anūyāja) here”— serves as an indicator for the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of two sets of four [libations] by means of the word ‘eight’ occurring in the sentence, “He takes eight [portions] in the upabhṛt ladle. And thus,

since the grinding of flour in the case of the flour-oblation (piṣṭakacarau) is already established through extension (atideśa) by way of ensuring the accomplishment of the substance to be offered— in accordance with the use of the word ‘caru’ here— it would be entirely purposeless to resort to its being an injunction.

Indeed, when it is possible for there to be a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*), it is not proper to accept a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and treat [the passage] as an injunction (*vidhi*) for the purpose of excluding grinding in the case of an offering to two deities (*dvidevatya*);
for since being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*) is more appropriate than breaking the syntactical unity, there is no purpose served by that [grinding] in the case of an offering to two deities.
Furthermore, as stated by Pārthasārathi: "Since even in a vessel of ground flour (*piṣṭaka-caru*) a clear cooking (*viśadapāka*) is possible, the word *caru* denotes cooked rice (*odana*)."
That is not so; for when flour is thrown into a pot filled with water and cooked, clarity (vaiśadya) is impossible.

Indeed, when the flour has been turned into a mass by the water, the perception of the counter-correlate and the correlate of mutual exclusion does not arise, whereby it could attain clarity in the form of being unjoined with one another.

Therefore, in the case of cooked rice (*odana*), because the grains of rice themselves exist separately from one another, their lack of mutual contact is clearly perceived. This is evident from the traditional practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*): when preparing a pot of rice that has not yet been drained, they add a copious amount of water to ensure the removal of stickiness, whereas for rice that has already become such [cooked], they add only a sufficient measure of water; this is done precisely to avoid the state of being mutually adhered.

If the designation "caru" were applied merely by virtue of being cooked internally by steam without being drained [of liquid], then since clarity (vaiśadya) would not be required, the status of being "odana" (boiled rice) would not be contingent upon clarity; consequently, the usage of the term by ritualists (*yājñika*) would apply to that very case [of *caru*].

Since this is observed in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vārttika*, and the *Nyāyasudhā* on that point, the ritualists' own attempt to justify their usage regarding *odana* that is cooked internally by steam without being drained is also untenable.

As for what has been stated here by the authors of the *Prakāśa*: "Just as in the case of flour (*piṣṭaka*), when it is rice (*odana*), its status as denoting a 'pot'—which would otherwise follow from common usage—is set aside by its being denoted by the word *udāna* [as established] in the Arthavāda;

likewise, since the flour-oblation (*piṣṭaka-caru*) is prepared by that very same process, its status as denoting both rice and flour, which is based on common usage, would also be set aside. Furthermore, according to the view of Miśra, once the capacity [of the word *caru*] is grasped in respect to rice in general, there is no contradiction; therefore, its denotation of a specific kind of rice—one that is not drained and cooked by internal heat—is justified by the usage of sacrificial experts (*yājñika*)."
For it was stated in the *Ktādhikaraṇa* that when there is a perception of a general [term], that which presents a required specific [meaning] is indeed favorable and not contradictory.

However, for you, because of the superior authority of the *arthavāda* even over Vedic usage—as in common worldly usage—it would be improper to claim that [the term] denotes *odana* (boiled rice) and flour, as that would contradict [the *arthavāda*].
This is contrary to the *Śāstradīpikā* regarding the tenth book (*dāśamika*) of the *Adhikaraṇas*.

For in that context, since the ritual manual (*yājñika-prayoga*) speaks of rice cooked with internal heat that has not been allowed to leak out, and because the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) occurs there—

following the hearing of the word *caru* in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) prior to the injunction— it is understood that the purpose of the *arthavāda* is precisely to exclude the sense of "mere pot" by strengthening that [primary meaning]. Thus, in accordance with the word *caru* established at the beginning of the section, one should assume that the general term refers specifically to that particular [type of cooking], so as not to contradict the *arthavāda*.

Since there is no evidence for the word *caru* having its own inherent power (*śakti*) to denote [the oblation], it is inconsistent to postulate that its meaning is determined by the usage of ritualists (*yājñika*)— who require a specific referent— for the word generally denoting boiled rice (*odana*), based on the force of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). For this very reason, in that particular section (*adhikaraṇa*), the mixed authors stated that the usage of ritualists extends as far as boiled rice, treating it as being on the same level as the explanatory passage.

However, even in the view of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, who holds that the word *caru* has its primary denotation (*śakti*) ending with cooked rice (*odana*), there is no presentation of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) as a means of grasping the word's power to denote rice— by way of refuting the view that *caru* denotes a cooking pot (*sthālī*) in the section concerning the *trivṛt-caru* and the horse-hair (*aśvavāla*)—
because the determination of the meaning of the word *caru* is already established through the well-known usage of ritualists (*yājñika-prasiddhi*), and thus [the arthavāda] would serve no purpose.

For this very reason, in the tenth book of the *Śāstradīpikā*, the fact that the term refers to a cooking pot (*sthālī*) is refuted on the grounds that the practice of a more trustworthy sacrificer (*yājñika*) possesses greater authority than the common usage of the term for a cooking pot.

Nor is it correct to argue that—because there is no absence of denoting "rice up to its limit" (the entire meal), because it would contradict the *arthavāda*, and because it would be simpler to take it as denoting the "pot"—the usage by ritual experts (*yājñika*) would also be sublated; for there is no contradiction. Just as in your own view there is no contradiction because [the word] depends on the general [category], so too here, by intending a similarity to rice and for the purpose of excluding items such as unrefined gruel, soup, and vegetables which might otherwise be included, no contradiction is possible. Otherwise, since there is no distinction in usage, one would have to choose between the pot well-known in common worldly usage and that well-known among ritual experts.

If [the term *grahaṇa*] were intended merely for the purpose of removing doubt, it would follow that its meaning is already established by the rule "in cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] by the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) and so forth.

Consequently, since the word *caru*, whose meaning is already determined, is here determined by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it would not fall under the scope of the principle concerning doubtful matters; this would contradict the statement in the *Śāstradīpikā* regarding the section on the *trivṛt-caru* and *aśvabāla*. Therefore, since the meaning must be stated as being determined solely by the technical usage of the sacrificial experts (*yājñika-prasiddhi*) in order to override common worldly usage, the reliance upon the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not for the sake of grasping the primary denotative power (*śakti*), but rather for the sake of attaining clarity.

Furthermore, in this view, since the word *caru* is accepted as denoting that [offering] even when it is prepared from flour—just like boiled rice cooked over heat—the lack of contradiction is established by postulating that the intended meaning is *caru* in the form of boiled rice (*odana*). This is done to prevent the consequence of accepting both meanings [flour-preparation and boiled rice] simultaneously under the term *caru*, which would undermine its status as a synonym for the cooking vessel (*sthālī*) based on the common usage of ritualists (*yājñika*). In reality, however, once the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *caru* is determined to reside in the cooking vessel, the word *odana* appearing in the concluding portion must be interpreted in accordance with the determination made in the opening portion.

Since the praise is also possible through the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being the means for preparing the rice-porridge (*odana*), it is not possible to subvert its denotative power on the basis of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); thus, the cessation of its being a word for "cauldron" (*sthālī*) is indeed difficult to establish.

Furthermore, has it been determined prior to the understanding from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that the word *caru* denotes a specific kind of rice that has not been strained, by setting aside its denotation as a cooking vessel?

If the first case is true, then because the determination of the meaning of the general term in the explanatory passage is achieved by that very [prior] determination, it would be difficult to justify the claim in that particular section (*adhikaraṇa*) that the determination of the word *caru* is made by the explanatory passage itself.

If the second case is true, then even if the requirement for a specification is satisfied by a determined qualifier, it cannot be satisfied by one that is undetermined; thus, it is improper to argue that there is no contradiction because the word *caru* serves to provide the specific detail based on the established usage of ritualists (*yājñika*).

Since it is untenable for [the usage] to be a restrictive factor merely by virtue of being well-known among ritualists (*yājñika*) without its capacity to denote meaning or its capacity to convey the intended sense (*tātparya*),

just as the usage of Mlecchas is sublated by the usage of Āryas, so too the common usage of Āryas is sublated by the more trustworthy usage of Āryas who possess a greater familiarity with the performance of rituals, due to the equality of the underlying logic.

Thus, because the common meaning is established in this way, once it has been determined at the outset— by refuting the sense of "contained in a pot"— that [the term *caru*] denotes only that which is cooked by internal heat without being drained, then, in accordance with that, it is appropriate for the word *odana* (cooked rice) occurring in the concluding portion to employ a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on similarity; therefore,
it is logical that the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) refers specifically to that which is composed of clearly distinct grains of rice.
However, even by this much, [the word *caru*] does not possess the capacity to denote the aspect of being made from rice-grains characterized by clarity (*vaiśadya*);

for if that were the case, it would follow that in *caru* offerings made of mung beans, barley, and so forth, the word *caru* would have to be used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*) in its infinite instances,
since the status of being "rice-grain" (*taṇḍulatva*) is accepted— based on common worldly usage and the scriptures— only for grains whose material source is *vrīhi* rice.
For this very reason, the author of the Vārttika stated that the ground for the application of the word [‘odana’] is simply that which is cooked by internal heat without being strained [of water].

By this, the inclusion of the qualification ‘having rice as its material cause’ (*taṇḍulaprakṛtikatva*)—which is written in all the commentaries for the purpose of excluding soup, vegetables, and the like—is refuted; for even if over-extension (*ativyāpti*) were avoided, under-extension (*avyāpti*) would result in the case of dishes made from mung beans and so forth.
Furthermore, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to round, hard objects made of rice-grains that are well-known in the world as "fruits" (*phala*).

Therefore, since it must be stated that the exclusion of those [objects] is achieved by accepting the term as an *upalakṣaṇa* (indirect indicator) for "being distinct from soups, vegetables, and the like," it is logical that the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) serves to indicate that very indication.

Moreover, in the *Nyāyasudhā* commentary, when demonstrating the purposefulness of the two words "not having leaked internal heat" (*anavastrāvitāntarūṣma*), the word "made of rice-grains" (*taṇḍulaprakṛtika*) was not employed; thus, the explanatory passage has the status of being for the sake of indicating the distinction from soups, vegetables, and so forth.

Since it has been established that [the passage] conveys the intended meaning of what I have stated, it is correct as stated in the *Nyāyasudhā* that an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) does not possess the capacity to convey word-meanings (*śaktigrāhakatva*). However,
even in both systems, the exclusion of flour-based sacrificial oblations (*caru*) such as those for Sarasvatī and others from the *Prāyaṇīya* rite remains difficult to justify.
Therefore, this must be resolved in a way that does not contradict any of the texts:
the word *caru* applied to a flour-offering (*piṣṭakacarū*) is purely figurative and not primary.

For this very reason, when the performance of a *caru* is required in Vedic (*śrauta*) or Smārta rites, only flour is used as its constituent by those who are qualified; thus, according to the maxim of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*), it is not accepted [as the primary substance] in all such cases.

Since the offering is accomplished even without grinding in the case of the *pauṣṇa-caru*, the prescription for grinding is established as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*); thus, by accepting the secondary sense [of the word], it results in a *piṣṭaka-caru* (a cooked offering of flour), and everything is consistent—so enough with this laborious effort. Precisely because the term *caru* is applied even to a flour-offering, he states that this is the ground for the application of the term *caru* without regard for clarity: "Therefore, what is called 'caru-ness'... [is as follows].
The rest is clear.
Thus ends the fourteenth section concerning the placement of the grinding of the *pauṣṇa* [portion] specifically within the *caru*.
— — — — — — (B1) (15th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.3 Pā.3 Adhi.15) "On account of the connection with one [deity] in a single [instance]. Jaimini 3.3.39:
Where Pūṣan is the deity accompanied by another;

Just as in the case of the Rājasūya sacrifice, regarding the statement "the caru offering for Indra and Pūṣan," when there arises the deliberation as to whether the grinding applies there as well, or only where Pūṣan is the sole deity— [the conclusion is reached] that,

in accordance with the explanatory passage (arthavāda) stating "for he is toothless," it is understood that the grinding is prompted by the very nature of Pūṣan; therefore, [it applies] to his specific form.
Furthermore, even in other literary sources, grinding is indeed appropriate because of its existence [in the archetype].
For this very reason, the reference to being ground half-way—expressed by the word *nema* in the injunction, "One desiring cattle should offer a *caru* to Soma-Pūṣan, half-ground"—is also consistent.

However, if it were suspected that, according to the principle of the first section of the ninth book (*navamādhyāya*), since there would be pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) regarding the essential nature of Pūṣan himself, it is necessary to resort to an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*), [then the following applies].

In that case, let it be so; for there exists, by the method previously stated, an inference of the sacrifice produced by the knowledge of the connection with *pūṣan* as ground for grinding, which serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). That [inference] also resides in the word *pūṣan*. However, in accordance with the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and other factors, one must accept a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) consisting in "the state of being for the sake of the transcendental result (*apūrva*) prompted by the divinityhood based on *pūṣan* as the substratum. Consequently, even in a sacrifice dedicated to two deities (*dvidevatya*), the ritual duty of grinding is possible.
And since this is the case, one should strive to achieve the successful completion of the cooking either by preventing obstacles or by means of gradual placement [of the grain].

Having reached the conclusion that [the division] is either by way of the vessel or by way of the [deity], it is necessary to resort to an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—namely, being a means to the *apūrva* (transcendental result)—in order to avoid meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*). Furthermore, the assumption that [the division] is mediated by the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is untenable without the presentation of Pūṣan as the deity.

Once that [deity] is presented, the avoidance of meaninglessness is achieved simply by assuming mediation through that [deity]. And in the case of a dual-deity [sacrifice], this follows the principle of the section concerning the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇādhikaraṇanyāya*).

Since Pūṣan alone lacks the status of being a deity [in other contexts], the act of grinding occurs only where Pūṣan is indeed alone. Nor is it the case that—even if the deityhood that serves as the means for the *apūrva* (unprecedented result) is indicated by the word "Pūṣan" as a qualifier—the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) is intended as the mode of connection when that [deityhood] appears in relation to Pūṣan; for in that case, pervasion (*paryāpti*) is not intended.

Furthermore, one might ask: "Why is there no grinding (*peṣaṇa*) and so forth even in the case of a single deity for whom two deities are intended, since it is possible for Pūṣan also to possess the nature of being the object of reference (*uddeśya*)? This should not be said;

for when the qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) is pervaded by a property that subsists distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), it is impossible for a relation that subsists in only one [of the two] to serve as the relational content (*saṃsarga*).
Otherwise, there would result the absurdity of verbal cognitions such as "one possesses two-ness" or "one is two," just as one might say "one possesses the inherence of two-ness."

Therefore, since the deityhood that exists distributively (vyāsajyavṛtti) is a qualifier only through the relation of pervasion (paryāpti), and since that [distributive deityhood] is sublated in the case of Pūṣan alone, the grinding and so forth apply only there [in the case of joint deities], because deityhood residing solely in Pūṣan is the qualifier.
Furthermore, the state of being toothless is not contradictory, as it is merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda).

Furthermore, since even the state of not being ground is accepted as the object of injunction in that very same context, there is no lack of intelligibility because the injunction of a qualified efficient force (bhāvanā) does not result in a syntactical split (vākyabheda). // 3.49 //
Thus ends the fifteenth section concerning the fact that the grinding of the *pauṣṇa* [portion] is for a single deity.
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* composed by the venerable Khaṇḍadeva.

(B2) Regarding this, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* states: "In order to avoid meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), when the grinding (*peṣaṇa*) is prompted by the *apūrva* (transcendental result), there arises a requirement for a means (*dvāra*). Through the *bahuvrīhi* compound, Pūṣan himself, being the primary element, serves as that means; and he is qualified by his 'portion' (*bhāga*). Furthermore, according to the etymology ‘that which is divided (*bhajyate*)’ or ‘that which is served (*sevyate*)’, the portion is that which is to be served."

Furthermore, since a deity lacks the status of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), such [ownership] is impossible; thus, if [the term *puṣṇe*] were taken in its secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to [the sacrificer] himself, then according to the maxim "when something is offered with reference to two [entities], it belongs equally to both," ownership over half [of the offering] would be impossible for Pūṣan, just as in common worldly practice. Consequently, just like the status of being an enjoyer, the status of being able to dispose of [the object] at will (*yatheṣṭaviniyojyatva*) is also impossible for him. This is because, just as for one whose father is living, there exists a restriction against disposing of paternal wealth at will toward another person, so too [is there a restriction here].

It was stated that the door referred to by the word "portion" (*bhāga*)—namely, ownership as expressed in the Smṛti: "He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of Brāhmaṇas"—is applicable even when [the deity] is not previously engaged [by a sacrifice], thus supporting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there should be grinding in a rite for two deities.

However, this is untenable because, in the ninth book, once the corporeal form of the deity has been refuted, there is an absence of both being an enjoyer and being subject to disposal at will; likewise, there is an absence of any obstruction to its being disposed of for another's sake. Thus...
Having set aside what has been established by the author of the *Prakāśa*, [it is argued as follows]:
although, even when [the compound] is analyzed as an *apūrva*-based formation (*apūrvaprayuktatve*), Pūṣan alone—being the primary member—is the verbal door (*dvāra*) due to the *bahuvrīhi* compound;

nevertheless, because Pūṣan himself cannot directly undergo grinding (*peṣaṇa*), and because [the injunction] would otherwise be purposeless (*ānarthakya*), the word "portion" (*bhāga*) indicates, through a reversal of the qualifier and the qualified, that the sacrificial offering (*havis*) which is the means of the sacrifice is indeed the door.
It is not a deity; for even if it were the door [to the sacrifice], the sacrificial offering (havis) must necessarily be the door.
Pūṣan, however, is merely an indicator of the offering;

in that regard, since there is no possessive suffix (taddhita) or compound (samāsa)—such as those found in "āgneya" or "aindrapīta"—which would indicate Pūṣan's independence [from the offering], he cannot function as a qualifier by means of excluding connection with anything else.
However, since this is merely by way of excluding what is non-yoga, this very [definition] exists even in the case of a rite dedicated to two deities.
To refute this, he says: "That too [is included] in the word 'pūṣan'."

When, by means of a sentence, there is an injunction of something in relation to a specific objective (*uddeśya*), and when the contingency arises that such an injunction would be purposeless (*ānarthakya*) regarding the connection with that objective as presented through the word’s own expressive power (*śabdaśakti*), then—by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the status of being a means to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result)—within the very word denoting that [objective], the objective is enjoined in that form toward the thing to be enjoined; thus, that [action] alone becomes the medium (*dvāra*) toward that *apūrva*. As in: "One threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn avahanti*).
In such prescriptive sentences (*saṃskāra-vākya*) as these, this [interpretation] is both established and logical;

for once the connection of threshing and the like with the *apūrva* is understood through the context itself, the specific [grain] mentioned in the sentences on threshing and so forth—such as the word *vrīhi* (rice)—is merely provided as a means.

Thus, here, because the sacrifice is indicated by the word "portion" (*bhāga*) precisely through its connection with Pūṣan, the *apūrva*, although presented by that [word], is not the direct object of the injunction.
Because there is no word expressive of that [deity],
the word "portion" (bhāga) thus serves as the means for the sacrificial oblation (havis) which accomplishes the sacrifice;
in its absence, that [deity] itself would be the object of reference (uddeśya) according to the literal expression.
And that is not possible,
because it would result in the violation of the principle of single thrust (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*);

for even if Pūṣan were a qualifier merely by way of excluding what is non-conjoined (*ayogavyāvṛtti*), it would lead to the same reason [for invalidity] as in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*)— namely, the consequence of a qualified object of reference (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*).

Since you and others have established in the *Bālaprakāśa* that the injunction is made solely with the deity Pūṣan as the objective by means of a traditional connection (*paramparā-sambandha*), and since the present investigation proceeds precisely on the basis of that [establishment], it is untenable for the oblation (*havis*) to be the intended object here. Thus, the avoidance of meaninglessness occurs through the word "Pūṣan" itself—which serves to designate the intended object—by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva-sādhanatva*), and specifically by way of the deity; therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not proven.

As for the critique by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*—that because the corporeal form of a deity has been refuted, there is no lack of restriction regarding the deity’s being employed at will by another, and thus Pūṣan cannot serve as a "door" (mediator) when qualified by such ownership—that too is to be disregarded, because even for one who maintains that the deity is a word (*śabda-devatā*) and does not accept a corporeal form, they must still accept a specific relationship that generates the conventional usage of terms like "the god's property. Since one must necessarily postulate whatever specific relationship makes that usage possible, it is precisely Pūṣan as qualified by that very relationship who serves as the door; such is the intended meaning [of our position].

For this very reason, as stated by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, since ownership—defined as the power to employ another according to one's will—is of no use toward the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), it cannot function as a "door" [to that result]. Consequently, accepting that the term *pūṣan* itself indicates the status of being a means to the *apūrva*, he establishes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in a different manner, stating: "But on the other hand... (*paraṃ tu*).
The rest is clear.

And here, the purpose [of the discussion]—namely, that the rule regarding grinding applies even in the case of an offering to two deities—was stated by the Bhāṣyakāra during the very presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is quite clear that this is not the case because there is no authoritative means of proof (*pramāṇa*) to establish it.

In that regard, the author of the Vārttika has stated in the *pūrvapakṣa* that even the favoring of the non-primary [deity] is permissible according to the maxim of "eating from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyabhojinnyāya*); but here, however...

Regarding what was stated by the venerable teacher— that because Pūṣan is included on account of his equality with Indra, it is indeed possible to perform the grinding of everything, and this indicates another purpose as well— the intended meaning is as follows: since, when the grinding of everything is performed out of regard for Pūṣan, the term *caru* can still be applied even to a ground *caru*, the non-contradiction between the deity Indra and the sacrificial material is established according to the maxim of "eating from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyabhojinyāya*).
There is the grinding of everything.

Furthermore, even if the word *caru* were conventionally restricted to boiled rice that has not been strained, then by performing the grinding out of deference to Pūṣan, there would result the destruction of Indra’s own substance in the form of the boiled rice; in that case, whose benefit would there be?

Thus, in this state of doubt, because the primary element has not yet encountered any contradiction, just as in the *adhvarakalpā* sacrifice there is an adherence to the properties of the primary *āgnāvaiṣṇava* offering, so too here, due to the necessity of adhering to the properties of the *aindra* (Indra-related) oblation, total grinding of the grain does not apply; therefore, since there is no contradiction only in the case of taking ground flour for the *caru* offering, [that is what should be done].

If the application of the "rule of the one who eats from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyabhojinī-nyāya*) were established, then just as in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) total grinding would indeed be possible; thus, no difference in purpose between the prima facie and final views could be established.

Therefore, although a contradiction might arise under the alternative of taking rice-grains for the *caru* offering, since that can be resolved by partial grinding (*ardhapeṣaṇa*), there should not be a destruction of the deity Indra's material [by total grinding]. Consequently, the distinct purpose of the prima facie view is established as being precisely this: that grinding should be only partial.
For where there is a total contradiction of the secondary sense, there the primary sense alone is to be accepted.

In the case of the *adhvara-kalpa*, since the ritual meaning of the scripture consists solely in the single act of touching the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) intended for Sarasvatī—which is situated in the middle of the clarified butter (*ājya*) materials—the purpose is accomplished even by the *vṛdhanvatī* mantra; thus, there is no sublation (*bādha*) of that [mantra]. However, in this present case, if one were to favor the primary [deity] Indra, it would follow that the grinding of the offering for Pūṣan would be entirely sublated. Therefore, partial grinding (*ardhapeṣaṇa*) is appropriate. This very point must be accepted as the purpose, established through the application of the "Kāṃsyabhojin-nyāya" (the maxim of the one who eats from a bronze vessel).
Therefore, it is precisely for this purpose that the motive is stated here.
Thus ends the fifteenth section concerning the fact that the grinding of the *pauṣṇa* offering pertains to a single deity.

Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Prabhāvalī*, a commentary on the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*, composed by Śambhubhaṭṭa, disciple of Khaṇḍadeva— the ornament of the circle of poets and the foremost leader who has crossed the ocean of the glorious Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsās.
Here ends the section [concluding with] "navītāntam."
